talks.title: Attacking SCCM with SCCMHunter | Garrett Foster
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Attacking SCCM with SCCMHunter | Garrett Foster.
talks.summary:
Overview: Garrett Foster of SpecterOps presents at Wild West Hackin' Fest on attacking Microsoft SCCM using the SCCMHunter toolset.

Key Topics: SCCM architecture and excessive enterprise trust in endpoint management; community research on SCCM attack paths; distribution point discovery via WDS service connection points; and BloodHound graph integration.

Technical Details: Foster demonstrates identifying SCCM distribution points by querying Active Directory for WDS service connection point child objects. SCCMHunter automates enumeration and exploitation of SCCM misconfigurations.

Takeaways: Endpoint management platforms like SCCM represent high-trust infrastructure that attackers actively target. Red and blue teams should assess SCCM configurations and monitor for unauthorized queries.

talks.title: Announcements & Evolving ROADtools for Entra ID Recon & Tokens | Dirk-jan Mollema
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Announcements & Evolving ROADtools for Entra ID Recon & Tokens | Dirk-jan Mollema.
talks.summary:
ROADtools Overview

Dirk-jan Mollema presents ROADtools for Microsoft Entra ID enumeration and token operations. Released in 2020, the open-source toolkit centers on ROADlib authentication flows, ROADrecon for tenant reconnaissance, and ROADtx for token exchange.

Red and Blue Team Utility

ROADrecon runs from low-privilege accounts to enumerate tenant data useful for both red-team mapping and blue-team analysis when the Azure portal hides relationships. ROADtx handles refresh tokens, access tokens, cookies, and memory-extracted credentials.

Azure AD Graph Deprecation

The tool relies on graph.windows.net's Azure AD Graph API, including an internal version exposing conditional access policies without privileged roles. Microsoft is deprecating this API in favor of the more restricted Microsoft Graph, which limits visibility into internal Entra properties.

Privilege Analysis Demo

Mollema previews detecting hidden global-admin privileges through user "Bob," demonstrating how ROADrecon analysis surfaces authorization paths not obvious in standard portal views.

talks.title: Breaking Entra: Identity Attacks You Can Recreate | Jonathan Elkabas
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Breaking Entra: Identity Attacks You Can Recreate | Jonathan Elkabas.
talks.summary:
Identity Is Not the Whole Perimeter

Jonathan Elkabas argues “identity is the new perimeter” understates the problem: buying credentials bypasses technical controls, and non-human identities dominate modern tenants. Microsoft reports far more workload identities than human users, many over-permissioned.

Entra Identity Sprawl

He breaks down service principals behind enterprise apps, system- and user-assigned managed identities for Azure resources, and newer agent identities tied to Copilot and AI services—calling the overlapping terminology organized confusion attackers exploit.

Midnight Blizzard Case Study

The talk revisits APT29’s Microsoft breach starting from password spray against a legacy test tenant and escalating to executive email access, illustrating how minor misconfigurations chain into tenant compromise.

Entra Goat Lab

Elkabas introduces Entra Goat, a deliberately vulnerable Entra ID environment for safely practicing attack paths end to end. The session demos misconfiguration chains attackers use in the wild and encourages hands-on recreation in isolated labs.

talks.title: MQL for Email APT Hunting | Bryan Campbell
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in MQL for Email APT Hunting | Bryan Campbell.
talks.summary:
Platform overview

Brian Campbell of Sublime explains MQL (Message Query Language) for email threat hunting, supported by Autonomous Security Analyst and Autonomous Detection Engineer components for adaptive defense.

MQL and enrichments

MQL expresses attacker TTPs with organizational context, NLU, computer vision, OCR, link rendering, WHOIS, ML scoring, and deep attachment analysis via File Explode/Strelka across nested archives, macros, HTML smuggling, and encrypted zips.

Risk scoring

Multiple weak signals are weighted into one interpretable severity score to reduce false positives and catch sophisticated campaigns that evade single-indicator rules.

APT29 example

He details Russian espionage email tradecraft—thread hijacking, secure-document lures, OAuth consent abuse, and inbox-rule forwarding—and walks through a diplomatic spearphish using HTML smuggling to drop IMG/ISO/LNK/DLL chains designed to bypass attachment-only controls, with MQL focused on detecting the HTML dropper.

talks.title: From Lure to Alert: Implementing Canary Tokens in M365 | Ryan O'Donnell
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding From Lure to Alert: Implementing Canary Tokens in M365 | Ryan O'Donnell.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Ryan O'Donnell describes piloting mailbox-based canary tokens in Microsoft 365 using native audit telemetry rather than third-party tripwires.

## Motivation and Threat Model
After initial cloud compromise, actors like Storm 2372 run crude keyword searches—"password," "admin," credentials—across stolen mailboxes. O'Donnell targets this predictable post-compromise behavior to shrink dwell time below industry medians.

## Implementation Details
Lure emails are planted in hidden folders such as Recoverable Items, which remain searchable even when not visible in the UI. Testing with Graphrunner confirmed keyword searches surface canary content. Day 12 of the first pilot produced an alert at 11:47 p.m. based solely on mailbox operations—no EDR or malware signals.

## Takeaways
M365-native canary tokens can detect intruder mailbox reconnaissance early, but require careful lure placement, tuning, and validation that hidden folders remain indexed.

talks.title: Nikto @ 25 | Chris Sullo
talks.teaser: Traces the history of web scanners and walks through the Nikto 2.6 release, including its new matcher language and LFI checks.
talks.summary:
Chris Sullo, the maintainer of the Nikto web scanner, opens with a short history of web scanning. He traces early CGI scanners from the late 1990s, such as cgiscan.c and Whisker, and the rise of commercial crawlers around 2000. He explains that Nikto began in 2001 as a quick tool for checking one file across a corporate network, then grew into a full scanner. He also argues that older checks still find problems on aging applications.

The core of the talk covers the Nikto 2.6 release, which Sullo built with an AI coding assistant while reviewing every change. Major updates include a domain-specific language for response matchers that cuts false positives, cross-platform local file inclusion tests guided by a platform profiler, and a random user agent for each request. Speed rose about 10% and eight plugins were removed. He also shows practical options: a save flag that records raw requests and responses for each positive, a replay utility that can send them through a proxy, and a custom 404 string that filters pages returning the same content for everything.

He closes by covering the database format, where users can add their own checks in a separate file, and upcoming work such as a scan results manager, a partly working Nuclei conversion, and possible new engines. In audience questions, he encourages users to report false positives on GitHub. His takeaway is that for penetration testers, accuracy matters more than raw speed, and saving evidence makes findings easier to defend.

talks.title: You Used to Call Me On My Shell Phone | Jacob Swinsinski
talks.teaser: Shows how to write Windows shellcode by hand, resolve API calls at runtime, and chain it into a buffer overflow exploit.
talks.summary:
Jacob Swinsinski introduces Windows shellcode for people new to it, based on a months-long research effort that he found harder than it should have been. He defines shellcode as machine code that runs after a memory corruption bug such as a buffer overflow, and contrasts Windows with Linux. Because Windows has no direct syscall route for shellcode, it has to resolve Windows API functions at runtime. He walks through finding kernel32.dll by traversing the process environment block and its module list, then resolving exported functions from there. He notes that the structure offsets used for this stay fixed across executions. He also covers register roles, bad characters, null bytes and NOP sleds, and how assembled code is extracted as a byte array and tested in a C loader.

The talk moves from a message box payload in a live demo to a reverse shell built from the same logic. For a real target, he picks Phone Server, an open-source messaging application, and finds a buffer overflow in a function that copies input into a 2,000-byte buffer with no bounds checking. Fuzzing with an input of 2,001 bytes showed the return address being overwritten, and longer input reached the instruction pointer, which he confirmed in a debugger. The working exploit combines a NOP sled, the shellcode and a Netcat listener to capture a reverse shell over the network. He also described writing a custom encoder for Metasploit's SGN encoder to build an x86 exploit from an ARM Mac.

The audience Q&A covered why Windows keeps some internals undocumented, how locally executed shellcode fits post-compromise use, and how to size a NOP sled by stepping its length while watching registers in a debugger. The main takeaway is that Windows shellcode is larger than its Linux counterpart, but the resolver stub can be reused across payloads once it is tested in a disposable Windows lab.

talks.title: Hack the Notes: Exploring Pen-Test Documentation | Christian Duncan
talks.teaser: Offers practical tips on taking notes, capturing screenshots and structuring pen test reports so readers can act on findings.
talks.summary:
Christian Duncan, a security consultant with an offensive background, argues that documentation takes up a large share of almost every security task, whether the output is a client report, a blog post or a write-up of a new attack path. He stresses that the organization, flow and details of what is written shape how readers make decisions about their own risk.

The core advice is to write notes as the work happens rather than afterward. Each entry should record what was done and why, so the timeline stays intact when the report is assembled. Notes should follow a chronological structure that tells the story of what was discovered and how it was reached, which gives clients insight beyond a list of vulnerabilities. Screenshots get particular attention: each one should prove a specific point, be cropped to the relevant content, and be annotated with a red box, arrow or short label. Stray cursors and off-center captures should be removed or retaken.

Clear documentation builds trust with readers and reduces the back-and-forth needed to explain findings. Poor documentation, with missing steps, unclear screenshots or disorganized notes, creates confusion and weakens confidence. The speaker closes by noting that this is a skill that is never fully mastered and invites feedback from the audience.

talks.title: Tools of the Trade: Tips & Tricks for Testers OTG | Phil Miller and David Fletcher
talks.teaser: Walks through portable gear for on-site pentests, from travel routers and Pi-based KVMs to organized physical testing kits.
talks.summary:
Phil Miller and David Fletcher argue that testers should plan their on-site gear before a trip, so they do not arrive missing a needed cable or adapter. They suggest building purpose-based kits, such as a Wi-Fi kit, a physical testing kit, or an everyday carry bag, kept packed and ready. Early items include a large backpack, a travel router that can run VPNs and handle captive portals, and portable monitors and external input devices.

The middle covers specific tools. One example is a network access control bypass: read the MAC address of a phone on a wall port, clone it with MAC Changer, and plug the laptop in its place, since VoIP phones are often poorly segmented. Other gear includes a Flipper Zero, a Wi-Fi Pineapple pager, and a low-cost photo printer for making a badge with a face photo. A PiKVM, a Raspberry Pi based remote keyboard, video and mouse device, lets a tester control a customer's laptop from their own machine and capture screenshots. A Pi 5 with a 4G LTE hat was shown as a remote box, and Pangolin as an identity-aware access tool built around WireGuard.

The closing Q&A covered carrying lock picks and a multi-tool through airport security, and on-site access using a fake badge and a plausible manner. The takeaway is to assemble kits before travel, label them, and test every device before arriving at a customer site.

talks.title: I'm In Your Logs Now, Deceiving Your Analysts and Blinding Your EDR | Olaf Hartong
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in I'm In Your Logs Now, Deceiving Your Analysts and Blinding Your EDR | Olaf Hartong.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Olaf Hartong demonstrates how Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)—an operating system facility designed originally for performance monitoring and debugging rather than security—can be manipulated to deceive security analysts, forge alerts, and blind Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) agents. Because security tools such as Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike, and Elastic rely extensively on ETW for visibility beyond standard kernel callbacks, fundamental architectural traits of ETW create exploitable weaknesses that allow unprivileged or low-privileged actors to spoof telemetry or exhaust logging capacities.

### Key Topics
- **ETW Architecture and Security Products**: ETW connects providers (applications or drivers generating events), session controllers/the ETW kernel, and consumers (such as EDR agents). EDR vendors prefer ETW for stability (avoiding crash-prone kernel drivers), granular filtering, dynamic configuration, and broad coverage across hundreds of providers.
- **Event Spoofing Without Elevation**: ETW allows any user-mode process to call `EventRegister` with a provider's GUID and emit events using `EventWrite`. While ETW attaches the authentic originating Process ID (preventing PID spoofing), it does not track which process registered or emitted the event, enabling attackers to inject arbitrary synthetic logs.
- **Abusing Ingestion Caps to Blind Sensors**: Cloud-connected EDRs implement event capping to manage costs, performance, and bandwidth. Hartong discovered that by generating synthetic queries (such as random LDAP lookups) until hitting local or global 24-hour caps (e.g., 1,000 events), real offensive actions (such as SharpHound or AD Explorer activity) are completely dropped from telemetry.
- **Buffer Exhaustion**: Trace sessions use kernel non-paged memory buffer pools. By launching an unconsumed trace session with maximum pool configurations and flooding events, the ETW kernel tells providers that buffers are full, dropping telemetry across all concurrent sessions listening to that provider—including the EDR.

### Technical Details
- **Permissions and Registration**: ETW access control primarily protects event consumption via Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL) strings, leaving event emission largely unrestricted. Users in the `PerformanceLogUsers` group (which non-elevated accounts are often added to, such as when Visual Studio is installed) gain broad tracing rights.
- **Telemetry Injection Nuances**: Writing custom events required accounting for Windows little-endian byte ordering and specific event header structures that off-the-shelf consumer-focused packages omitted. Using these techniques, Hartong was able to forge LDAP queries, AMSI events, and fake antivirus/ransomware detections.
- **Tooling Released**: Hartong developed research utilities including *ProvMon* (to monitor provider registrations) and *Bamboozle EDR* (to automate event spoofing, telemetry flooding, and trace buffer exhaustion).
- **Vendor Response**: After reporting to Microsoft, initial remediations only addressed the specific ransomware detection proof of concept and introduced signature detections against the POC binary, leaving the core architectural issues and 98+ other providers unpatched.

### Takeaways
- **Defensive Blind Trust**: Security analysts must recognize that endpoint logs and SIEM data derived from ETW cannot be inherently trusted as immutable, ground truth evidence.
- **Detection Opportunities**: Defenders can monitor for abnormal telemetry patterns—such as rapid volumetric spikes followed by total silence in specific log tables—or attempt provider registration monitoring (though registration logging is inherently noisy).
- **Architectural Resolution**: Because event emission abuse and buffer suppression stem from kernel-level design choices within ETW, full remediation requires deep architectural adjustments by Microsoft rather than superficial signature blocks.

talks.title: # ClickForClickOnce - Generate Configurable Clickonce Payloads | Debjeet Banerjee
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding # ClickForClickOnce - Generate Configurable Clickonce Payloads | Debjeet Banerjee.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Tool Shed presentation, Debjeet Banerjee ("DB"), a malware developer for Black Hills Information Security (BHIS), introduces **ClickForClickOnce**, an open-source framework designed to automate the creation of configurable Microsoft ClickOnce payloads for penetration testing and red teaming. Historically, ClickOnce was used by organizations to distribute self-updating Windows applications with minimal user interaction via a link. For red teams, it offers an effective initial access vector requiring just two user clicks (Open and Run), leaves no artifacts in standard browser download directories, avoids SmartScreen blocks typically seen on EXEs or DLLs, and experiences comparatively fewer detections. However, manual ClickOnce payload creation via Visual Studio on Windows is time-consuming and difficult to automate under engagement deadlines. ClickForClickOnce solves this by offering an automated web interface packaged via Docker.

### Key Topics
- **Architecture and Interface:** ClickForClickOnce runs in a Docker container using a Caddy web server (serving static content and zipping artifacts) and a FastAPI backend to handle build configurations. A simple web UI allows operators to build customized payloads without wrestling with complex tool setup or dependencies.
- **Configurable Payload Options:** 
  - *Naming:* Tailoring the application display name (e.g., matching a target organization's IT tooling) to make execution prompts believable.
  - *Size Inflation:* Artificially inflating file size (typically to 200–300 MB) to bypass or delay immediate EDR scanning. The tool inflates the text section up to ~10 MB (to avoid excessive entropy spikes) and appends random data in resource files for the remainder.
  - *AppDomain Injection:* Running payloads under Microsoft-signed binaries (such as TzSync, PowerShell ISE, ServiceHub, or powershell.exe) to execute shellcode without forced DLL injection.
  - *Configurable Actions:* Chaining actions including shellcode execution (configurable in `program.cs`, with a default 8-minute delay to counter EDR inspection of read-write-execute memory allocations), dropping files to disk, and executing OS commands (supporting environment variables).

### Technical Details & EDR Detections
- **Execution Chain:** Delivering a `.application` file prompts the user to open and run it. The browser invokes Windows ClickOnce handler `dfsvc.exe`.
- **EDR Test Results:** Field testing showed strong success with zero detections against Microsoft Defender (MD), SentinelOne, and Sophos. In contrast, CrowdStrike Falcon and Cylance regularly detect the process. The speaker highlighted that detections are rarely triggered by the payload itself; rather, `dfsvc.exe` triggers a call to `rundll32.exe`, which EDRs flag or block outright before shell execution. When shells are established, subsequent beacons are sometimes blocked due to network indicators. Banerjee observed that post-CrowdStrike-outage shifts have pushed EDR focus heavily toward network behavior, domain fronting, and URL/CDN reputation (such as burned Dev Tunnels).
- **Browser & Formats:** While modern browsers handle `.application` files, older browsers can utilize `.appref-ms` files, which can also be embedded in documents.

### Takeaways & Defensive Considerations
- **Detection Strategies:** Defenders can identify malicious ClickOnce usage by detecting signed binaries (like `powershell_ise.exe`) executing from user AppData directories instead of `System32`. Monitoring for `.exe.config` files associated with AppDomain injection, unusual DLL sideloads, and unexpected `dfsvc.exe` spawning of `rundll32.exe` provides reliable detection opportunities.
- **Application Allowlisting:** Although AppLocker can challenge ClickOnce execution, operators can bypass restrictions by using generated artifacts (`.exe.config` and payload DLLs) combined with environment variables to force AppDomain injection when whitelisted executables launch.

talks.title: GDIOCSpider - Extracting and Identifying IOCs from the GDriveverse | Noah Dunn
talks.teaser: A live demo shows a Google Drive scanner that extracts typed IOCs via configurable regex rules and exports defanged results to CSV.
talks.summary:
The session introduces GDIOCSpider, an open tool that connects to Google Drive over OAuth or a service account, downloads selected files, and hunts for indicators of compromise in their text. The speaker frames two motivations: mining large libraries of DFIR reports to rediscover where an IP or hash appeared before, and reviewing a drive that may have been tampered with or holds unexpected artifacts.

Most of the walkthrough is configuration and a terminal demo. Users steer folder and file scope, delimiters, supported MIME types, strict versus lossy regex matching, exclusion lists, optional defanging, and console versus CSV output. The run summarizes scanned paths, prints each IOC with its type and value, and aggregates counts by type. Sample output is opened in a spreadsheet with file paths and IDs, then traced back to a synthetic incident document and a CSV to show cross-file correlation.

Practitioners should treat the design as pipeline-first: bulk identification stays on traditional regex (with AI reserved for odd edge cases), PDFs lean on MuPDF for text extraction, and downloads beat streaming for reliability at scale. Planned extensions mentioned include Beam or Dataflow automation, more types, and faster regex. Q&A covers pattern sources on GitHub, path-based exclusions, multi-drive service accounts, hash coverage without Base64, shared-drive visibility, and Google API trash-folder pitfalls.

talks.title: Hunting for Stupid | Mary Ellen Kennel
talks.teaser: Shares threat hunting habits, from turning threat reports into low-noise detections to documenting hunts as proof of work.
talks.summary:
The talk takes its name from a manager's request to "hunt for stupid", meaning the careless mistakes privileged staff can leave behind, such as misconfigurations, credentials in the clear and hardcoded passwords. The goal is to find these before the wrong people do. The speaker describes where hunt ideas come from: a daily cyber news webcast that draws on a CISO-focused podcast, and friendly working relationships with the vulnerability management team, who know the weak spots in an organisation.

Each hunt should end in a low-noise, high-fidelity detection use case, but those use cases need upkeep because logs and indexes change over time. The speaker uses the Pyramid of Pain as an indicator model. She says hashes, IP addresses and domains matter less in large organisations, where threat feeds ingest them, but matter more for small teams. Her worked example is a report on an APT41-linked set of about 25 Chinese-language pen testing tools. Her method is to identify each tool's name, where it is downloaded from, what artifacts it pulls down and which command-line switches are unique, while checking for Mac or Linux versions. She says AI chatbots now help her formulate queries faster.

She stresses documenting each hunt as it happens, with a header, a screenshot showing the tool, the time range, the query syntax and the number of hits, so the work can be shown later as proof. She compares note-taking tools and uses plain Word herself. She closes with threat hunting frameworks, naming PEAK, MITRE ATT&CK, the Diamond model and ADS.

talks.title: LinkedIn Landmines The Hidden Risks of Accepting Every Connection | Alexis Julian
talks.teaser: Maps common LinkedIn abuse patterns and gives practical vetting, privacy, and visibility steps for connection requests and recruiters.
talks.summary:
Accepting every LinkedIn connection looks harmless but opens paths to credential theft, malware, fraud, and impersonation. The presentation cites a network poll in which 89% of 171 respondents—mostly security staff—had seen fake or compromised accounts trying to connect.

Through recurring scenarios around a fictional user named Carl, the talk walks fake recruiters offering roles: a sign-in portal that harvests LinkedIn credentials and hijacks the account for malicious posts; a job attachment that enables macros and installs a keylogger while still showing a plausible description; a prolonged hiring scam that ends with requests for direct deposit data; and a newer duplicate executive profile used for impersonation. It explains how attackers use search filters, premium and recruiter tooling, scraping with tools like Selenium or Beautiful Soup, and rich company “People” pages plus email naming conventions to pick targets. Overshared profiles can expose contact data, org structure, and certification hints that strengthen follow-on campaigns.

Practitioners are urged to weigh personal risk tolerance, watch for authenticity signals, limit cross-platform jumps, enable two-factor authentication, add selective profile disinformation where appropriate, and—above all—review LinkedIn visibility settings regularly on desktop.

talks.title: Thirteen Steps to Being Unbroken: Infosec for the Underfunded | Tarah Wheeler
talks.teaser: Confronts underfunded incident-response burnout and offers thirteen hygiene questions that close most small-organization security gaps.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a widening gap between threat pressure and the capacity of small municipalities, businesses, and critical-infrastructure operators. Drawing on WannaCry work with United Kingdom National Health Service responders, it describes leadership failures during hospital shutdowns, chronic under-staffing, and lasting harm to people doing incident response. It argues that United States cybersecurity support has weakened since 2017, citing reduced proportional funding, cuts affecting CISA and programs such as CIS and the multi-state ISAC, stalled software bill of materials work, and recent attacks on cities including Saint Paul.

Enterprise compliance expectations fall on organizations with handfuls of staff, often served only through managed service or managed security providers. Ransomware demands against small firms rose from roughly five hundred to one thousand dollars in Bitcoin as criminals treat them as easy targets. Anecdotes span water utilities with six employees, cancelled cyber insurance at a coffee shop, a Black Basta chain involving a law firm and MSP, and a Colorado accounting firm breached with a fifteen-hundred-dollar response budget while sensitive tax records were held for ransom.

The closing prescription rejects waiting for government rescue or full NIST adoption. Instead it offers thirteen plain-language assessment questions on passwords, access, insurance awareness, downloads, phishing signals, MFA, updates, and device hygiene. The speaker reports these questions closing most gaps for small clients and urges practitioners to support peers, route organizations to MSSPs where possible, and explain controls with analogies matched to each business’s world.

talks.title: "Everything is a Proxy if You Try Hard Enough"- Old RFCs, New Exploits | Ken Pyle
talks.teaser: Shows how loosely specified HTTP and DNS behavior lets requests tunnel SMTP and turn web proxies into SSRF pivots.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a look back at early internet standards, arguing that RFCs left gaps that only became exploitable decades later. The speaker points to vague rules around HTTP methods, default port assignments, and DNS name limits, and describes how many protocols are simply text parsed over raw sockets. Because a service is largely a parser, the port and the processing logic matter more than the nominal protocol.

The core demonstration sends an HTTP TRACE request with an SMTP conversation in its body to port 587. One side treats the message as a malformed HTTP request, while the other parses the SMTP commands and delivers an email. The same parser mismatch is shown through public web proxies that fetch arbitrary URLs, a content delivery service that can be coaxed into requesting arbitrary ports, a Windows Spotlight endpoint, and an Exchange Online draft-preview request that acts as server-side request forgery. Changing a DNS record's address to a loopback or private address lets the attacker reach internal hosts and scan ports, and short TTLs help evade caching. Recursive DNS lookups triggered by many subdomains are shown to multiply outbound requests.

The speaker closes by arguing that these problems are built into the protocols and are hard to fix with patches alone. He urges designers and defenders to think through the consequences of a standard before shipping it, and says the findings were responsibly disclosed to Microsoft.

talks.title: Exploiting AI: A Case Study on Voice Biometric Penetration Testing
talks.teaser: Shows how cloned voices and spoofed numbers defeated a bank's voice verification and a live help desk's password reset.
talks.summary:
The talk covers two penetration tests that used AI voice clones against phone-based authentication. In the first, a bank's IVR matched a caller's spoken phrase to an enrolled voice print and checked the calling number for spoofing. The team cloned volunteers' voices from roughly 10 to 20 seconds of audio each, mapped the prompt library over about three hours of calls, and passed the voice check on most test accounts with default settings. Spoofed numbers were not flagged, and repeated attempts never triggered a lockout.

The second case targeted a live help desk. Using a podcast episode as source audio, the team cloned a CIO's voice and loaded a soundboard with clips grouped by purpose, such as identity details, firm statements, pressuring lines and stalling phrases. The first call lasted about two minutes and got two admin accounts reset, with new passwords emailed to the executive. The client then pulled that agent off the phones and reinforced awareness training. A follow-up call failed after a clip misfired, and the agent hung up to call back and verify the caller.

The takeaways are that light reconnaissance and cheap tools can defeat both automated voice checks and people. Voice biometrics should not stand alone, number spoofing controls and lockout policies need to be in place, and help desks need firm callback verification before resetting admin credentials, even when the caller sounds like an executive.

talks.title: Cyber on a Shoestring: Building Wagyu Career Skills and Experience on a Ramen Budget | Evan Kirstein
talks.teaser: Shows how to build cybersecurity experience on a small budget with home labs, scoped practice, portfolio projects and community ties.
talks.summary:
Evan Kirstein opens with the problem many newcomers face: employers often say they want proof of skills rather than degrees or certifications, yet getting that proof usually seems to require a job. He offers a four-step cycle called the 4P framework (prepare, practice, prove, participate) for building relevant work on a tight budget, using free or low-cost courses, tightly scoped lab exercises, written artefacts and community engagement.

He then divides the field into lanes (blue team, red team, GRC and OSINT) and suggests choosing one lane to focus on while staying familiar with the others. For a home lab, he starts with a laptop running virtualisation and works up to a used workstation with enough RAM for Security Onion, with pfsense used to segment the network. He describes daily drills such as reconnaissance, exploitation, writing a Sigma rule from the resulting alerts, then hardening and retesting. Lane-specific portfolio pieces include an OSINT investigation report, a GRC policy built in CSO Assistant, and checks for cloud identity and access misconfigurations.

The closing section covers resumes, interview stories framed as situation, task, action and result, and before-and-after metrics such as scan results and detection rates. He urges viewers to contribute to local groups, Discord communities and open-source projects by offering value first. He ends with a call to action: pick one lane, ship one mini project this month, and build a few portfolio pieces this quarter.

talks.title: Dungeons & Dragons: The Security Tool You Didn’t Know You Needed
talks.teaser: Shows how role-playing games can make incident response tabletop exercises more engaging, and introduces the Hack Back framework.
talks.summary:
Traditional security training, including many tabletop exercises, is often boring. Participants disengage, protect their own turf, fight the scenario, or run through checklists without much real discussion. The speakers argue that game-based learning works better, pointing to research cited in the talk that links it to effective learning, and to role-playing games, where people step outside their normal job, laugh, and speak more openly.

They present Hack Back, a role-playing framework for tabletop exercises built around rounds, per-round actions, characters with skill modifiers, and d20 rolls for uncertain outcomes. An incident master acts as facilitator, keeps the scenario moving and adds storytelling. Pre-made characters are deliberately exaggerated so players quickly take on a role. The sample run starts with a Friday afternoon alert that an administrator account from marketing has signed in while its owner is on vacation, and players weigh options such as blocking the account, revoking sessions, or checking logs. They also described Malware and Monsters, a creature-collecting game built around real malware families that teaches incident response and malware history.

The main takeaway is that fun and engagement make exercises more honest and memorable, and that the format can be adapted to risk management, zero trust concepts, mixed technical and non-technical teams, or sales audiences. The framework is still rough, with rules and facilitator guidance being documented, and the source is planned for release once it is easier to use. The speakers invited contributions and feedback.

talks.title: Elicitation: Weaponizing Social Engineering for Covert Access Operations | Dorota Kozlowska
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Elicitation: Weaponizing Social Engineering for Covert Access Operations | Dorota Kozlowska.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Dorota Kozlowska, a penetration tester with Black Hills Information Security (BHIS) working in the Anti-SoC continuous penetration testing team and a Certified Covert Access Specialist, presents on using social engineering elicitation during covert access operations. The presentation explores how physical penetration testing integrates with social engineering to expose vulnerabilities in physical security controls (such as locks, barriers, cameras, and guards) and human procedures. Kozlowska emphasizes that elicitation leverages human psychology—including the desire to be helpful, ego, and the instinct to correct errors—to subtly extract sensitive data without raising suspicion.

### Key Topics
- **Physical Penetration Testing Fundamentals:** Kozlowska underscores the necessity of having a documented scope and a "get out of jail free card" signed by leadership before entering a target facility. Working in pairs allows teams to stage distractions (e.g., dropping documents in a bank lobby to draw eyes away from turnstiles). Testers must discreetly document their findings through approved photo or video capture while respecting agreed-upon rules of engagement.
- **Phases of Social Engineering:** Kozlowska outlines the attack lifecycle across reconnaissance, engagement, exploitation, and execution. Reconnaissance involves gathering intelligence on employee names, roles, shift habits, org charts, and floor plans. Engagement focuses on rapport-building and establishing plausible pretexts. Exploitation involves influencing targets to breach normal processes or reveal restricted data, leading to the execution phase where objectives (such as accessing a server room or placing a flag) are achieved.
- **Psychological Foundations of Elicitation:** Elicitation differs from direct interrogation; it feels like casual conversation. Attackers exploit psychological principles such as reciprocity, social proof, perceived authority, sympathy for a confused individual, and foot-in-the-door consistency.

### Technical Details
- **Elicitation and Framing Techniques:** Operators utilize subtle challenges, innocent inquiries, and false information testing (deliberately offering inaccurate claims so targets instinctively correct them to defend accuracy). Framing techniques shape how inquiries are perceived:
  - *Praise & Ego Framing:* Complimenting a target's expertise so they reveal proprietary system architectures.
  - *Challenge Framing:* Provoking detailed technical explanations by expressing doubt that a system works a certain way.
  - *Sympathy / Helpless Persona:* Posing as a confused new hire or contractor struggling with access.
  - *Presumed Familiarity & Third-Party Framing:* Dropping internal tool names, Active Directory groups, or colleague names to validate procedures without formal requests.
- **Mirroring and Active Listening:** Replicating a target's tone, pacing, posture, and language creates rapport and encourages unguarded venting or disclosure of operational workarounds.
- **Technical Access Mapping:** Kozlowska demonstrates how an attacker can incrementally map an enterprise access path without triggering helpdesk alerts—such as chatting with IT support to confirm VPN clients (e.g., AnyConnect vs. Fortinet), confirming Active Directory group naming conventions with HR, and checking MFA trust models (e.g., Duo vs. Okta) with developers.

### Takeaways
- **Operational Tradecraft:** Operators should maintain confidence, stick strictly to timelines, avoid lingering unnecessarily, retain plausible backstories, and remove all physical equipment during exit.
- **Defensive Strategies & Awareness:** Organizations must train employees that casual inquiries can be weaponized. Red flags include subtle testing of procedures, repeated rephrased questions, excessive flattery, and artificial urgency. Defensive responses include deflecting, refusing to over-explain or educate, answering with clarifying questions, generalizing responses, adhering strictly to workplace rules, and reporting suspicious encounters quietly.
- **Ethics & Continuous Testing:** Elicitation must adhere to ethical boundaries and legal frameworks (such as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, GDPR, and wire fraud laws). Continuous red-team-inspired testing is vital as technologies and communication mediums evolve.

talks.title: Death by Dashboards - Moving the Needle on What Actually Matters | Tim Medin
talks.teaser: Shows how security dashboards and incentives can reward busywork, and how to measure risk that actually improves defense.
talks.summary:
The talk questions whether security teams measure and reward the right things. The speaker argues that managers favour dashboards, and that counts such as open vulnerabilities, mean time to resolution and blocked attacks can push staff toward busy work that does little to lower real risk. Scanner output often misses the bigger weaknesses, such as misconfigured Active Directory, weak passwords and systems without MFA.

Several remedies are offered. Findings should be validated before they reach a report, since one false result can lead a client to discard an entire test. CVSS was never meant to set remediation priority on its own, so teams should adjust scores using exposure, data sensitivity, compensating controls and system criticality. Work can be handed out in small monthly batches, and accepted low-risk items can be moved to an informational category or an appendix. In one password example, an organisation piloted a longer 14-character policy without forced rotation, and the speaker recalled that most staff then chose it. For phishing, the speaker asks what a click rate would actually change in practice.

The talk also draws on incentive failures: a bounty on cobras that led people to breed them, a rat-tail bounty in Hanoi, and developers who created easy bugs to fix. The closing advice is to measure whether attacks are caught earlier in the kill chain, and to report mitigated risks to executives so they can see progress.

talks.title: Strengthening Cybersecurity Potential: Investing in People Instead of Tools! | Markus Schober
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Strengthening Cybersecurity Potential: Investing in People Instead of Tools! | Markus Schober.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Markus Schober, founder of Blue Cape Security and former principal consultant at IBM X-Force, argues that strengthening cybersecurity resilience requires prioritizing investments in people rather than continually purchasing new tooling. While leadership often leans toward capital expense investments in point solutions, tools without skilled operators lead to underutilization, alert fatigue, and critical detection gaps. Schober presents a practical blueprint for developing structured onboarding, hands-on training, and career advancement paths to improve retention, operational efficiency, and overall security capabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Tool-First Mindset vs. Foundational Competency**: Security tools provide an abstracted layer that lacks human context and critical thinking. Relying solely on tool outputs without understanding underlying fundamentals causes analysts to misinterpret alerts or overlook real intrusions.
- **The SOC Fatigue and Turnover Crisis**: Referencing data from a Tines report ("Voice of the SOC Analyst"), Schober highlights that 71% of analysts experience burnout, 64% spend over half their time on tedious manual tasks, and 64% consider switching jobs within a year. Repetitive, shallow triage with unclear development paths drives talent drain.
- **Underutilization and Maintenance Overhead**: Organizations often operate tools at only a fraction of their capability because analysts are not trained to tune them. Furthermore, managing and maintaining automation and point solutions requires significant ongoing human resources.
- **Real-World Breach Lessons**: Schober reviews a CISA advisory where an agency suffered a multi-week intrusion due to ignored EDR alerts, unpatched vulnerabilities, and an unexercised incident response plan that failed to provide third-party responders with necessary access. In another instance, an outsourced MDR team dismissed valid ransomware alerts running from `AppData\Local\Temp` as false positives due to a lack of basic technical knowledge, leading to an entire enterprise network being shut down.

### Technical Details & Training Roadmap
To illustrate transforming a security team from basic triage to advanced capabilities, Schober outlines a multi-year "Crawl, Walk, Run" maturity framework:
- **Foundations (Crawl)**: Focuses on core enterprise architecture, including Windows domains, domain admin/service accounts, authentication event analysis, credential attacks, and living-off-the-land binaries.
- **Detection and Investigation (Walk)**: Expands into host forensics, disk and memory analysis, log triage, and implementing dedicated collection tools such as Velociraptor. Analysts learn to operationalize detection rules (YARA, Sigma) and perform initial malware triage.
- **Offensive Emulation and Specialization (Run)**: Analysts operate command-and-control (C2) frameworks and ransomware simulators to see attacks from the red-team perspective. Capabilities mature into cloud incident response, threat intelligence operationalization, purple teaming, and simulated cyber-range exercises.

### Takeaways
Effective workforce enablement relies on active, hands-on learning rather than passive listening. Practicing and operationalizing skills in lab environments drives substantially higher knowledge retention. By establishing structured onboarding, guided career roadmaps, and frequent practical workshops, organizations empower analysts to maximize existing tool investments, adapt to evolving attacker tactics, and dramatically boost operational resilience.

talks.title: Baselining for Bad Things with Surveyor! | Tre Wilkins
talks.teaser: Shows how to baseline remote admin tools across EDR data with the open-source Surveyor tool, so unusual installs stand out.
talks.summary:
Tre Wilkins argues that teams must know what is in their environment before they can prioritize risk. Baselining answers questions such as who runs PsExec, who uses network scanners or sniffers, and when they do. He focuses on remote monitoring and management software, which helps IT but is easy for attackers to abuse. He described a financially motivated actor that impersonates IT support, and a customer case where a user was tricked, a second remote tool was deployed after a failed attempt, and the intrusion ended in ransomware.

The core of the talk is Surveyor, an open-source Python tool that queries EDR platforms and summarizes the results. Searches live in JSON definition files, so analysts need not write native EDR syntax. Prebuilt files cover remote admin tools, scanners, sniffers and file sharing. Batch mode checks lists of hashes, IPs or domains. In a seven-day run against SentinelOne, several RMM tools appeared in one environment. The CSV output records endpoint, user, process path and command line. In OpenSearch, a widely installed tool looked routine, while Quick Assist on a single endpoint stood out for investigation. Surveyor can also run in AWS, with Lambda, Step Functions and a front end, to query environments in parallel.

He urged attendees to baseline their environments, verify expected activity, investigate anomalies, and contribute improvements upstream. For hardened environments, he suggested testing controls with Atomic Red Team. In questions, he said screen-sharing software and network sniffers belong in the inventory too, and that the tool has been used with threat intelligence IOC lists. Statistical deviation analysis would need a separate tool.

talks.title: Tool/Game: KC7 | Jibby Saetang
talks.teaser: Walks through KC7, a free browser game teaching log investigation and pivoting to newcomers without technical backgrounds.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents KC7, a free, browser-based investigation game built as story-driven training for people with no technical background. Players work through a fictional clothing company, Celestial Cowboy Couture, whose designs were copied and sold online. Early questions teach the query pane and show how to take one indicator, such as an IP address or user agent, and pivot from it to related records.

As the scenario unfolds, a suspected insider turns out to be a compromised login. The walkthrough decodes an encoded PowerShell command in CyberChef, counts logins to find a second affected employee, and finds that the CEO's machine ran discovery commands and had a backdoor added. In the later open-ended section, the speaker shows a password spray, where many failed logins share a similar pattern, and a shared user agent tied to 47 successful logins that suggests 47 people may be compromised. The attacks are modeled on real threat actor techniques mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and hidden in generated log noise.

The talk closes with ways the project is used beyond the game. A week-long camp for middle schoolers used a Kung Fu Panda scenario and a hospital ransomware exercise, and schools can set up a classroom tenant to track student progress. Log files are published on GitHub in JSON so teams can load them into their own tools. The speaker asks attendees to share the game so people outside traditional security paths can get into the field.

talks.title: CULTivating Growth and Connection | Wade Wells
talks.teaser: Explores loneliness risks, digital and in-person ties, and steps to grow infosec communities via meetups and mentorship.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing personal threat models for social participation—geography, neurodiversity, and comfort with travel—and cites public health data linking weak social ties to higher mortality, dementia risk, and mental illness. It contrasts the benefits of peer support and healthy behaviors with downsides such as obligation, online “empty calories,” comparison on social media, and stereotypes that make newcomers wary of security culture.

The middle section diagnoses why many practitioners avoid networking: awkward greetings, jargon, fear of public forums, and the escalating effort from lurking online to leading meetups or speaking. A tongue-in-cheek “social ATT&CK”-style map walks through reconnaissance on local groups, preparing conversation topics, building trust, and volunteering until teaching and broader industry impact become possible. Practical pointers cover meetup directories, Defcon groups, college clubs, starting small at events, and books on conversation and emotional intelligence.

Closing material treats mentorship as often informal, warns that most mentees focus on jobs, and stresses geolocation, tone-setting, and avoiding paid dynamics when unnecessary. The speaker urges supporting local communities, sharing detections and knowledge openly, and continuing a friendlier era in which collective communication lifts the whole field.

talks.title: Hiding in Plain Sight: Shellcode Obfuscation Techniques | Mike Saunders
talks.teaser: Compares shellcode obfuscation methods like XOR, delta encoding, and jigsaw shuffling by how often antivirus engines flag them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why shellcode loaders need to hide their payloads from antivirus and EDR, and how the speaker tested a range of obfuscation approaches. Each sample held an obfuscated payload and its decoding routine, with nothing executed, and was scored by how many of 72 VirusTotal engines flagged it. An unobfuscated Meterpreter payload was caught by 27 engines, while simple Base64 drew 18 and ROT13 drew 7.

Stronger-looking options did not always fare better. A single-byte XOR was flagged by 8 engines, a multi-byte XOR key by 2, and AES by 8, which the speaker linked to the high entropy that encryption adds. Because high entropy can get a binary blocked, the talk also covered mixing payload bytes with word-based data to lower overall entropy. Other methods included reversing byte order, storing bytes as UUIDs, IPv4, IPv6 or MAC addresses, shuffling bytes with a position map, and delta encoding, which was flagged by only 2 engines. Many detections targeted the decoding routine rather than the bytes, so changing the console subsystem or adding junk code could break those signatures.

The main takeaway is that no technique beats every product. A practitioner should identify which engines the target environment uses, then test candidate methods in a lab before relying on them. Storing the payload in a resource section or a separate file, and hiding data with steganography, were also raised as ideas to explore.

talks.title: TOOL: RITA | Chris Brenton
talks.teaser: Shows how the open source RITA tool hunts for command and control beacons in Zeek logs, including running it on Windows.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces RITA, an open source threat hunting tool built to find command and control channels, where a compromised host regularly calls out to an attacker's server. It works from Zeek logs and analyzes 24-hour windows, so slow, infrequent beacons still leave enough data points to surface. The backend has moved to ClickHouse, which the speaker says raised throughput from roughly 5 to 10 gbit to about 100 gbit in testing, and the whole tool now runs in Docker containers.

Results now appear as severity levels instead of raw scores, supported by context signals: prevalence, meaning how many internal hosts reached a destination; first-seen time, kept for 90 days; rare user agent strings and JA3 TLS hashes; and MIME types that do not match the requested file extension. Behavioral checks look for regular timing, including jittered beacons, and for a double-plateau pattern from sleep and task cycles. Analysts can allow-list known benign destinations, and notes can record why something like remote access software is present.

The closing section demonstrates a hacky way to run Zeek and RITA on Windows: WSL2, dumpcap writing rolling pcap files from the Windows interface, a daily cron job feeding Zeek, and a screen session for scheduled imports. The main limitation is that the Linux VM cannot see the host's network interface directly. The takeaway is to combine timing, rarity and context signals rather than rely on signatures alone.

talks.title: Demystifying Deep Fakes | Anmol Agarwal
talks.teaser: Explains how GAN-generated images, videos and cloned voices work, and which free tools help spot them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining deepfakes as AI-generated or AI-altered images, video and audio, and notes that they are used to spread misinformation and to support social engineering. It explains generative adversarial networks: a generator turns random noise into an image, a discriminator scores whether the result looks real or fake, and the two keep competing until the output is convincing. A website that produces fake faces is shown as an example, with the mismatched background as a giveaway.

The middle section argues that visual cues such as odd hands, strange expressions, inconsistent shadows and reflections are becoming less reliable, so people should lean on tools and process. A deepfake video of Morgan Freeman is used as a case study. The speaker recommends checking whether several independent outlets report the same story and running suspicious images through a reverse image search. A free video scanner correctly flagged the clip, and the speaker stresses that its results combine machine learning with human analysts. For audio, a free open-source detector flagged a golf-themed clip of presidential voices at 96.4% confidence, while the same tool could not catch the Morgan Freeman video's audio, which was only identified visually.

The closing part covers mitigation: watermarking and provenance tracking by industry, public awareness, and legislation. US rules are fragmented by state, with Tennessee's ELVIS Act cited, while the EU is presented as having the most developed framework, including disclosure rules for synthetic content. The practical takeaways are to verify sources, treat urgent requests for money or personal data with suspicion, and combine several detection tools rather than trusting one.

talks.title: TOOL: Halberd | Arpan Sarkar
talks.teaser: Demonstrates an open source web app for running cloud attack techniques against Entra ID, M365, Azure and AWS.
talks.summary:
Arpan Sarkar presents Halberd, an open source tool for security testing across multiple cloud platforms. Its goal is simple testing for organisations without large budgets or specialist skills. The tool runs as a local Python web application covering Entra ID, M365, AWS and Azure, with GCP planned. Techniques are grouped by MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and new techniques or attack surfaces can be added with little effort.

The demo starts with a device code flow technique, which produces a code that a lured victim enters to hand over a token for their account. The token is then used for discovery, which lists users, and for a reconnaissance dashboard that maps the applications, roles and groups the account can reach. Using a privilege escalation module, the speaker creates credentials for an application and authenticates as it, then searches a victim's chat messages and finds stored AWS keys. Those keys are loaded into the tool, which lists S3 buckets in AWS.

The automator chains techniques into playbooks with delays and saved settings, which can be scheduled, shared and imported, with an example based on a Midnight Blizzard campaign. Trace logs and a generated report summarise executed techniques, success rates and activity per identity. The speaker notes Halberd is not a substitute for full red team work but suits quick detection checks. Large environments take time: user enumeration reached 200,000 users in about five minutes, and incremental output is being built.

talks.teaser: Walks through pentest methods against GraphQL APIs, from schema discovery to batched login brute force and injection.
talks.summary:
The talk covers attacking GraphQL APIs from a penetration tester's point of view. It starts with the basics of how GraphQL queries, mutations, fields and objects work, and why developers favor it, since clients receive only the fields they request. The recon phase covers finding GraphQL endpoints through Nmap's detection script, endpoint wordlists and proxied traffic in Burp, plus scanning with graphql-cop to get a picture of the API's weaknesses.

When introspection is enabled, the full schema can be dumped and mapped in GraphQL Voyager, which the speaker compares to BloodHound for its view of objects and permissions. When introspection is disabled, the talk shows how field suggestion messages can be abused, with Clairvoyance automating the process of rebuilding the schema from them. Attacks follow: batching many login attempts into one mutation to get around rate limits, OS command injection through a debug field whose only argument is a string, reading a password file that way, and SQL injection in a query filter, confirmed by a SQLite error message.

The speaker stresses that introspection and suggestions are often treated as features rather than vulnerabilities, that authentication must be coded by the developer, and that staging and production configurations can differ. The takeaway is to assume an API sits behind any web application, internal ones included, and to test each endpoint for schema exposure, batching and injection.

talks.title: Never Say Anything: NSA Hacking for Defense at Scale | Tony Sager
talks.teaser: Traces three decades of NSA defensive work and argues that defenders must translate findings into business risk terms.
talks.summary:
Tony Sager opens with a personal history of computer security as he lived it, starting with his entry into the National Security Agency in 1977 and moving through work in cryptography, vulnerability analysis and red and blue team testing. He describes how the field shifted from mathematics toward the messy reality of operating systems and networks, and how an early IT-focused red team exercise showed senior defense leaders how quickly a determined nation-state could disrupt military systems.

The middle of the talk covers his conclusion that finding flaws alone rarely gets them fixed. He describes the release of NSA security configuration guidance to the public in 2001, the Cyber Defense Exercise that grew out of a service academy contest, and the idea that the best place to solve a problem is often upstream, where systems are configured and bought. He argues that each assessment is a sample of a wider population, so results should be shared in a standard format, and that vulnerabilities should be judged by their context rather than treated as alarms.

He closes by urging practitioners to translate technical findings into the business and economic decisions that organizations actually make, since most people will not understand threat reports written in technical language. He points to nonprofit work through the Center for Internet Security as a model for giving benchmarks away for free, and encourages attendees to volunteer across the community.

talks.title: PowerPug! - a Tool to Help People Use a Single Group | Jake Hildreth
talks.teaser: Outlines Protected Users adoption barriers in Active Directory and shows how the PowerPug PowerShell module automates prerequisite checks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why most organizations ignore Active Directory’s Protected Users group despite built-in hardening: in roughly two hundred environments the speaker has assessed, fewer than five percent use the group fully. The group blocks NTLM and weak Kerberos, limits delegation abuse, and shortens credential lifetimes, but those controls clash with legacy apps, IP-based administration, seamless SSO, old RDP setups, and service or computer accounts nested in privileged groups.

The middle walks through a manual readiness path: verify forest and domain functional levels, refresh stale admin passwords, turn on logon auditing, hunt NTLM and weak encryption in DC events, mark accounts sensitive, then add a single admin and test before wider rollout. That workflow is labor-intensive and easy to get wrong.

PowerPug is introduced as a PowerShell Gallery module that inventories the forest, flags logging gaps with paste-ready remediations, correlates weak logons with admin accounts, and emits commands to add only candidates that pass the checks. Live demos cover a small lab and a messier multi-domain lab with mixed functional levels. The close stresses incremental adoption, rotating old passwords first, and keeping computer and service accounts out of the group.

talks.title: Gravwell CE for Logs: The Truth Is In There | Corey Thuen
talks.teaser: Shows how Gravwell Community Edition ingests syslog and Sysmon, searches with pipe-based modules, and triggers home-lab style alerts.
talks.summary:
Corey Thuen introduces Gravwell Community Edition as a free log analysis platform aimed at practitioners who want a Splunk-style workflow: ingest first, structure and question the data later. He outlines installation via apt, default two gigabytes per day of ingestion, and a form-based fifty gigabytes per day license for personal or light commercial use, plus a shared demo environment for hands-on exploration.

The walkthrough centers on search syntax that mirrors familiar command-line tools: tag filters, grep with invert logic, RFC 5424 syslog parsing into tables, stats and charting, regex extraction on messy Ubiquiti-style logs, auto extractors, and kits such as Sysmon dashboards. He chains modules in a microphone-on example, describes open-source ingestors including Simple Relay for syslog and a lightweight Windows agent as an alternative to Windows Event Forwarding, and sketches home-lab sources—Sysmon, access points, Zeek, netflow, and lookups—that enrich Wi-Fi and endpoint visibility.

He closes with automation that runs when scheduled searches return results, illustrating beer-kegerator temperature alerting and starter flows for malicious-domain detection with email or webhooks. The takeaway is that the same free stack supports security telemetry, household monitoring, and ad hoc analysis without writing application code beyond searches.

talks.title: Threat Hunting with a Chorus of Strings | Jonathan Ham
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Hunting with a Chorus of Strings | Jonathan Ham.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Wild West Hackin' Fest in Deadwood, speaker Jonathan Ham explores low-fidelity network threat hunting under extreme operational constraints. Presenting a scenario where legacy packet captures (collected via WinPcap/WinDump) cannot be parsed by modern libpcap-based tools, Wireshark, or TCPDump, Ham sets out to prove that meaningful threat detection can still be achieved using nothing but the basic Unix utility `strings` against raw binary packet capture files.

### Key Topics
The talk centers on detecting three distinct cyber attack scenarios using only `strings` without protocol reconstruction or packet disassembly:
- **Watering Hole Attack & Portable Executable (PE) Identification:** Spotting cleartext HTTP traffic, file download artifacts, and dynamically linked libraries (DLLs) indicative of an executable transfer.
- **ICMP-Based Data Exfiltration:** Recognizing non-standard, obfuscated, and base64-encoded payloads transmitted within ICMP Echo Request packets.
- **DNS C2 Tunneling (iodine):** Hunting IP-over-DNS tunneling through character length profiling, 8-bit ASCII analysis, and identifying abnormal query names.

### Technical Details
- **Scenario 1: Watering Hole & PE Detection:** Ham runs `strings -n 12` (filtering for sequences of at least 12 printable ASCII characters) and pipes output to `less`, using regex matching for HTTP `GET` and `Host` headers. The investigation reveals requests to `lab.jhamcorp.com`, retrieving assets and ultimately `notepad.exe`. Grepping for `.dll` strings confirms the payload is a Portable Executable. Inspection of sequential strings reveals server responses with `Content-Type: application/x-msdos-program` and file size metadata. Ham highlights an anti-malware evasion trick where the standard compiler string `This program cannot be run in DOS mode` was altered using a hex editor to evade basic string-matching heuristic detections while keeping the executable functional.

- **Scenario 2: ICMP Data Exfiltration:** Outbound ICMP is often permitted enterprise-wide despite regular users having no business need to ping external resources. Ham demonstrates how data exfiltration tools (such as `hping3`) chunk stolen files into small payloads (e.g., 200 bytes) to avoid triggering legacy Snort rules for oversized ICMP payloads (rules frequently disabled due to MTU path discovery false positives). Even when an attacker compresses (gzip) and base64-encodes the data before transmission, running `strings -n 12` on the packet capture immediately exposes unnatural, repetitive, non-standard text blocks in the ICMP payload space, confirming anomalous activity.

- **Scenario 3: DNS Tunneling via iodine:** The `iodine` tool tunnels arbitrary IP traffic over DNS by gzipping packets and encoding them (using base32, base64, or base128) into DNS query names, typically utilizing NULL, TXT, or private resource records. Normal network traffic rarely exhibits long printable domain names (typically under 30 characters). Ham analyzes internal vs. external tunnel captures using `strings` with 7-bit ASCII and 8-bit encoding (`-e S`). While standard traffic contained zero strings longer than 60 characters, the base128-encoded DNS tunnel traffic yielded thousands of strings exceeding 20, 40, 80, 100, and even 200 characters in length. Recurring domain patterns (`giveyouup.jhamcorp.com`) allowed the discovery of the C2 tunnel endpoint.

### Takeaways
While relying solely on `strings` hides transport-layer metadata, source/destination IPs, ports, and protocols, it is sufficient to prove anomalous network behavior and validate hypotheses of malicious activity. Ham emphasizes that any system compromise will fundamentally alter its network and host behavior. When standard tools fail, primitive utilities can provide sufficient indicators to direct deeper file system and host-based forensic investigations. Ham also notes benchmarking findings that `ngrep` parses packets an order of magnitude faster than piping raw `strings` to `grep`.

talks.title: Two Cyber Guys And an Al Walk Into a Bar | Derek Banks, Joff Thyer
talks.teaser: Walks through AI's history from early neural networks to large language models, then demos AI on a suspicious command.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the staffing shortfalls and workload pressure facing security teams and asks why artificial intelligence matters to the field. Joff Thyer and Derek Banks trace the technology's history, from the term's coinage in 1955 and early neural networks built to cancel telephone echo, through the hardware limits of that era, to the transformer models and GPU growth behind today's large language models. They also explain how models were measured against standardized exams and how their capability has been compared to a student's progress.

The middle of the talk looks at projected gains in compute and algorithm design, along with concerns about the quality of internet training data, alignment and the electricity demands of large compute clusters. Banks then argues that much useful AI work does not depend on large language models and relies on older machine learning methods. He explains supervised learning for labelled tasks such as spam or phishing classification, unsupervised learning for anomaly detection, and neural networks as layered weights that are adjusted during training. He also defines tokens and context windows.

The talk closes with a live demo using an open-source, prompt-driven command-line tool. The presenters feed in an unfamiliar Windows command that sets up a background SSH tunnel and ask the model to explain its flags. The demo was cut short for time, and the presenters then request a detection rule idea. Their takeaway is that model output should be checked like a colleague's work rather than trusted outright. They close by previewing a longer course on AI for security professionals.

talks.title: Workshop: How to Triumph at Tech Support | Bill Stearns | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Offers a practical process for troubleshooting customer issues and keeping frustrated users informed, from ticket triage to closing.
talks.summary:
This workshop is a process-focused guide for people who handle technical support for software. The speaker frames the job as two roles: a translator who moves information between frustrated customers and developers, and a puzzle solver who builds a hypothesis from incomplete details. He stresses listening, being honest when an answer is not yet known, and imagining what the customer is seeing on their screen.

The middle of the session covers the working method. Handle one problem per ticket and start with the most critical issue. Collect the software version, operating system, hosting platform, exact error messages, and any recent change such as a reboot, upgrade, or firewall edit. Where possible, rebuild the customer's environment, or compare a working system against a broken one setting by setting. Swapping in an older component version can serve as a temporary workaround. He also recommends a shared notes document, a searchable toolkit of troubleshooting queries, a non-production copy of the product for practice, and ticketing and scheduling tools that support several team members across time zones.

The closing section covers communication. Give status updates even when nothing has changed, avoid promising fix dates, and write fixes with clear prerequisites and steps. Keep language simple for customers who use English as a second language. Confirm with the customer that the problem is actually solved, and ask for feedback when a ticket closes.

talks.title: So My Credentials Have Been Leaked, Now What? | Dwayne McDaniel | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how to respond when leaked credentials surface, from validating exposure to rotating secrets and writing playbooks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that leaked credentials, which the speaker uses to mean API keys, passwords, connection strings and certificate files, keep turning into breaches. It draws on several cases. An Uber super admin was phished, and hardcoded credentials in PowerShell scripts then made it easy for the intruder to move laterally. A developer's unpatched media server let attackers reach a vendor's infrastructure and, from there, customer environments. A contractor's push of a repository to public GitHub exposed a key to a Toyota data server holding data on roughly 296,000 customers, which went unnoticed for about five years.

Citing 2022 findings from a secret sprawl report that counted more than 10 million hardcoded credentials in public GitHub repositories, the speaker urges engineers to assume breach. When a leak is suspected, the advice is to check whether the secret is still valid, how old it is and where it was exposed, then work out which systems depend on it. Next, notify the owning teams and security staff, report the incident so the organisation can help, and rotate the credential once a recovery plan and possible downtime are understood.

For prevention, the talk recommends keeping secrets out of code, storing them in environment files that are reliably excluded from version control, and using a vault or a cloud provider's secret manager. Git pre-commit hooks can block commits that contain credentials. Teams should also write playbooks from past incidents, run retrospectives, and automate steps where possible.
