talks.title: Burp, Not Just For Browsers | Samantha Peters | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how to proxy Postman, Python scripts, and iPhone app traffic through Burp Suite for centralized pentest artifacts and tooling.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by reframing a common assumption: Burp Suite is not limited to browser traffic. After a brief recap of proxy listeners, loopback binding, and Firefox CA installation, the focus shifts to routing other clients through the same workflow.

Postman is wired to a custom proxy so API calls appear in Burp with full request and response detail, including benefits of Repeater, Intruder, and project-scoped logging. Python examples use environment variables or per-request proxies with the requests library; a short directory-busting loop against a Hack The Box target illustrates capturing many responses in Burp for quick triage. Mobile setup binds Burp to all interfaces, pairs an iPhone on the same Wi‑Fi, installs the PortSwigger CA, and demos background traffic from a free-to-play game.

Practitioners should treat Burp as a hub for documentation and analysis across tools. Limitations matter: some apps detect MITM proxies, while others may expose cleartext API traffic when proxied successfully.

talks.title: Zero to Hero: Hacking Your Way to Your First Pentest Gig | Christian Villapando | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Zero to Hero: Hacking Your Way to Your First Pentest Gig | Christian Villapando | WWHF 2023.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at WWHF 2023, Christian Villapando shares guidance on how aspiring security professionals can break into the field and secure their first penetration testing gig. Speaking remotely from Manila, Villapando draws from his background as a pentest consultant for a US-based Fortune 100 company, master's student at the SANS Technology Institute, member of the Philippine CTF team Hacktivate, and advocate providing free cybersecurity training. He emphasizes that breaking into pentesting is achievable regardless of one's current age or background, provided one focuses on foundational skills, hands-on practice, and active community involvement.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Penetration Testing**: Villapando defines pentesting as an authorized attempt to access computer systems to improve an organization's security posture by identifying attack paths before malicious actors do. He clarifies that pentests are point-in-time assessments.
- **The Reality of Daily Pentesting Work**: Contrary to popular media portrayals of non-stop hacking, a pentester spends considerable time on non-hacking activities. These include client communication, scope definition, troubleshooting connectivity issues, writing reports as testing progresses, and providing post-delivery support and presentations.
- **Career Paths**: Aspiring professionals can enter the industry as full-time employees (at pentesting service firms or internal enterprise security teams), contractors paid by the hour for set durations (such as 3–6 months), or independent consultants running their own business, which provides more autonomy but relies heavily on industry reputation.
- **Types of Assessments**: Common assessments include web applications, external network testing, internal active directory assessments, wireless testing, mobile pentesting, and product or IoT embedded device testing. Web application testing is highlighted as the most common engagement and the usual entry point for beginners.
- **Core Fundamentals & Prerequisites**: Success requires solid grounding in computer networking (understanding concepts like TCP and the three-way handshake), operating systems (especially proficiency in Linux over standard Windows interfaces), and scripting or application development languages (recommending Python for scripting, alongside exposure to languages like PHP or Java). Those transitioning from other IT or infosec roles should also familiarize themselves with broader concepts like security controls, red and blue teams, and incident response.

### Technical Details & Learning Strategies
- **Training Platforms**: Villapando advocates leveraging free and paid learning resources, mentioning PortSwigger Web Security Academy for web application security, Hack The Box, TryHackMe, and material from SANS and OffSec.
- **Certifications**: While industry figures like Dave Kennedy and John Strand no longer need certifications due to their established reputations, certifications can help beginners pass initial HR screenings to land their first interview, though they are not an absolute requirement.
- **Goal Setting**: To maintain consistent progress, learners should set structured goals: daily goals (learning two current infosec news items or exploits), weekly goals (studying technical fundamentals like TCP RFCs), monthly goals (participating in a CTF), and quarterly or yearly goals (completing an online course or passing an exam).
- **Documentation and CTFs**: Writing public write-ups (e.g., documenting vulnerable machines on platforms like Medium) helps build communication skills and document personal growth. Hands-on CTF participation (such as competing in the DEF CON Red Team Village CTF) reinforces technical skills under realistic scenarios.

### Takeaways
To land a first pentesting role, candidates should focus heavily on troubleshooting fundamentals, gain hands-on practice via CTFs and labs, document their progress, and network within the community. For those already in IT or infosec, volunteering for dirty work, vulnerability assessments, or internal testing tasks can provide crucial visibility and experience. Pentesting ultimately balances technical hacking with communicating business risk to clients.

talks.title: I’m OK, You’re OK, We’re OK: Living with AD(H)D in Infosec | Klaus Agnoletti | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Explores how ADHD shapes work in infosec, from career setbacks to coping strategies and why employers should adapt.
talks.summary:
Klaus Agnoletti talks about living with ADHD while working in information security. He was diagnosed in 2019, and the talk explains the condition as he experienced it: an inattentive presentation without hyperactivity, which made concentration hard and kept costing him jobs for years before he understood why. He describes an iceberg model of common misconceptions, along with a list of traits such as difficulty switching tasks, weak time sense, and choice overload, and reflects on how repeated short employments and firings pushed him to change direction.

The middle of the talk covers coping. He mentions stimulant medication that helped him stay awake and focus, music designed for concentration, and a daily breathing routine that quiets his mind. He moved from security advisory into community management at an open source startup, then went freelance, which let him choose his own work and hours. He also notes that a diagnosis stays on record in Denmark and can affect things like life insurance.

He closes with practical lessons: understand the condition, know your strengths and weaknesses, and tell colleagues how your brain works. He argues employers should judge quality and timing rather than where someone sits, since flexibility is also good business. Each person's ADHD differs.

talks.title: Campfire Talk: 5 Ways to be Successful in a Fortune 5 SOC | Ben Renz, Vidur Ravella | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shares career and burnout lessons from two engineers who worked in a Fortune 5 security operations center.
talks.summary:
Two speakers who worked together in a Fortune 5 security operations center share what they learned while working around the clock in that environment. The talk covers managing up: setting a clear agenda for one-on-one meetings, raising promotion goals as a shared plan rather than an ultimatum, and recognising when a manager relationship is not a good fit. It also argues for following genuine interest across the field rather than chasing one role, such as red teaming, and for judging candidates by hands-on experience rather than certifications alone.

The middle section covers work-life balance and burnout. The speakers describe working very long weeks early in their careers, learning to decline unpaid extra hours, and taking mental health days. They recommend building a community both inside and outside the employer, through conferences, online channels and social events, and leaning on teammates when investigations get hard.

They then describe the daily grind of the SOC: a follow-the-sun team with about 36 people in the US and around 15 in India, with tickets arriving from phishing reports, user clicks, endpoint alerts and frequent war rooms. To cut the repetitive alert load, they built an internal automation layer around their SIM that handled roughly 30,000 tickets a week. The talk closes with advice to treat the job as just a job, make time for travel and other interests, and work smart rather than long hours.

talks.title: Immunity, Free Speech & the (Potential) Death of Internet: Section 230 | Kelli Tarala | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Traces how Section 230 grew from early publisher liability cases and why lawmakers and courts still debate it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the First Amendment and the limited immunity that publishers and distributors of written material have long held. A 1950s Los Angeles obscenity case against a bookshop clerk is used to show how strict liability for other people's content could force shopkeepers to read every title they stock. The speaker then covers a 1990s lawsuit against the online service Prodigy, where a court treated the service as a publisher of an anonymous user's post on a message board rather than a passive carrier. Congress responded with the safe-harbor provision in the Telecommunications Act of 1996, so that websites, including small businesses, would not be treated as publishers of content their users posted.

The middle of the talk lays out arguments on both sides. Supporters say the law protects free expression, supports technology platforms, and reduces the load on courts that would otherwise hear endless defamation claims. Critics say it does not address harmful content, misinformation, uneven content moderation, or declining platform accountability. The speaker also reviews two Supreme Court cases arising from terrorist attacks, Twitter v. Taamneh and Gonzalez v. Google, which were decided without ruling on Section 230, leaving the question open.

The closing section encourages practitioners, especially those in governance, risk and compliance roles, to explain the law to non-technical family members and colleagues and to read sources from different perspectives. The speaker suggests a shared responsibility model, in which providers and users both take due care. Recommended reading includes a book on the history of the 26 words, EFF resources, a legal paper proposing fixes, and SANS reading room papers. The speaker stresses that the talk is not legal advice.

talks.title: Magnets for Needles in Haystacks: Using MITRE ATT&CK w/ Risk-Based Alert | Haylee Mills | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how aggregating low-fidelity observations into risk scores can cut noisy SOC alerts and surface attacker behavior.
talks.summary:
Mills presents risk-based alerting, which she also calls aggregated abstraction alerting. Traditional one-to-one detections fire on routine activity and bury analysts in false positives. Instead, individual observations from many log sources are written into a shared risk index with scores, and an alert fires only when scores pile up against one object within a time window.

She walks through building it with Splunk's collect and lookup commands, though she says any tooling can do the job. Each observation carries a risk object, a threat object, source type, original event time, risk message, and ATT&CK tactic. Scores can be adjusted by asset priority or critical vulnerability counts. Two cases illustrate the point. An Acrobat process spawning a browser was harmless alone, but paired with a proxy connection to an uncategorized site within five minutes it reliably caught phishing. Reconnaissance commands scored low individually, and when several ran on one host they signaled a red team or a real compromise.

Reported results include alert volume drops of 30 to 90 percent, with one deployment going from about 1,500 alerts a week to 100. Purple teaming also improved, since red team fingerprints justified requests for new data sources. Mills advises a phased rollout, often taking three to six months to reach production, and suggests reviewing threat objects to spot noisy or rare behavior.

talks.title: The Truth is Out There: Unveiling Secrets with Open Source Intelligence | Joe Gray | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Surveys open source intelligence tools, search engines and the privacy habits investigators need, with ethics and bias checks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a historical tour of intelligence gathering from public sources, from wartime broadcast monitoring to journalists who noticed late-night pizza orders at the Pentagon during Desert Storm. The speaker argues that the same habits of watching public signals still shape investigations and crowdsourced research today.

The middle of the talk covers tools and judgment. The speaker favors working from the command line and Linux where possible, but says a browser is enough to start. Search engines beyond the usual one are presented as useful because each returns different results, and regional engines matter when the target is in another country. Mapping services, Recon-ng, Sherlock and Jupyter notebooks come up as examples, though the speaker insists that human reasoning matters more than any tool. Misinformation, disinformation and bias get attention, with advice to check your own assumptions and verify claims against several sources. Generative AI is discussed both as a way to speed up work and as a source of fake personas, and bot networks are described as a growing threat to trust online.

The closing section focuses on responsible practice. Investigators should collect only what a report needs, protect their own data with a password manager and a VPN, and consider isolated or cloud systems for research. Legal limits differ by country, sector and licence type, and privacy rules such as GDPR shape what can be stored. The speaker recommends practising with CTF events, reading published indictments and keeping good notes, and says investigators should know their limits and step away when the work becomes distressing.

talks.title: Lost Underground | Ray and Mike Felch | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Lost Underground | Ray and Mike Felch | WWHF 2023.

talks.title: Cybersecurity for the "Have-Nots" of the World | Jake Williams | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Gives small and mid-sized organizations with little security staff a budget-conscious way to prioritize their defenses.
talks.summary:
Jake Williams opens by contrasting security advice written for large enterprises with the reality of small and medium businesses, often 1,000 to 2,500 employees with fewer than ten IT staff and no dedicated security team. He argues that generic best practices and costly consulting engagements, such as a risk assessment that produces an unaffordable remediation list, rarely fit these organizations. He frames the problem as limited time and money, where every build-or-buy choice means giving up something else.

He then walks through steps he considers realistic at this scale. These include an affordable EDR product, moving off on-premises Exchange and file shares to hosted services, and disabling DNS over HTTPS so that monitoring stays useful. For visibility he describes running Security Onion on inexpensive hardware fed by a network tap, enlarging Windows event logs, and enabling print server logging to answer insider questions. Other suggestions include rotating network storage units to keep one offline backup, using a third-party patching tool, and disabling USB mass storage. He advises against managed threat hunting from an EDR vendor, commercial awareness training, phishing simulations and CTI feeds for these organizations.

He closes by urging realistic goals, with detection valued over prevention when resources are thin. When constraints leave no workable set of controls, he says consultants should tell the client so rather than sell an plan the organization cannot carry out.

talks.title: Six Ways to Defend Better RN | David Kennedy | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Presents six defenses: command-line telemetry, environment-tuned detections, day-one rule churn, and layered deception traps.
talks.summary:
Organizations often chase multi-year strategies, commodity tools, and buzzwords while business and adversaries move faster than security programs can adapt. The speaker contrasts slow governance and boxed EDR deployments with what red teams actually exploit: predictable defaults, weak behavioral baselines, and detection pipelines that take weeks to change. Examples include commodity C2 that evades stock signatures when lightly renamed, and a customer that caught a long-running engagement by alarming when non-technical users ran technical tooling.

The core framework centers on coverage through environment-specific “landmines”: map normal admin and user behavior, alert on deviations such as unexpected PsExec or living-off-the-land binaries on ordinary accounts, and shrink alert noise by focusing on long-tail anomalies rather than endless commodity rules. Detection engineering should run like agile development—rules from hunting or intelligence into production within a day, with consistent processes for analysts or MSSPs. Threat intelligence, hunting, and detection work should be one coordinated investment, not scattered projects.

Six actionable themes emphasize visibility and command-line telemetry (for example Sysmon and ETW), fast detection churn, layered deception (decoy domain admins in memory, bait SPNs, fake share credentials), and applying offensive tradecraft in reverse. Deception rarely appears in enterprise programs yet yields high-fidelity signals with little user impact. The closing message is that dwell time drives damage; enough bespoke detections and traps make sustained stealth costly even when vulnerability management and staffing remain imperfect.

talks.title: Destroying Fog of War: Realistic End-to-End Attacks and Detective Controls | Jeff McJunkin WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how a short attacker path through an MSP environment can be caught with cheap detective controls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that most breaches end with attackers reaching sensitive data, and that defenders only win if they detect and remove an intruder before that goal is reached. Jeff McJunkin describes common ways in, including exposed remote services, phishing, and access through managed service providers, and notes that a single internet-facing service with weak single-factor login can be enough.

The live demo follows an attacker from a publicly indexed remote desktop host at a local managed service provider. A credential found in a large breach-data file opens a session, and client folders on the machine reveal documents. Files are then staged and uploaded to an unauthenticated file-sharing site, and a local account with a default password turns out to be an administrator. Along the way, the presenter points out that built-in discovery commands such as net user and NLtest, along with remote support tools, are common first steps in real intrusions.

For defenders, the suggestions include alerting on new remote support installs and outbound connections, disabling tools such as Quick Assist when they are unused, and limiting Office macros to users who need them. Canary tokens tied to a registry key can alert on reconnaissance commands, and calls to a renamed copy of net.exe can themselves be a signal. The takeaway is to add one detective control at a time, roll back anything noisy, and keep shortening the time between an attacker's first foothold and a response.

talks.title: Rethinking Penetration Testing | Mike Saunders | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Compares red teams, assumed breach and purple teams, and explains which test suits a client's maturity and goals.
talks.summary:
Mike Saunders argues that the traditional internal network penetration test, which relies on port scans and exploitation from a single box, does not prepare organisations for how real attackers operate. He notes that vendors use many overlapping names for red teams, assumed breach and purple teams, so buyers often do not know what they are getting.

A red team is a long, goal-focused attack on a mature environment, starting from outside with phishing or physical access, and it tests how the blue team responds rather than the tools. It demands extensive research into the target's email protections, staff and endpoint defences, and it is expensive. An assumed breach begins after a user has already been compromised, so testers can move faster and cover more ground, either openly as full-knowledge testing or quietly to check whether detections fire. Purple teams are collaborative, goal-driven exercises in which testers and defenders work through scenarios together, which requires real blue team time. Throughout, he stresses using a representative workstation and account, and deciding with the client whether EDR should be enabled.

His recommendation is that most clients with some maturity should start with assumed breach, while immature programmes should first fix patching and hardening through internal and external tests. Before buying, organisations should set goals, budget and defender availability, because a red team rarely fits a one-week budget.

talks.title: Six Things DevOps Wants from InfoSec | Naomi Buckwalter | WHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows security staff how to earn developer trust with specific guidance, verified findings, and hands-on help in CI/CD.
talks.summary:
Naomi Buckwalter, a director of product security at a software security vendor, frames the friction between developers and security teams as marriage counseling. She opens with a familiar scene: a team hands a near-release application to security and gets back a long list of findings that threatens the schedule. She then walks through six things developers reportedly want, beginning with empowerment through training, tools, integrations and ownership.

The middle of the talk covers the practical asks. Checklists should name approved libraries, allowlist-based regular expressions and a clear definition of done rather than vague rules. Security staff can do research for developers, such as comparing identity providers in a spreadsheet, and build internal tools that fit existing pipelines. Findings should be validated against the team's own code before they are passed on, and reviewed GitHub Actions can be pinned to specific commit hashes or forked and patched. Early threat modeling built around confidentiality, integrity, availability and non-repudiation helps catch risk before implementation. CVSS scores alone do not show business impact, so teams should add their own context.

The closing sections urge security staff to learn how software is built, including languages, frameworks and pipelines, and to read the code. Postmortems should be blameless, questions work better than nagging, and developers need access limited to their tasks while still having room to make mistakes. Security champions inside development teams help embed security into daily work. The core message is to be specific, collaborate, and treat developers as the people building the product.

talks.title: Building a Winning Team Culture | Heath Adams | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Actionable guidance on compensation, remote teamwork, transparency, and hiring to build resilient security company culture.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames team culture for security organizations that operate largely outside traditional offices. It opens with the speaker’s path from help desk and pentest roles into founding a training company that grew to roughly twenty-two people with no reported voluntary turnover, arguing that people matter more than short-term profit and that replacing staff costs more than paying fairly.

The middle walks through policies the company tried, including moving away from unlimited PTO toward fixed vacation time, flexible hours without petty clock-watching, revenue sharing for client referrals, and rewarding employee innovation with a revenue share on new programs. It also covers adapting management to different personalities through one-on-ones, motivation questions, and avoiding destructive hires, plus weekly open-book financial updates so bonus expectations are not vague.

The close turns to collaboration tools, shared calendars, documentation, peer support, public recognition in chat, community reputation, self-care, and continuous learning. Practitioners are urged to know their market value, interview employers about culture, and expect transparency, balance, and training investment from leadership.

talks.title: Workshop: Incident Response for Humans | Nathan Case | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Walks developers and non-specialists through incident response using a tabletop game about a merged company under attack.
talks.summary:
Nathan Case presents a condensed incident response workshop for developers and people without a security background. The talk defines an incident as any event that damages an organisation and introduces a repeating observe, orient, decide, act loop, illustrated with someone adjusting their stance on ice. Teams take on defender and attacker roles in a tabletop-style game built around a fictional company merger.

As the scenario escalates, defenders deal with spearphishing, corporate spyware, laptops mining cryptocurrency, and suspicious outbound traffic. Some teams have endpoint detection and others do not, which changes what they can see. Later, a machine in another country keeps reporting production, and insiders complicate decisions. The speaker then describes a real case in which an intruder stayed inside a company for about two years, until a second group's activity triggered ransomware that encrypted systems five times and recovery took months. A separate example involves an operator who noticed a temperature running five degrees above where it should be, because cooling was slower than expected.

The session closes on after-action reviews. The speaker urges responders to write notes during an incident, keep copies of logs, and be candid in the review, since fear of blame lets people steer attention away from the root cause. A five whys style of questioning is suggested for finding out why something happened. Attendees leave with a simple, repeatable routine that works for beginners and experienced responders alike.

talks.title: Workshop: MITRE ATT&CK and the ATT&CK Navigator (Part 2 of 2) | Carrie Roberts | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Walks through the ATT&CK Navigator to visualize emulation coverage, combine threat group layers, and share results.
talks.summary:
MITRE's ATT&CK Navigator is a free, open-source web tool that draws techniques from the ATT&CK matrix as colored layers. The presenter notes it can be self-hosted, so sensitive coverage data stays inside an organization. The demo opens with a layer built from Atomic Red Team test counts, where techniques with ten or more scripted tests are shaded dark red, and shows how sub-techniques expand, get annotated and get filtered by platform.

The middle of the talk covers layer mechanics: custom scores and color palettes, comments and links attached to techniques, JSON export and import, and loading community layers from a raw GitHub URL. The presenter then builds separate layers for three threat groups, scores them, and combines them with a simple sum formula. Techniques shared by all three groups show up in green, which gives a practical way to decide what to prepare for first. A browser extension, ATT&CK Powered Suit, is also shown for jumping from a technique ID on a web page straight into the ATT&CK site.

The talk closes with a brief look at MITRE's ATT&CK Evaluations, which publish vendor results without scores and need configuration context to read fairly, and at MITRE's micro emulation plans, which are simpler downloadable executables than full adversary emulation plans. The takeaway is that the Navigator works well as an at-a-glance coverage view for management and as a shared plan for detection and red team work.

talks.title: Workshop: MITRE ATT&CK and the ATT&CK Navigator (Part 1 of 2) | Carrie Roberts | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Introduces the MITRE ATT&CK matrix and how the ATT&CK Navigator maps an organization's coverage against it.
talks.summary:
The session is a hands-on introduction to MITRE ATT&CK, a knowledge base of adversary behaviour built from observed real-world attacks, and to the ATT&CK Navigator, a tool for overlaying coverage on the matrix. The speaker starts with the wider MITRE ecosystem, contrasting CVEs, which are tied to a specific software version, with CWEs, which are general weakness categories. Caldera is introduced as a command-and-control style tool for emulating attacker behaviour safely on test endpoints.

Walking through the Enterprise matrix, the talk explains tactics as attacker goals, such as initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, credential access and lateral movement, and techniques as the methods under each goal, each with its own number. Brute Force serves as a worked example: password spraying is one of its four sub-techniques, and the speaker describes how trying one season-and-year password across thousands of harvested usernames gets into a few percent of accounts, while lockout policies make classic guessing impractical. Each technique page lists mitigations and references, and the group, campaign and software sections show which threat actors and tools have used a given technique, including a 2016 Ukrainian electric power campaign.

The closing part points to the group and software pages for finding actors that target a particular industry, and to the all-techniques page for placing new test ideas. Atomic Red Team scripts are tied to these same technique numbers. The practical takeaway is a shared vocabulary that lets teams prioritise defences and check coverage against one common reference.

talks.title: Workshop: Point and Shoot to Continuous Auditing in the AWS Cloud | Andrew Krug | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how to run Prowler and Scout Suite against an AWS account and move from point-in-time audits to continuous auditing.
talks.summary:
This hands-on workshop looks at what cloud auditing and compliance mean in practice, and why it is hard to map vague framework controls such as PCI DSS onto concrete AWS configuration. The speaker explains that newly launched managed services can outpace existing control mappings. Participants begin by signing in to a training AWS account through single sign-on with temporary, read-only credentials, and the talk notes that consultants should avoid relying on long-lived access keys.

The middle of the session covers point-in-time auditing with open-source tools. Attendees run Prowler and Scout Suite against the account, then feed the JSON output into TruffleHog to look for secrets left in the collected data. The speaker walks through common AWS exposures seen on real audits, including publicly readable S3 buckets, SQS queues and SNS topics, shared machine images and snapshots, and overly permissive IAM policies. He also describes how he triages findings by criticality and service, and warns that scans produce heavy describe and access-denied call volume that appears in CloudTrail.

The final part compares snapshot scans with continuous auditing. Attendees explore AWS Config, including conformance packs, public-access rules and advanced queries, then review a commercial cloud security posture management dashboard. The takeaway is to run more than one scanner, add context before handing findings to engineers, and move toward continuous monitoring as cloud environments change quickly.

talks.title: Demystifying Design: Making Infosec Look Good | Caitlin Cash | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how security teams can partner with designers to meet goals, give useful feedback, and choose when to use AI.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that design always serves a purpose and that a widening gap between creators and users—worsened by automation—makes cross-disciplinary collaboration harder. The speaker, a designer at Black Hills Information Security, describes joining the team through PRO v3 and why infosec practitioners should care about intentional visual and verbal choices rather than default aesthetics.

The core walkthrough treats projects like puzzles: define motivation and limits first, respect team morale and budget, pivot without losing the project's heart, and separate disposable work from material that represents a brand or earns revenue. Examples range from Coca-Cola Santa campaigns and artifact restoration to a sandbox ideation mindset and a screen-captured process building the Threat Hunting zine cover, with emphasis on information hierarchy, print constraints for screenshots, and goal-based feedback instead of personal taste.

The close ties design communication to security culture—writing for the reader's understanding, avoiding design by committee, and measuring success by whether the work kept its purpose. Q&A touches on logo pricing references, vetting platforms like Fiverr, community feedback over formal surveys, and managing designer burnout through personal creative work.

talks.title: AD (Addie) and DNS (Dennis): A Match Made in Heck | Jim Sykora & Jake Hildreth | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Maps integrated DNS abuse from node creation and DNS Admins to sinkhole, with hardening and a PowerShell zone audit module.
talks.summary:
Active Directory and DNS are described as mutually dependent: integrated zones store records as directory objects, so weaknesses in either layer can affect identity and name resolution across the forest. The presenters walk through established abuse lines, including dynamic updates and LDAP-created DNS nodes available to authenticated users, broadcast-name poisoning limitations, Kevin Robertson’s PowerMad-style wildcard poisoning, and Windows Server 2016 zone scopes nested under integrated zones. They compare forest, domain, and legacy zone partitions, noting that legacy layouts can inherit overly broad permissions at the DNS head object and that precedence rules let locally stored zones override stricter replicas.

On the offensive side, they revisit the patched DNS-admin DLL load that elevated to SYSTEM on domain controllers, stress that DNS Admins remain powerful through ownership and conditional forwarders, and outline “evil sinkhole” scenarios that locally override resolution for EDR, management, or security tooling. Newer DNS policies and query resolution features—often PowerShell-only—are framed as post-compromise redirection options. A dangling SPN concept ties Kerberos service names to DNS poisoning, though the chain is presented as ongoing research.

The defense half recommends disabling LLMNR, NBNS, and mDNS; pre-creating wildcard and WPAD records; shrinking and protecting DNS Admins; converting legacy zones; using DHCP service accounts for dynamic updates; auditing ACLs, scopes, and policies; and cleaning unused SPNs. They demo Blue Tuxedo, a PowerShell module that inventories zones, forwarders, admins, tombstones, and related misconfigurations, then tests and emits remediation commands, published on Triar’s GitHub for smaller environments.

talks.title: DevSecOps Worst Practices | Tanya Janca | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Fifteen anonymized DevSecOps anti-patterns from enterprise consulting, with rollout and tooling guidance to avoid them.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames DevSecOps as the security specialist’s work woven through a DevOps shop—not merely owning a few scanners in CI/CD—and argues that organizations rarely share how implementations fail, which slows industry learning. Drawing on patterns seen across more than four hundred anonymized client engagements, the speaker walks through fifteen recurring mistakes.

Early themes include the boy who cried wolf: high-noise tools blocking builds until developers disable them, including a case where expensive SAST was turned off pipeline-wide after false positives and long runtimes. Related pitfalls cover throwing untested tools into CI/CD, using the pipeline as artificial security gates, hiding scan results behind impossible access paths, runaway tests that burn time and cloud budget, and impossible SLAs that block releases despite incremental fixes. Further items address untrained staff on production-adjacent systems, security issues rotting in backlogs, all-negative security culture, notifications that shame entire organizations, fragmented bug trackers, SDLc coverage beyond CI gadgets, overly permissive pipeline permissions, automation limited to CI while ignoring the IDE, and reluctance to share incident lessons that could align resistant teams.

The close stresses testing tools before pipeline insertion, alerting before blocking, realistic dual SLAs for legacy versus new findings, training, positive reinforcement, and fitting security into developers’ workflows. Listeners get concrete rollout tactics and pointers to community resources and slide downloads.

talks.title: That Shouldn't Have Worked - An Intro to Evading AV/EDR | Corey Overstreet | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Surveys common ways to get payloads past Windows AV, EDR, sandboxes and allow-listing, from delivery to execution.
talks.summary:
Corey Overstreet presents an introduction to getting payloads past antivirus, endpoint detection and response, and application allow-listing. The talk aims to help red teamers reproduce execution steps and show defenders what they look like. The speaker stresses that evasion is a cat-and-mouse game, that simple changes should be tried first, and that delivery should mirror a real phishing download. Files fetched through a browser pick up the Mark of the Web, which can be avoided by wrapping the payload in an archive or encoding it inside a dropper.

The middle covers runtime and sandbox defenses. User-mode protections such as AMSI, ETW and API hooks can be patched, unhooked by reloading DLLs, or sidestepped with direct syscall stubs, though those calls can be monitored too. Sandbox evasion relies on long delays that outlast the sandbox, oversized files padded with zeros that compress back down, and checks for domain membership, host naming and debugger processes. For static detection, the speaker covers high-entropy blobs, encoding shellcode as dictionary words or identifiers, swapping default keys and names from public C2 frameworks, and breaking up the memory allocation and permission sequence.

The talk closes with common execution routes, including executables, MSBuild inline tasks, InstallUtil, MSI install actions, shortcut files, service binaries and proxy DLLs, many of which rely on Microsoft-signed binaries. Practitioners should take away that simple variations are worth testing first, that callbacks should be delayed and suspicious parent-child process chains avoided, and that the referenced blogs, code samples and courses are the place to go deeper.

talks.title: Mysteries of Lateral Movement | Olaf Hartong | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how to keep BloodHound attack paths current by feeding live Sentinel and Defender telemetry into a graph database.
talks.summary:
Blue teams rarely make use of BloodHound's attack-path data, the speaker argues, because full scans need permissions and planning, sessions change within minutes, and local admin changes often go unseen. Logon, role and alert events that reveal those paths already reach the SIEM. The talk introduces FalconHound, a toolkit that queries Microsoft Sentinel, Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Graph, Neo4j and the BloodHound API on a schedule, writes session relationships into the graph and ages them out.

The speaker, who describes himself as a non-programmer, built the Go tool with AI coding help and cautioned that generated code needs checking and that hosted assistants may retain input. Demos covered a compromised user who sat in nested groups with admin rights to a machine, and a server with a 2020 SQL remote code execution CVE that had a path to tier zero ownership. Other detections flagged new paths to high-value targets, raised alert severity for users near domain admin, and tracked uncommon sessions as possible lateral movement. Scale was a constraint: Neo4j Community Edition is single-threaded, and one large client produced about 5,300 new sessions every 15 minutes.

The recommended cadence is a run every 15 minutes for session data, while full BloodHound and AzureHound collections stay on a weekly to quarterly rhythm because logs miss some directory properties. The speaker noted that object ID handling for the newer BloodHound Community Edition was still in progress.

talks.title: Hacking the IR Team | Gerard Johansen | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Hacking the IR Team | Gerard Johansen | WWHF 2023.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Wild West Hackin' Fest (WWHF) 2023, Gerard Johansen from Red Canary discusses how organizations can break down silos between red teams (offensive testers) and blue teams (incident response/defenders) to drastically improve incident response (IR) capabilities. Johansen argues that traditional security models treat penetration testing as an annual compliance checkbox exercise that leaves immense technical expertise on the table. Instead of jumping directly into complex, expensive annual purple team exercises where teams often fail, he advocates for a structured, year-round continuous training pipeline centered on realistic threat emulation.

### Key Topics
- **Silos and Checkbox Compliance:** Many organizations view security testing through a governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) lens, tightly scoping annual penetration tests to minor vulnerability scans or running Responder. This fails to provide actionable value or prepare defenders for real adversary behaviors.
- **The IR Training Gap:** Incident response training is frequently limited to annual tabletop exercises or costly multi-day offsite boot camps. Because budgets often get cut first in soft markets and technical skills degrade rapidly over months, defenders lack exposure to live adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
- **The "4 Rs" of Training:** Johansen asserts effective IR training must be Realistic (emulating genuine adversary behavior), Relevant (drawing from real threat intelligence like Red Canary's Threat Detection Report or Mandiant M-Trends), Recent (regularly practiced because training decays quickly), and Repetitive (drilled continuously rather than once a year).

### Technical Details & Framework
Johansen outlines a progressive, year-long training framework combining offensive and defensive capabilities:
- **IR Plan Review & Premortem Analysis (1-hour drill):** Engage red team personnel to review incident response and disaster recovery plans, conducting premortem analyses to spot assumptions adversaries could break (e.g., discovering online flat-file backup data lakes that an attacker could easily encrypt).
- **Monthly Detection & Response Micro-Emulations:** Conduct focused, single-technique emulations rather than entire kill chains using tools like Atomic Red Team or Caldera. Examples include testing `rundll32.exe` execution, DLL search order hijacking, LSASS memory dumping, or testing readiness against frameworks like Impacket, Cobalt Strike, or PowerShell Empire.
- **Tabletop Drills & Key Assumptions Checks:** Link discrete micro-emulations into partial kill chains (e.g., executing lateral movement via RDP, SMB, or GoToMyPC, and validating if defenders can locate Event ID 4624 Type 10 logon events and NetFlow artifacts within 10 minutes). Red teams participate in tabletops to challenge flawed managerial assumptions (e.g., proving whether an attacker can eavesdrop on incident response Zoom/WebEx channels).
- **Annual Purple Team Validation:** Conduct a full purple team engagement at the end of the year to validate cumulative progress across patched detective controls, playbook adjustments, and triage response speed.

### Takeaways
- **Continuous Tempo Outweighs Annual Splurges:** Organizations gain far more defensive resilience from continuous, low-cost weekly or monthly micro-emulations than from an isolated annual penetration test.
- **Actionable Metrics for Leadership:** Track technique-level metrics (e.g., mapping results on a MITRE ATT&CK spreadsheet) focusing on detection rate and dwell time/time-to-detect (e.g., flagging tests where activity was undetected after 90 minutes).
- **Mutual Benefits:** Red and blue cross-collaboration exposes defenders to the live attacker mindset and tooling while teaching red teams defensive detection boundaries and EDR telemetry evasion.

talks.title: What The Hack is Going On? An Offensive Look at Modern Breaches | Tim Medin | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Explains how modern breaches start, from stolen credentials and phishing to consent grants, and where defenders should focus.
talks.summary:
Tim Medin looks at modern breaches from the attacker's side. Since pentest reports cannot be shared, he uses the Verizon data breach report as his main source. Most breaches there involve an external attacker, about one in five involve an internal one, and stolen credentials are a leading way in, while exploits rank far lower. He argues that the exploits that do work are often old, long-patched flaws, and that scanner severity ratings push teams toward the wrong fixes.

The middle of the talk covers credentials and social engineering. He criticises 90-day password rotation, complexity rules and predictable patterns, and cites the MGM breach, which began with a phone-based help desk password reset. He describes phishing with convincing pretexts, MFA fatigue from repeated push prompts, and OAuth consent attacks that keep access after passwords and MFA are changed.

For practitioners, the advice is to focus on the data and systems that would hurt the business most, since sensitive data is often reachable without domain admin. Defenders should run offensive tools against their own networks, clean up over-shared files and wrong permissions, enforce MFA everywhere, and speed up detection and response, because breaches will happen.
