talks.title: Tool Shed Demo: Aleph | Corey Ham | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Demonstrates the Aleph tool for indexing and searching breach and ransomware data sets, including entity extraction and mapping.
talks.summary:
Corey Ham opens with why breach and ransomware data sets are hard to use. A leak can run to terabytes and mix tens of thousands of file extensions, so raw volume is useless until the material can be searched. He presents Aleph as a tool built for journalistic work that loads such collections into one searchable index. He notes that plain keyword search cannot read binary formats like PDFs or JPEGs, and that some tools only read the first part of a large file.

The live demo runs the tool in Docker on a laptop, with single-user mode turned on to skip authentication. He creates an investigation, drags in a handful of sample files, and shows the browser view, which displays extracted text, metadata, checksums, and named entities found automatically during import. He searches for a person's name and for a password string, then loads a CSV from the command line. He maps its first name, last name and email columns to person entities so that each row becomes a linked record. He also covers recursive extraction of nested archives, the storage overhead of roughly double the source size, and the option of adding support for unsupported file formats through custom modules.

He closes with a walkthrough of the Ferrari data set from a ransomware leak. He loaded it with no manual parsing and got quick awareness of its contents, including marketing files, a video, and a scanned typed service document that the tool still made searchable. The takeaway is that a single container and a few commands can give an analyst immediate visibility into large, messy and unfamiliar data.

talks.title: Tool Shed Demo: Windows Commander and Exfiltrer (WCE) | Momen Eldawakhly | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Tool Shed Demo: Windows Commander and Exfiltrer (WCE) | Momen Eldawakhly | WWHF 2023.

talks.title: Tool Shed Demo: CTF 101: How to Play and Win | Roman Bohuk | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Explains capture the flag formats and challenge categories, then shows how to approach a basic web challenge step by step.
talks.summary:
This beginner-oriented talk introduces capture the flag competitions to people who have not played before. It first contrasts the main formats: attack-and-defense events, where teams defend their own services in real time while exploiting others, and jeopardy-style contests, where players solve independent challenges for points. Scoring is covered too, including static point values and dynamic scoring, where a challenge's value falls as more teams solve it. The case for practice is that hands-on tasks turn lectures into applied skills and build a habit of looking at how systems work from the inside.

The middle section walks through the common challenge categories. Web exploitation covers issues such as SQL injection, command injection and reading client-side JavaScript for hardcoded values. Cryptography ranges from simple encodings to weak ciphers and custom implementations. Forensics asks players to find traces in artifacts such as packet captures, memory dumps and Windows logs. Open-source reconnaissance involves gathering public information about a target, while reverse engineering and binary exploitation focus on taking programs apart and corrupting memory. Practical tips include reading titles and descriptions closely, starting with the easiest challenges, searching for unfamiliar concepts, and trying unexpected input to see how an application reacts.

The talk closes with a live walkthrough of an easy web login challenge. The presenter views the page source, finds the JavaScript function that checks the credentials, and reads the expected values from the code. The takeaway is that capture the flag events reward curiosity and persistence, and that beginners should not be discouraged when stuck, since many platforms offer free hints.

talks.title: Tool Shed Demo: Token Tactics: A Tactical Usage Demo | Steve Borosh | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Tool Shed Demo: Token Tactics: A Tactical Usage Demo | Steve Borosh | WWHF 2023.

talks.title: Tool Shed Demo: Pre2k | Garrett Foster | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how pre-created Active Directory computer accounts with default passwords can be found and checked over Kerberos.
talks.summary:
Active Directory computer accounts pre-created with the pre-Windows 2000 compatibility option get a default password matching the lowercase host name without the trailing dollar sign. Earlier published work described their markers: a logon count of zero, a UAC value of 4128, and authentication that works only over Kerberos. The speaker's team sprayed a list of about 98,000 computers under a client's rules of engagement and found roughly 1,100 valid machine accounts, some with logon counts above zero. Colleagues running internal tests reported valid accounts in at least seven out of every ten tests.

The talk demonstrated pre2k, a tool for finding and validating these accounts. Its authenticated mode can check every computer object or only those matching the markers, while its unauthenticated mode pulls host names over a null SMB session. Options added threading, sleep and jitter to slow guessing, and a save-and-stop-on-success setting that keeps the Kerberos ticket in the working directory. The speaker also noted that passwords longer than 15 characters are truncated to 14, a fix that raised one run from 1,100 to about 1,900 valid accounts. Accounts created with no password at all were shown to yield valid tickets.

The talk closed with related research: time roasting of computer accounts via NTP hashes, Kerberoasting machine accounts that carry service principal names, and lingering ACLs on pre-created accounts that could enable resource-based constrained delegation abuse. For defenders, the takeaway is to hunt for these accounts using logon count and UAC values and to reset their passwords.

talks.title: GraphRunner | Beau Bullock, Steve Borosh | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: GraphRunner demonstrates M365 post-exploitation via Graph API abuse, permissive defaults, and live privilege-escalation demos.
talks.summary:
The presenters describe GraphRunner as a post-exploitation framework for Microsoft 365 and Entra ID after initial access—typically phishing or stolen credentials—not for gaining that first foothold. It is built mainly in PowerShell, includes OAuth helpers and a minimal GUI, and centers on Microsoft Graph plus some undocumented endpoints such as estimate access for permission enumeration.

The talk walks through authentication via device code and app registrations, reconnaissance of tenant settings and conditional access, and offensive use of default policies that let users create groups, invite guests, and register apps. Demos cover joining updatable and public groups for Teams and SharePoint access, abusing dynamic membership rules, cloning security groups for watering-hole style deception, guest-based persistence, illicit consent and injected OAuth apps, shared mailbox discovery, and data extraction from mail, Teams, SharePoint, and OneDrive—including bypassing download blocks with immersive reader and Snaffler-style file hunting.

Practitioners are shown how Graph API power and permissive defaults enable privilege escalation, long-lived persistence through refresh tokens and app registrations, and quiet pillaging without marking mail as read. The session closes with public release of the tool on GitHub, a long blog write-up, and cloud pentest cheat sheet resources.

talks.title: Empowering the CS Workforce | Gerald Auger, James McQuiggan | WWHF 2023
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Empowering the CS Workforce | Gerald Auger, James McQuiggan | WWHF 2023.

talks.title: The Rita Award for Deadwood 2023 goes to...
talks.teaser: The segment recounts the Rita Award's roots and recognizes a member whose optimism and service echo its namesake.
talks.summary:
The segment introduces the Rita Award, named after the presenter's mother Rita, who helped shape Black Hills Information Security early on and was remembered for unflappable optimism and habitual help for others, from church community work to volunteering the family for moves and service projects. The speaker describes how that attitude echoed widely after her death, including a packed memorial in Rapid City, and how acquaintances often say she reminds them of their own relatives.

Each year the conference seeks someone who embodies the same spirit inside the information security community. The talk references educators and mentors who act as steady positive forces, including figures such as the Cyber Mentor and John Hammond, before turning to the current honoree.

The closing moment recognizes Gerald with applause as the recipient who carries forward that example of encouragement and community care. Listeners gain context on a recurring Wild West Hackin' Fest tradition rather than defensive techniques; the takeaway is how the event spotlights character and generosity alongside technical work.

talks.title: Closing Ceremony | John Strand | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Closing Ceremony | John Strand | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: I’m a Security Charlatan & So Are You | John Hammond | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for I’m a Security Charlatan & So Are You | John Hammond | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Backdoors and Breaches Live Demo | Jason Blanchard | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: A live tabletop walkthrough shows how attack and procedure cards train incident response teams through randomized breach scenarios.
talks.summary:
The session introduces Backdoors and Breaches, a card-based tabletop game meant to teach compromise chains and defender workflows without heavy prep. The presenter explains how red attack cards summarize initial access, pivot and escalation, command and control, and persistence, each pairing brief technique descriptions with realistic detection ideas and pen-test tooling references. A free online version lets remote teams run the same exercises.

Volunteers act as an incident response team facing a fictional help-desk escalation: an accountant installed software after a caller impersonated IT weeks earlier. Using blue procedure cards such as endpoint protection analysis, server analysis, network threat hunting, and endpoint analysis, they roll dice to see whether each step succeeds. Established written procedures grant modifiers; critical rolls inject chaos events that remove capabilities. The demo surfaces Active Directory weaponization early, while other chosen procedures fail for operational reasons the group must articulate.

The revealed chain combines social engineering, Active Directory abuse, domain-fronted command and control, and logon-script persistence. The closing lesson is to judge whether that bundle could happen locally, then drive mitigations, acceptance of risk, or further study when the answer is uncertain.

talks.title: Tool Demo - Locksmith | Jake Hildreth | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Introduces Locksmith, a script that finds risky AD Certificate Services settings and generates fixes for them.
talks.summary:
Active Directory Certificate Services is Microsoft's built-in public key infrastructure, easy to deploy and just as easy to misconfigure. The speaker focuses on abuse of certificate-based authentication, starting with disabled auditing, which he says he has never seen fully enabled across assessments. Other recurring problems are overly permissive access control lists and certificate templates that let low-privileged users supply a subject alternative name, a single step toward domain compromise. He also describes a certificate authority flag that changes template behavior, partly mitigated since May.

Locksmith scans an ADCS forest and reports findings, then goes further by helping fix them. Its basic mode runs as a normal user and exports results to a CSV file. A second mode outputs a one-line remediation for each finding, such as removing manager approval from a template or resetting dangerous flags and restarting the service. A third mode applies the changes when run with elevated rights on the certificate authority hosts. ACL remediation was still unfinished at the time of the talk.

Planned work includes a menu, better error handling, multi-forest support, alerts for missing auditing group policies, and an elevation check before fixes are attempted. In questions, the speaker argued that manager approval is the least disruptive fix, though it adds work for PKI administrators, and that limiting who can enroll in risky templates would help most. The takeaway is to audit first and change risky templates carefully, since fixes can disrupt certificate-dependent services.

talks.title: Tool Demo - Sirius Scan & Nmap Scripting Engine | Matthew Toussain | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Tool Demo - Sirius Scan & Nmap Scripting Engine | Matthew Toussain | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Tool Demo - KERnano | Ash Noor | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows an offline, no-install Python multi-tool with wordlist, Base64, URL checking and pentest command helpers.
talks.summary:
The speaker presents KERnano, a no-install Python multi-tool for Windows and Linux that bundles about ten utilities collected from tools used during CTFs and engagements. It was built so the tester could work offline and carry everything in one portable program, without depending on web-based utilities.

The demo starts with the Word Lister, which extracts the text from a two-page PDF and then produces a list of unique words with special characters and numbers removed. Next, an offline Base64 decoder is used on an encoded string, and a leetspeak tool converts a phrase back to plain text. The URL checker then reads a text file of three addresses, reports which ones are live, notes whether each has SSL enabled, and writes the HTTPS and HTTP sites to separate output files. One entry in the list was not a valid site, and the checker treated it as such.

The helper tool asks for a target IP and the tester's own IP, then writes a text file of commonly used commands for nmap, gobuster, Hydra, reverse shells and a Python HTTP server with those addresses already inserted. The speaker says this saved a few minutes of manual editing on every engagement. The tool is open source on GitHub, and the speaker mentions that some rough edges are still being worked on. The practical takeaway is a portable, offline toolkit for repetitive pentest tasks, with the source available to review.

talks.title: WORKSHOP: Advanced Passive DNS Search Techniques for Cyber Investigations | DomainTools | WWHF '22
talks.teaser: Shows how to pivot through passive DNS data using time fencing, wildcards and regex for investigations.
talks.summary:
This hands-on workshop introduces passive DNS as an investigation tool and explains how it differs from ordinary DNS lookups. Passive DNS records observations collected above recursive resolvers at cache misses, which makes it possible to go from an IP address to the domains that pointed at it over time, and from a name server or record value to related domains. The speaker walks through the DNSDB dataset and the Scout web interface, with attendees using API keys issued for the session.

The exercises start with standard searches by record type and the difference between left-hand and right-hand matching. Participants pivot from name servers, SOA contact emails, and SPF and DKIM values in TXT records to find domains that appear unrelated but share infrastructure. Wildcard subdomain enumeration is used to find lookalike login domains tied to phishing, and the speaker shows how public zones can expose internal IP addresses. Advanced options are covered next: time fencing to narrow results to an incident window, offsets for paging through large result sets, and de-aggregation to see how observation counts change over time, such as spikes that match a campaign.

The later section covers flexible search with keyword, glob and POSIX regular expression queries that match any label in a name. Examples include enumerating domain generation algorithm patterns and searching for brand names embedded in domains or text records. The speaker advises anchoring expressions, starting in standard search and pivoting, and using the command-line client for larger result sets. The main takeaway is that passive DNS adds enumeration and correlation value for threat hunting and red teaming, but its results carry no risk scoring, so analysts must judge what they find.

talks.title: What’s up Breaches! | Mishaal Khan | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Explores how investigators mine breach data to pivot identities, validate targets, and adopt layered privacy defenses.
talks.summary:
The presentation treats breach collections as a practical engine for digital investigations rather than password-check curiosities. It groups leaks, scrapes, hosted search portals, locally stored dumps, and stealer logs, arguing that full-field breach files beat redacted web lookups when you need phones, plates, addresses, and similar pivots beyond credentials.

Demonstrations move from Have I Been Pwned into local ripgrep over DriveSure and ParkMobile, correlating VINs and plates with decoders and state sites, resolving LinkedIn member IDs to emails via breach files and a People Data Labs API demo, and noting discovery paths such as Shodan for Elasticsearch, open S3 search, WHOIS-history breaches, password reuse to surface hidden accounts, and stealer packages with cookies, screenshots, and resumes. The speaker stresses safe acquisition, malware risk, and multi-terabyte storage, and contrasts vehicle data in parking apps with public records for attribution.

The close shifts to layered privacy—alias inboxes, MFA, unique passwords, virtual cards, opt-outs, and self-audits—and points listeners to OperationPrivacy.com. Audience questions cover rejected burner contacts, third-party APIs on payment masking services, and how intent and role affect handling stolen breach data.

talks.title: API Security Through External Attack Surface Management Phillip Wylie | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of API Security Through External Attack Surface Management Phillip Wylie | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Adversary Emulation or How I Learned to Stop Being Polite and Get Real Results | Adam & Katie
talks.teaser: Compares red team testing habits with real threat actor behavior and offers ways to make adversary emulation more realistic.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many offensive security exercises are shaped by goals that differ from how real threat actors operate. It reviews common testing approaches such as assumed compromise and penetration testing, and places them alongside the Pyramid of Pain and MITRE ATT&CK. The speakers note that climbing those models does not automatically make an exercise realistic, because real adversaries pursue intent such as theft or destruction, and techniques serve that goal.

A trade-off model of accurate, fast and inexpensive testing follows, where teams can usually choose only two. Next, detection data from a managed detection provider is compared across confirmed tests and confirmed malicious activity. Tools such as Empire, BloodHound and Metasploit showed up more often in testing, while reflective code loading, AutoIt, JavaScript and encoded PowerShell appeared more in criminal activity. Testers also tended to fire bursts of discovery commands in short windows, and some obscure living-off-the-land binaries were seen almost only in tests.

For solutions, the speakers recommend agreeing on goals, speed, accuracy and cost before an engagement, and deciding which behaviors matter to the organization. They suggest treating public test libraries as starting points that can be chained together, and using threat intelligence from internal incidents and external reporting to pick realistic behaviors. They close by urging testers to vary tooling, tempo and techniques so exercises better resemble real adversaries.

talks.title: The Ethics of Digital Surveillance | Kathryn Carnell | Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Examines how data brokers and everyday tracking erode user privacy, and what companies can do about it.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a cybersecurity instructor, treats user privacy as an ethics question rather than a compliance checklist. She argues that the internet grew out of a government and research setting, so its early norms about collecting user information never anticipated today's personal, everyday use. Many users, she says, do not realise how much of their activity is gathered and linked together.

The middle of the talk focuses on data brokers. She describes the kinds of details they aggregate, from contact information and purchases to health interests and real-time location, and cites figures such as roughly 4,000 brokerage companies worldwide and one firm said to hold data on 500 million consumers. Case examples include AOL's 2006 release of search logs that exposed one user, the stalking death of Amy Boyer after a broker sold her email address, and the marketing firm Epsilon, which faced charges over facilitating elder fraud schemes. She also covers family location sharing in Life360 and a Dutch review of Google Analytics.

She closes with practical mitigations: transparent, ongoing consent and opt-out options, short privacy statements that are easy to read, and collaboration between security, legal and design teams so users understand what is collected. Her message to practitioners is to raise these issues inside their own companies before lawmakers write rules without technical input.

talks.title: Less SmartScreen More Caffeine - ClickOnce AbUse for Trusted Code Execution | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse trusted ClickOnce deployments and signed .NET assemblies to run code while avoiding SmartScreen prompts.
talks.summary:
Nick Powers and Steven Flores examine ClickOnce, a Windows deployment technology for .NET applications, as an initial access option. They explain how the deployment and application manifests control installation, and why a freshly built unsigned payload tends to trigger SmartScreen, application control and endpoint analysis. They also note that EV code signing grants immediate reputation but is costly and vetted, and that a reused signing certificate can later link an operator's payloads together.

The main technique is to find signed ClickOnce deployments already in circulation, decompile them and backdoor a dependency that is not strongly named, or use app domain manager injection, so the host signature stays intact. Integrity fields in the manifests can be nulled or removed, and Mage can generate fresh manifests. The speakers then show that an arbitrary .NET assembly can be wrapped as a deployment when its embedded application manifest lacks the assembly identity line, a check in system.deployment.dll that never matches because processor architecture is missing. A demo ran code inside a Microsoft-signed assembly, and they released Assembly Hunter and ClickOnce Hunter to automate searching for candidates.

For defenders, the closing section suggests monitoring dfsvc.exe child processes and unsigned module loads, baselining the local app data location where ClickOnce applications are stored, and flagging uncommon signed applications that make internet connections. Group Policy or registry settings can also block ClickOnce from running files downloaded from the internet zone.

talks.title: Pentesting Azure Container Services | Sergey Chubarov | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers reuse cached Kubernetes credentials and tamper with Azure container images to reach other containers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short tour of Azure's container services: a registry for images, Container Instances for small standalone workloads, and AKS for Kubernetes. The first attack path is simple. Cached Kubernetes credentials on a developer or administrator workstation can be copied to another machine, which then reaches the cluster without any login.

A second path chains several misconfigurations. With overly broad pull and push rights on a registry, an attacker can download an image, unpack its layers, add a preloaded library that opens a reverse shell, update the recorded file hash, and push it back under the latest tag. A test instance started from that image connected back as expected. Inside a Kubernetes pod, the service account token could read some API groups but not go deeper, and scanning the internal network revealed a database accepting connections without authentication.

Mitigations covered restricting push and pull rights, limiting registry access through private links or IP allowlists, and using separate hardened admin workstations. Content trust can require signed images, and vulnerability scanning catches outdated software, though not a deliberately planted payload. Running without root and applying network policies keeps containers isolated from one another by default.

talks.title: Getting the most out of Sysmon | Amanda Berlin | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how free Sysmon telemetry reveals credential dumping, NTDS theft and Exchange compromises, and how to test detections.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a ransomware case in which a PsExec command ran over a VPN and the victim had almost no logs. Domain controllers were not sending Windows logs, and a shared admin account lacked multi-factor authentication. The speaker argues that Sysmon, a free Microsoft tool, records far richer process, network and registry activity than default Windows logging, so it should be installed before an incident.

Several cases show which event IDs reveal each technique. Credential dumping through the comsvcs.dll MiniDump export appears in process creation events. Extracting the NTDS.dit database with ntdsutil shows up across process creation, process access and registry events. A COMSPEC variable paired with an encoded PowerShell command is tied to a registry change, and remote thread creation exposes injection. In an Exchange ProxyLogon compromise, IIS spawning PowerShell served as an indicator, supported by domain admin enumeration and a web client download string. Statistical outlier analysis across customer data and MITRE ATT&CK mapping in Vector with Atomic Red Team tests round out the detection-building approach.

The closing advice is to audit logging gaps, deploy Sysmon with a modular configuration and a log shipper across endpoints, and retest detections regularly, since rules, parsers and agents can quietly break.

talks.title: WORKSHOP: Threat Hunting using Active and Passive DNS | DomainTools | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for WORKSHOP: Threat Hunting using Active and Passive DNS | DomainTools | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Is the PKI sky falling? | Rick Davis | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: ADCS and PKI attack research maps misconfigurations to monitoring, HSM use, and assessment practices for enterprises.
talks.summary:
Public key infrastructure stayed out of the spotlight for years, but a dense wave of research and tooling since roughly 2020 changed that picture for Windows enterprises. The session walks a timeline from PKINIT certificate abuse and user-controlled keys through Will Schroeder’s AD CS white paper, which cataloged escalation paths such as misconfigured templates, vulnerable PKI objects in Active Directory, SAN abuse, CA ACL mistakes, and NTLM relay against certificate services. Follow-on work turned theory into repeatable chains: PetitPotam-style relay against vulnerable HTTP endpoints on ancillary AD CS roles, and later Certifried-style spoofing tied to machine naming and template fields, with patches requiring coordinated updates on every domain controller and enterprise CA.

On the offensive side, the speaker ties those findings to a small set of tools that cover template enumeration, Kerberos and smart-card abuse, and end-to-end AD CS exploitation in Python and other ecosystems. The through-line is that most issues are misconfiguration rather than novel code bugs, yet they routinely lead to domain-scale compromise comparable to losing a domain controller or the CA’s private key—the “golden certificate” scenario.

Practitioners are urged to inventory forgotten CAs and AD objects, document the environment, and treat PKI as tier-zero infrastructure with DR and business continuity planning. Defense guidance covers enabling CA and object-access auditing in both places it is required, monitoring Cert Publishers and CA admin groups, template change events, and registry edits on CAs and ancillary IIS-based roles, plus HSM protection for CA keys, administrative tiering, training for security operations and incident responders, and hands-on assessments rather than checkbox reviews.

talks.title: Gone In 60 {Seconds,Minutes,Hours} Learning from 3 live, realistic end-to-end breaches | WWHF '22
talks.teaser: Follows three live, end-to-end breaches from exposed spreadsheets to Exchange exploitation and a phone-based domain takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through three end-to-end breaches, each staged live, to show how real attackers differ from the scripted behavior of many penetration tests. The first breach needed no exploit: a search of an index of publicly exposed cloud storage turned up a spreadsheet holding student IDs, Social Security numbers and dates of birth, which opened with a plain download.

The second breach targeted on-premises Exchange servers exposed to ProxyNotShell. A scan found many unmitigated hosts, and an exploit script used credentials from combined breach data to gain code execution. The speaker then used a built-in Windows transfer tool to fetch a payload that altered the boot loader. The third breach started with a phone call that talked an employee into opening Quick Assist and sharing a six-digit code. The attacker used built-in OpenSSH to build a SOCKS proxy into the network, cracked a Kerberoastable service account hash offline, reached a domain controller over RDP, and pushed a Group Policy script that forced BitLocker encryption at reboot.

The takeaways are that attackers often rely on simple, scalable methods, so internet-facing services and single-factor remote access deserve priority. Severity scores alone are a weak guide; the speaker suggested asking whether a flaw gives an attacker a shell and whether an exploit exists. Defenders should restrict remote assistance tools, watch for unusual use of built-in administrative commands, deploy canary tokens, and pair prevention with detection and response.

talks.title: Tool Demo - BBOT | The Techromancer | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: A demo-heavy session shows how BBOT runs recursive OSINT—subdomains, ports, screenshots, and Nuclei—in a single pipeline.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces BBOT, a Python command-line OSINT framework from Black Lantern Security aimed at penetration tests and bug bounties. It is positioned as hacker-focused alternative to SpiderFoot, installable via pip, with more than sixty modules and recursive workflows: each discovered asset triggers the same modules again on that asset within defined scope.

Most of the session is live demonstration against SpaceX-related targets. Examples include a minimal HTTP probe that collects DNS and link data, automatic download of module dependencies through Ansible, simultaneous output to text, JSON, CSV, and Neo4j, graph visualization of relationships between domains, web spidering that surfaces paths and secrets, subdomain enumeration paired with technology fingerprinting, and GoWitness screenshots. The speaker describes scope controls such as strict mode and scope distance, cites a benchmark where BBOT reported more subdomains than common tools for a medium-sized company domain, and notes Nuclei integration plus custom web modules, including a recent engagement where operators obtained shells via a Telerik-related module.

Practitioners should leave with a picture of one-command OSINT that replaces phased manual runs, optional Neo4j for relationship analysis, and configuration hooks for depth, targets, and scan naming.

talks.title: Adversaries Rising Looking Ahead in Security | Dave Kennedy | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Adversaries Rising Looking Ahead in Security | Dave Kennedy | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: The Complete GRC Analyst Day in the Life | Gerald Auger, PhD | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Complete GRC Analyst Day in the Life | Gerald Auger, PhD | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Writing Ransomware for Kicks | Joff Thyer | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through building a simulated ransomware tool with fake data, IOC profiles and a Discord-controlled remote bot.
talks.summary:
Customers often ask red teams to emulate ransomware during assumed-compromise tests, but encrypting real production data is a hard sell. This talk covers a Go tool built for ransomware simulation that recursively encrypts and decrypts files, generates fake directories and documents containing made-up personal-looking details, and can be driven remotely.

Files are encrypted with a random AES key, which is itself protected with RSA, and SHA-256 hashes of the originals are stored in SQLite so decryption can confirm each file. Keys are written to disk, into alternate data streams on Windows, as a challenge for defenders. To mimic real families, the speaker added indicator profiles in YAML built from public malware samples, with URL and command entries that only run harmlessly. Endpoint protection quarantined the plain profile, so it was stored encrypted instead.

The live demo generated fake data, encrypted it with a ransom page, decrypted it with hash checks, and then issued commands through a Discord bot. The closing advice is to use the tool only on scoped, authorized engagements, keep the keys, and test restores, since restores matter more than backups.

talks.title: Security Exclusions, Endpoint Controls, and You | Jake Williams | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Security Exclusions, Endpoint Controls, and You | Jake Williams | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Connor McGarr | “Hey Cortana - Do We Still Care About Binary Exploitation?" | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Surveys how Windows mitigations like CFG, CET, ACG and HVCI have reshaped exploitation and why red teams use it less.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why binary exploitation has become less common in red team work on modern Windows. It starts with the early years, when stack overflows could be exploited with hard-coded addresses in memory that was readable, writable and executable. It then covers DEP and ASLR, which pushed attackers toward code reuse and information leaks, and notes that exploitation volume still peaked around 2010, years after those defenses arrived.

The middle section examines defenses against control-flow hijacking. Control Flow Guard checks indirect calls against a bitmap of valid targets, but it allows exported functions and so can be bypassed. Extended Flow Guard adds prototype hashing to narrow this, though it currently falls back to CFG. For return addresses, the hardware shadow stack in Intel CET compares the stack copy against a protected copy, replacing the abandoned software RFG. For shellcode, Arbitrary Code Guard blocks writable-executable memory in user mode, and HVCI applies similar rules in the kernel, enforced by the hypervisor through extended page tables. The speaker also shows how a data-only attack can copy the SYSTEM token into a command shell, and how kernel data protection guards some static and dynamic data.

The closing takeaway is that these mitigations make exploitation tedious. Attackers must build payloads from return-oriented programming or rely on data-only corruption, which is harder for EDR to flag, so red team research has shifted toward C2 frameworks and social engineering. The mitigations are free on supported hardware, though ACG adoption is limited by JIT engines and poorly written drivers.

talks.title: Tool Demo - DolosJS | Forrest Kasler | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Tool Demo - DolosJS | Forrest Kasler | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Tool Demo - Vajra - Your Weapon To Cloud | Raunak Parmar | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Demos an open-source framework for enumerating and attacking Azure and AWS environments, from user discovery to OAuth phishing.
talks.summary:
Vajra is an open-source framework for enumerating and attacking cloud environments, named after the weapon of Lord Indra. At the time of the talk it supported Azure and AWS, with Google Cloud support planned. Because the session was 20 minutes long, only part of the feature set was shown live.

On the Azure side, enumeration modules check valid usernames and subdomains and list Azure AD and resource management data, while attack modules cover phishing, password spraying and brute force. In the demo, an access token from the Azure CLI was used to pull Azure AD users, roles, groups and owners, which could be exported to Excel. The phishing module displayed mail and OneDrive files from a consented victim account, and a refresh token allowed repeated access. For password spraying, the speaker advised trying fewer than ten passwords per account, since Microsoft locks accounts by default at ten attempts. A container finder listed publicly readable storage files.

For AWS, the tool enumerates IAM users, groups, roles and policies from access keys, and lists storage, compute and network resources; Lambda source code can be downloaded where the key has permission. An S3 scanner finds public buckets from a wordlist, and a misconfiguration review run with a security audit role reported 49 checks passed and 59 failed in the demo. The talk ended with a note that GCP support and some phishing setup steps were left to documentation. The takeaway is a tool for auditing cloud accounts and reviewing identity and access settings.

talks.title: Tool Demo - Riverside | Kaitlyn DeValk | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Tool Demo - Riverside | Kaitlyn DeValk | WWHF Deadwood 2022.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk at WWHF Deadwood 2022, Kaitlyn DeValk presents Riverside, an open-source network security visualization tool she began developing during her Master's in Computer Science at the University of Maryland. Drawing from her background as a U.S. Coast Guard officer conducting penetration testing, vulnerability assessments, and red teaming at Coast Guard Cyber Command, DeValk discusses the persistent challenge of outdated, static network maps and the lack of accessible visualization tools outside expensive commercial software. Riverside was created as a proof-of-concept to offer real-time and historical network visibility through an interactive graphical interface.

### Key Topics
- **User-Informed Interface Design**: DeValk conducted interviews with network administrators and security analysts to understand user preferences, gathering feedback on diagram layouts (node-link diagrams, hierarchical views, and tabular formats).
- **Architecture and Data Ingestion**: The system relies on standalone Golang agents running packet capture via Berkeley Packet Filters (BPF) and deep packet inspection (DPI) to extract netflow data. Data is forwarded via gRPC to a Golang server, stored in PostgreSQL, and communicated to a JavaScript front end via WebSockets.
- **Interactive Temporal Visualization**: A dynamic timeline tracks real-time traffic while allowing users to scrub backward to inspect historical network states.
- **Visual Encoding and Customization**: Network nodes and edges visually reflect operational metadata, including protocol-based edge coloring, communication duration, frequency-based node transparency, and analyst customization.

### Technical Details
- **Backend & Communication**: Both the agents and the central server are written in Go. Agents capture network traffic similarly to tcpdump, requiring elevated permissions, and communicate with the server over gRPC (tested locally on port 1533). Configurations are handled via YAML files. The server uses the Gin framework for API and session management, while an ORM facilitates database management with PostgreSQL (deployed via Docker). Data models include tables for hosts (agents), remote hosts, and netflow records.
- **Packet Inspection**: The agent uses the `go-dpi` library for deep packet inspection to classify protocols (tracking roughly 12 protocols, such as DNS colored purple, SSL/HTTPS colored green, SMB, FTP, and RDP, falling back to gray/unknown if unclassified).
- **Visual Representation**: Agent nodes are differentiated from remote nodes (which default to gray). Edges show directionality (single or double-sided arrows) and throughput. Edges widen as continuous communication persists. Nodes incorporate a transparency mechanic where frequently communicating hosts fade, making rarer or newer connections stand out. Users can modify node labels, shapes, and colors during incident triage.
- **Compatibility**: Agents were tested across operating systems including Windows 10, Windows 11, Linux (Ubuntu, Kali, Pop!_OS), and within virtual machine environments.

### Takeaways & Future Work
Riverside is presented as a supportive tool to augment network visibility rather than a complete replacement for security toolsets. While the backend and binaries were released on GitHub, planned enhancements include front-end data filtering, visual timeline stamping for investigator actions, automated clustering for network segmentation, integration with external threat intelligence APIs (such as GreyNoise), and testing at larger enterprise network scales.

talks.title: Tool Demo - SWAIN AtlasSuite | Andrew Heishman | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Presents a free Microsoft 365 tool that searches, purges and blocks phishing email using Purview content search.
talks.summary:
Andrew Heishman presents Swain, a free, open-source command-line program for Microsoft 365 that lets small and mid-sized teams search, purge and block email during an incident. Drawing on his experience in healthcare, banking and manufacturing, he explains why many shops struggle with email response: inherited hardware limits, multiple login portals, restrictive tool rules and weak search syntax.

Swain drives Microsoft Purview's Content Search, normally used for e-discovery, through PowerShell cmdlets. Users run a search with around 30 to 35 parameters, including sender, recipient, subject and attachment name, and wildcards catch campaigns that vary their sender strings. A purge can be soft, moving messages to users' deleted-items folders, or hard, moving them into the Exchange Online quarantine where retention later removes them. A separate option adds addresses to the tenant block list. Authentication uses Microsoft's own MFA prompts rather than locally stored credentials.

Requirements are an Exchange Online mailbox and an E3 license, with no need for E5 or Defender. The e-discovery manager role covers search and purge, and the Security Administrator role is needed for blocking. The speaker reported purging about 1200 emails in four minutes. In questions, he acknowledged that the tool has no technical control separating who can search from who can purge, a concern in larger organisations, though roles can be assigned separately. He presents it as a quick win for one-person shops.
