talks.title: Six Things No One !@#$%^& Told Me About Pentesting | Jason Downey | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Offers a pentester's candid career lessons on reporting, imposter syndrome, Active Directory skills and client trust.
talks.summary:
Jason Downey, a consultant at Red Siege, presents six lessons from his first years as a penetration tester after moving into security from network engineering. He starts with how early work tends to go badly, how entry-level postings and imposter feelings discourage newcomers, and why prior experience from networking, development or sysadmin roles still adds value. He argues that even experienced testers cannot master every domain, so specializing and playing to existing strengths matter more than trying to know everything.

The middle of the talk covers what the work looks like in practice. In one internal engagement, a domain controller that had not been patched since 2017 was found within hours of starting. In another, a client wanted to know whether its customer service process could stop money being withdrawn, and the speaker obtained funds using a colleague's name and publicly available details, which required long waits on hold with the bank. He stresses that real environments rely on Active Directory and multi-step kill chains rather than single-box puzzles. He recommends learning networking fundamentals, password spraying, recon, and practicing in home labs such as Game of Active Directory and DetectionLab, plus comparing command and control frameworks. He also urges writing reports as you go, respecting scope and rules of engagement, especially in hospitals, and understanding a client's environment early.

He closes by noting that red and blue teams share the same goal of making environments safer, and that reputation, friendships and relationships with clients shape a career in the field.

talks.title: How I Was Bored One Night and Found Two CVEs | Joe Helle | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through finding web vulnerabilities in open-source projects and filing them as CVEs to build a security career.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that entry-level security roles are hard to reach and that certifications and blogs have lost their signal as more people earn them. A published CVE, in contrast, shows initiative, a repeatable research method, and the ability to communicate with vendors. The talk began as a spare-time project aimed at helping mentees get into penetration testing.

The method starts with picking open-source projects that can be installed locally, such as desktop applications or Docker-based tools, and staying within your own systems administration skills. In one example, a hotel management application produced reflected cross-site scripting and several SQL injection issues in under an hour, tested with Burp Suite Pro and then with a free alternative. The speaker then covered the disclosure path. Before filing, check whether the vendor is a CVE Numbering Authority, since those vendors handle their own CVEs. Notify the maintainer first, confirm the issue is not already known, and request an identifier from MITRE with a public reference. For GitHub repositories, a bug bounty platform that acts as a CNA can manage the process, and the speaker described a Rails rate-limit bypass found in the Rack Attack library that way.

The closing advice was to treat CVEs as proof of work that employers can see, to publish the write-up, and to help others follow the same path. The question period covered contract developers, what happens when a vendor disputes a finding, and how security policies on repositories make disclosure easier.

talks.title: Building an Unlicensed 802 11 Particle Accelerator | Travis Kaun | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Blends a Ghostbusters proton prop with rogue APs, wand-driven spectrum scans, deauths, and WPA handshake capture for portable Wi-Fi testing.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes turning a Spirit Halloween replica proton pack into a portable wireless test rig he calls the Pontoon pack. After a Christmas gift sparked interest from his kids, roughly three months of soldering and microcontroller experimentation added servos, displays, and attack hardware without a fixed blueprint—mostly learning Arduino basics and power management along the way.

Under the shell sit a Mark 7 Wi‑Fi Pineapple for rogue and evil‑twin access points, a Raspberry Pi driving an e‑ink interface, Pwnagotchi-derived handshake harvesting with customized quotes, and a detachable wand with its own microcontroller for real-time 2.4 GHz spectrum views, target selection, and deauthentication on both 2.4 and 5 GHz. High-gain and Yagi antennas, dual 12 V and 5 V supplies with rocker switches, and a themed skin round out the build; he also points builders to Wokwi for wiring practice before soldering.

A recorded walkthrough shows busy-channel graphs, picking targets such as a local DMG network, entering deauth mode, and capturing reauthentication handshakes for offline cracking. Shipping damage left some antennas and displays inoperable at show time, but the talk frames the pack as a hands-on bridge between hobby electronics and familiar Pineapple-style workflows practitioners already use in the field.

talks.title: Honey, I Shrunk the Perimeter | Ian Garrett | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Explains why classic network perimeters fail today and how to shift toward visibility, identity, and per-asset controls.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that castle-and-moat perimeter security no longer matches how people and data actually move. Remote and hybrid work, cloud and SaaS sprawl, BYOD, and countless vendor and HR tools mean infrastructure and sensitive information often sit outside any clear network boundary, with many unknown ingress and egress paths.

Citing breach-cost research, the speaker notes that a large share of incidents stem from internal IT failures, human error, and supply-chain exposure rather than classic external perimeter breaks. Once an attacker passes the edge—often via phishing—flat internal trust enables lateral movement across devices and accounts while inward-only malicious activity never triggers perimeter-focused tools. Insider risk is framed less as deliberate spies than over-broad permissions and everyday accidental data spillage. Partnerships and integrations extend access beyond questionnaires alone, and data loss prevention is criticized when deployed as an expensive, slow first line rather than a late-stage control.

Practical direction centers on defense in depth, internal visibility, and shrinking the logical perimeter by securing networks, devices, applications, data, and users as distinct assets. Identity should gate each access decision, with granular rights down to individual files where possible, plus consistent internal logging. The closing emphasis is pairing visibility with control at the most specific asset level organizations can sustain.

talks.title: Campfire Talk | You’re Not Broken…Just Different Don’t Let Undiagnosed Neurodivergence Ruin You
talks.teaser: Highlights undiagnosed neurodivergence, risky self-medication, and how infosec leaders can foster safer, more productive workplaces.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames neurodiversity as brains that operate outside a medical “normal” baseline, noting that a large share of people—especially in security—may be undiagnosed. Drawing on decades without a label, he describes how untreated ADHD, anxiety, and depression fed self-sabotage, strained relationships, and escalating alcohol use until a 2017 crisis led to therapy, psychiatry, and formal diagnoses at age 48.

He contrasts feeling “broken” with being “beautifully different,” emphasizing skills plus medication where appropriate, hyperfocus as a usable strength, and weekly therapy even when things seem fine. Online screening tools, specialists who work with ADHD and autism, and peer communities on social media are offered as starting points. He also warns that masking and informal coping wear people down, and that late-life dismissal—“you’ve learned to cope”—misses the cost of those masks.

For managers, he urges psychologically safe teams: flexible schedules, sensory-aware workspaces, mental health days without interrogation, and openness about struggles. He cites higher output from supported autistic hires and shares how disclosure at a new employer enabled honest bad days. The close covers AA sobriety tokens, conference craving triggers, and Q&A on stigma, self-diagnosis, women’s underdiagnosis, and resources such as neurodiversityhub.org and Psychology Today therapist search.

talks.title: Incident Response Playbook Perfection | Amanda Berlin & Jeremby Mio | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Incident Response Playbook Perfection | Amanda Berlin & Jeremby Mio | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Resume Writing Workshop | Kip Boyle, Frank Victory, & Joshua Mason | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how to tailor a security resume to a job description, get past applicant tracking systems, and win an interview.
talks.summary:
The session is aimed at people working in or moving into cybersecurity who want their resumes to lead to an interview. The panel argues that a resume has one job: to get the hiring manager to start a conversation. They describe applicant tracking systems as the first filter, suggest that free online resume simulators can show how a document will be read, and recommend plain, machine-readable formatting with no tables or columns. The opening should be a headline and a short summary that states the role being sought and the value offered.

The middle of the talk treats tailoring as necessary work rather than optional polish. Speakers advise mirroring the wording of each job description honestly, using the employer's own job titles, and writing a certification equivalent in parentheses when a requested credential is missing. Old or irrelevant history, extra degrees and long lists of tools with no context should be cut, and the resume should stay within one or two pages, with a longer version held back for when someone asks. Every claim should be something the candidate can explain in an interview, because interviewers often question resume entries directly.

The workshop then moved to live reviews of resumes brought by attendees and sent in by remote participants. Feedback focused on turning vague duties into impact statements tied to the posting, such as stating the number of clients or alerts handled and the outcome, and on moving self-study like lab exercises into an experience section with the tools used. The takeaway for practitioners is to be truthful, targeted and easy to skim, and to treat the resume as a first work product that shows how the candidate will do the job.

talks.title: Thanks For The Memories Why I Am Leaving Information Security | Douglas Brush | WWHF Deadwood
talks.teaser: Reflects on three decades in information security, the reasons for stepping away, and how to plan a career exit well.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why the speaker, after roughly 30 years in IT and security, has decided to leave the profession. The decision is presented as a considered change rather than anger or cynicism. The speaker traces a path from home computers in the early 1980s and online bulletin boards to computer repair, forensic testimony in court, and leading penetration testing and incident response teams, then asks what should define a career once job titles fall away.

The middle of the talk covers the strain behind the decision, including a business unit closing, a divorce, a serious car accident and the deaths of several family members and friends, which made the speaker rethink working until burnout. Several industry frustrations follow: symptoms get treated rather than root causes, hiring filters out capable people with non-technical backgrounds, and tool sprawl adds cost and risk without reducing workload. Vendor cold outreach and conference habits are criticized as wasteful.

To close, the speaker outlines a plan of taking time off, finishing one more engagement, and leaving the field within a few years, working backward from a chosen end point. The advice to the audience is to take regular breaks, plan an exit early, make new mistakes, and tackle bigger problems such as water scarcity rather than repeating the same fixes.

talks.title: Roll for Stealth Intro to AV EDR Evasion | Mike Saunders | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through practical ways to get payloads past AV and EDR static checks, including strings, entropy, and compiler optimization.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces how antivirus and EDR products flag payloads before they run, focusing on the static stage when a file is written to disk or loaded into memory. The speaker sets aside runtime evasion, unhooking and command-and-control traffic obfuscation, and concentrates on brittle signatures triggered by default templates, variable and function names, suspicious strings, and DLL import declarations.

Several fixes are demonstrated. Renaming imported functions through an entry point alias and using generated two-word names avoids common signatures. A multi-byte XOR loader was flagged only after the compiler optimized the routine into a known pattern, and turning optimization off cleared the detection. Shellcode was disguised as UUID-formatted strings, split into even and odd index arrays, or stored as dictionary words that map back to bytes at runtime. Because encrypted shellcode has high entropy, a machine-learning engine blocked one loader until low-entropy padding was added. The speaker also released a tool called jargon that encodes shellcode as English words, and reported using it on an engagement against a Cobalt Strike beacon.

The takeaway is that many detections are fragile, so small structural changes can restore a payload, though results need retesting after every update. The speaker notes that rebuilding the Cobalt Strike artifact kit can change file signatures, and points to vendor training for deeper evasion topics.

talks.title: What’s Old is Gold | Brian Halbach | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through legacy printers, file shares and network protocols that still open doors on pentests.
talks.summary:
Brian Halbach argues that older penetration testing techniques still produce results on real engagements, even when they are no longer the newest research. He frames the material as anecdotal, gathered from conversations with consultant pentesters, and describes his viewpoint as an internal network tester working from a grey-box position.

The middle of the talk covers services that keep appearing on client networks. Printers with default credentials can expose or redirect directory credentials, and one changed display message led to a payload on an executive assistant's laptop. SMB null sessions still turned up on a forgotten domain controller, Kerberoasting variants still produced domain admin access, and anonymous FTP was found on building control devices. TFTP-hosted phone and router configurations, spanning tree and HSRP manipulation, and clear-text credentials for mail protocols were also covered, each tied to a point about business impact.

The talk closes with password permutation of old breach dumps, combined social engineering, physical and dumpster-based testing, and web application issues such as request smuggling. The main takeaways are to scan with a clear methodology, check legacy services on every engagement, and work closely with the blue team. The closing Q&A added audience suggestions and tooling questions, including a discussion of SMB tooling.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from Building a Game Proxy | John Askew | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Lessons Learned from Building a Game Proxy | John Askew | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: Wireless Attack Killchain for N00bs | Dennis Pelton | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Walks newcomers through a Wi-Fi attack kill chain, from finding targets to rogue access points, handshake cracking and defenses.
talks.summary:
Aimed at newcomers, this talk frames a Wi-Fi attack as a kill chain: identifying the target, dispatching forces, initiating the attack and then taking over the network. It opens with how access points broadcast their names and how clients advertise networks they have joined before.

Reconnaissance covers war driving with a monitor-mode wireless card and GPS, pairing captured network names, channels and security settings with locations, and checking the public wigle.net database. Dispatch covers rogue access points, including Karma-style fakes that answer any probe with a matching name, and deauthentication frames that push a client to reconnect to a stronger fake AP, which can also reveal hidden SSIDs. For initiation, he explains how the WPA2 four-way handshake leaks values that can be checked offline with aircrack-ng against a password list, and describes a key-reinstallation attack on clients that skip the final step, a method he has not run himself.

Defenses include learning these techniques, turning off automatic reconnection or setting it to ask, placing employee phones on a guest network, running rogue AP detection, keeping access points out of sight and choosing strong passwords. He notes that 802.11w must be enabled to block deauth spoofing and that WPA3 resolves both deauth and Karma abuse, though adoption remains very low.

talks.title: Why Developers Hate Infosec | Bronwen Aker | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Explains why pen test reports frustrate developers and offers ways to make findings clearer, more useful and easier to act on.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who edits penetration test reports for a living after years of web, desktop and mobile development, argues that developers tend to resent security testers. Testers break software that was built to spec, then leave dense, hard-to-act-on reports, while developers work under tight deadlines with little security training. The talk treats changing how testers communicate as the part they can control, since they cannot control their customers.

Two stories illustrate the point. A forced upgrade of an older web platform, prompted by the end of SSL support for that version, took a department of over 25 people months and finished only two weeks before the deadline. Later, an e-commerce launch drew a seven-page complaint email from a sales executive that listed what was wrong but never said what he wanted. The speaker suggests that reports name current versions, end-of-life dates, CVEs and public exploits, and show how far a system lags behind the latest release, giving staff material to take to management.

To close, the speaker urges selling security as a feature, citing how a Volvo engineer's shared seat belt design became a legal requirement, and suggests A/B testing safety messaging. Other ideas include supporting universities and CTF events, inviting developers to security gatherings, sharing personal motivations, and exploring retainer-style mitigation services. The message is that the community can change how the industry works together.

talks.title: I got an Alert Now What? | Kellon Benson | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: A practical workflow shows analysts how to read alerts, prove or disprove threats, and drive containment through recovery.
talks.summary:
The presentation answers a question many new security staff ask: when an alert fires, what should actually happen beyond searching a hash and closing the ticket if it looks clean. The speaker frames alert handling as testing a hypothesis, then walks through a repeatable path from initial context through decision and response.

Using an example where Excel launches regsvr32 and suspicious DLLs, the talk shows how to parse what the alert logic really means, collect hashes and process-tree pivots without drowning in rabbit holes, and use open intelligence carefully—especially searching VirusTotal by hash rather than uploading customer files. Legitimate binaries can still enable abuse, while malicious samples may map to a family such as Emotet, which informs impact (credential theft, follow-on malware, likely email delivery). Response follows contain, eradicate, and recover: isolate hosts, block malicious hashes but not universal system tools, scope the environment, re-image or remediate endpoints, and pull related messages from mailboxes.

When data is thin, the same mindset applies: widen the process tree, chase network indicators, ask where activity came from and where it went, and compare behavior to baselines for user, host, or organization to spot false positives. The closing emphasis is documenting team policy for sensitive lookups, knowing when to escalate, and building a culture where junior analysts can say they do not know.

talks.title: Vulnerabilities are a Sirius Problem! | Matthew Toussain | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how to cut scanner noise using exploitation data, CPE matching and an open-source vulnerability database.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a frustration many testers share: vulnerability scanners return long lists of findings, and most of them never matter to real attackers. The speaker uses a fully patched system flagged for TLS 1.0 as an example of an item that creates compliance work but little real exposure. He argues that only a tiny fraction of the tens of thousands of CVEs issued each year are used in attacks, and that the major commercial scanner vendors keep their vulnerability data closed, which leaves practitioners unable to add their own context.

He then looks at what helps decide what to fix first. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog lists flaws seen in real attacks, and public exploit modules, blog posts and online discussion can show which issues are active. Lateral exposure matters too: Log4j had a higher CVSS score than EternalBlue but limited spread potential, while EternalBlue was tied to WannaCry. He shows why the nmap scripting engine lacks a real vulnerability database, and how NVD data can be queried through a Go-based API, enriched with exploitation tags, and matched against CPE identifiers for installed software.

To gather those CPEs automatically, he demonstrates an agent that reads the Windows registry, and notes edge cases such as per-user installs that can be missed. He introduces Sirius, an open-source scanning engine in alpha that can import existing scanning libraries, with scanning working on Windows for now. The practical takeaway is to build a vulnerability database that reflects your own environment and to contribute to shared, open-source scripts and data.

talks.title: Evaluating OSINT Data Sources and Tooling - Build vs Buy | Corey Ham | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Evaluating OSINT Data Sources and Tooling - Build vs Buy | Corey Ham | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: A case for threat informed penetration testing | Dan DeCloss | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding A case for threat informed penetration testing | Dan DeCloss | WWHF Deadwood 2022.
talks.summary:
Dan DeCloss presents a business case for integrating threat intelligence with penetration testing programs to shift organizations from reactive to proactive security postures. He begins by establishing that traditional penetration testing and threat intelligence functions, while valuable, operate largely independently and sub-optimally.

Traditional Limitations: Standard penetration testing engagements typically occur infrequently (often annually), are broadly scoped, and apply baseline methodologies uniformly across engagements. While comprehensive, these generate voluminous findings and multiple attack paths, overwhelming blue teams with prioritization decisions. Reports can feel overwhelming, leaving defenders unsure where to begin remediation. Meanwhile, threat intelligence remains largely reactive—teams ingest threat feeds, extract indicators of compromise (IOCs), and push them into detection systems (SIEMs, firewalls) to identify known threats post-discovery. This keeps organizations in a responsive posture. Additionally, collaboration between red and blue teams is typically limited, as consulting firms move to next engagements or internal teams work in isolation.

The Core Problem: DeCloss frames the mission as making organizations and the world safer, identifying security gaps, and demonstrating measurable improvement. Traditional approaches leave teams fatigued by alerts, struggling to prioritize, and unable to articulate security progress to executives.

Threat-Informed Approach: The solution involves merging threat intelligence with continuous, iterative penetration testing. Rather than relying solely on annual assessments, organizations break testing into small, recurring cycles—for example, every two weeks. This approach applies threat intelligence to scope pen testing engagements, identifies actual threats relevant to the organization, and emphasizes context: understanding how a specific threat would execute in that environment, considering business model, compensating controls, and industry factors. Collaboration between red teams, blue teams, and threat intelligence teams (purple teaming) ensures all disciplines inform test plans and interpret results together. Agreed metrics measure progress over time, demonstrating trends in detection and defense capabilities.

Continuous Testing Model: Rather than eliminating annual assessments, the approach layers continuous testing atop them. When urgent intelligence emerges (e.g., Uber MFA fatigue breach), teams rapidly develop test plans. Otherwise, threat intelligence feeds into a backlog of known threats to iteratively test. This produces what DeCloss terms "fight while we train while we fight while we train"—constant readiness through ongoing validation.

Case Study: An anonymous large organization conducts weekly purple team exercises incorporating threat intelligence feeds. When the Uber breach surfaced, they quickly developed a test plan, validated controls with the blue team, identified gaps, and remediated—then communicated concrete findings to their board, replacing vague assurances with demonstrable actions. This improved board confidence and team morale.

Context as Critical: DeCloss emphasizes that applying threat context is paramount. Threat intelligence on specific threat actors or ransomware variants means nothing unless teams ask: How would this threat execute in our environment? Do these TTPs apply to us? What would success look like for an attacker here? This mirrors vulnerability management—a severity rating means nothing without understanding asset importance and compensating controls.

Measurement and Culture: By measuring outcomes against specific threats, teams show demonstrable progress, combat alert fatigue, and justify investments in tooling or personnel. Research shows purple teams adopting this approach report better morale, clearer understanding of true gaps, and stronger business cases for resources.

Key Takeaways: Adopt a programmatic approach with continuous, iterative testing and metrics. Integrate threat intelligence to drive test scope, not just reactive alerting. Build purple teams merging red, blue, and threat intelligence functions. Apply threat context to understand relevance before testing. Maintain annual/broader assessments for compliance and other attack paths. Measure and celebrate wins to demonstrate value and prevent fatigue. Move the majority of effort from reactive firefighting to proactive validation of known threats.

talks.title: Game One! | Kelli Tarala | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Maps privacy harms, new laws, and NIST frameworks so security teams can support day-to-day privacy operations.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing privacy as an expanding duty for information security staff, not a separate adversary to security goals. Using a football-themed structure, she walks through foundational privacy ideas drawn from legal scholarship: limited access to the self, secrecy, control over personal information, personhood, and intimacy in how relationships are disclosed. She then groups privacy harms into physical, economic, reputational, psychological, autonomy, discrimination, and relationship impacts, stressing that privacy work centers on human consequences rather than purely technical controls.

The middle of the session connects that foundation to organizational reality. Federal momentum around the American Data Privacy and Protection Act is described as stalled, while the Transatlantic Data Privacy Framework is positioned as the successor to earlier EU–U.S. transfer mechanisms after surveillance concerns. State comprehensive privacy laws and rising consumer rights requests are pushing legal and compliance groups to hand operational privacy tasks to security teams. She presents the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and NIST Privacy Framework as complementary tools with heavy overlap in protect, detect, respond, and recover, and notes similar “security first, privacy add-on” patterns for ISO programs.

Closing guidance focuses on practical readiness: maintain awareness of legislation, run data inventory and mapping, perform gap analysis, and use assessment scorecards when executives ask for posture. She encourages collaboration with legal, compliance, and engineering groups, highlights privacy-by-design resources, and points practitioners toward IAPP training and certifications. Audience questions briefly contrast SP 800-53 privacy controls with the Privacy Framework’s harm- and data-flow orientation, and she expresses skepticism about major new federal privacy law passing within the next year or two.

talks.title: Exploiting Persistent XSS | Ken Pyle | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Exploiting Persistent XSS | Ken Pyle | WWHF Deadwood 2022.

talks.title: It’s just Kerberos delegation… Trust me… | Darryl Baker | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding It’s just Kerberos delegation… Trust me… | Darryl Baker | WWHF Deadwood 2022.
talks.summary: Darryl Baker walks through Kerberos ticket flow, PAC verification quirks, and why unconstrained delegation hands attackers real TGTs. He contrasts constrained, protocol-transition, and resource-based constrained delegation, then chains RBCD with standard-user machineAccountQuota to impersonate domain admins via S4U2self and S4U2proxy. He demos krb RelayUp coercing SYSTEM over LDAP, parent-child trust S4U hops, and hybrid Entra Connect and Application Proxy delegation risks. Mitigations focus on machineAccountQuota zero, LDAP signing, channel binding, EPA on AD CS, Defender for Identity patterns, and advanced audit alerts for object creation and RBCD writes.

talks.title: Hackers Helping the Helpers | Ray Davidson | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: A veteran practitioner outlines Michigan's volunteer cyber corps and urges peers to strengthen local government resilience.
talks.summary:
The session frames cybersecurity as volunteer public service rather than packet chasing or malware glamour. The presenter ties personal resilience—recovery, family loss, and community support—to a call for practitioners to expect state leaders to invite them into formal civilian cyber response programs, and to understand how those efforts evolve from one person's vision into rules, law, and process.

The core story is the Michigan Cyber Civilian Corps: born from 2010-era fears about grid and infrastructure shocks, it trains qualified volunteers to help roughly 2,500 local public entities that are often cyber-poor, especially in rural counties with minimal IT staff. The talk walks through Merit Networks and state takeover, the Michigan cyber civilian act and later amendments (background checks, advisor on-ramps, vulnerability-as-incident), Cyber Partners for proactive placement, membership tests and certifications, training from early incident-response courses through RangeForce, and official deployment coordinated with the Michigan Cyber Command Center after local governments report ransomware or similar hits.

It closes by comparing peer programs in Wisconsin, Ohio, Texas, and other states, noting growing national interest through the National Governors Association and MS-ISAC, and urging attendees to build social infrastructure—meet people where they are, mentor youth, and volunteer beyond emergencies, as illustrated by long hours aiding local COVID vaccination efforts.

talks.title: Hackers In The Boardroom | Alyssa Miller | WWHF Deadwood 2022
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn to engage corporate boards using recon, reframed metrics, and success stories drawn from a pen tester's playbook.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by describing a new role as chief information security officer and why many security leaders still struggle once regulation pushes cyber onto board agendas. Fear-based framing, breach platitudes, equating security only with enterprise risk, and dashboards of blocked attacks or open flaws tend to make directors disengage or fund insurance instead of programs.

The core method treats the board like an engagement target: research directors’ backgrounds, infer what they really want to know versus what they ask aloud, and prioritize a short story over raw numbers. Metrics belong in appendices; the live deck should explain resilience, containment, and whether leadership can sleep at night. A failed health-grade metaphor and a breach postmortem that only listed gaps illustrate how crises backfire when successes go unmentioned.

The close extends the same mindset to persistence: maturity snapshots, multi-year roadmaps, and initiatives tied to revenue or efficiency so the board invites regular updates. The intended takeaway is that curiosity and tradecraft need not disappear at the executive table; they become the way to translate technical work into language executives will fund.

talks.title: Jake Williams, Jorge Orchilles & Daniel DeCloss | Panel Discussion-WWHF Purple Team Roundup | Talk 5
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Jake Williams, Jorge Orchilles & Daniel DeCloss | Panel Discussion-WWHF Purple Team Roundup | Talk 5.

talks.title: Kaitlyn Wimberley | Birdwatching: Canary Users in the Forest | WWHF Purple Team Roundup | Talk 4
talks.teaser: Shows how to build decoy Active Directory user accounts that alert on password sprays and Kerberoasting.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces canary user accounts in Active Directory as a low-effort form of cyber deception. A canary is a decoy account made to look like a real user, so any use of it signals an attack, much as a canary warned miners of gas. The speaker presents canaries as a complement to firewalls, EDR and other fundamentals rather than a replacement, and argues that even small deployments add useful visibility.

Setup guidance covers a long random password, logon hours set to deny all access, optional host restrictions, and matching naming, descriptions, groups and OUs so the account looks ordinary. Required logs must be audited on workstations and domain controllers. For a password spray canary, failed logon events (4625) for the account flag any single attempt, regardless of how slowly the spray runs. A PowerShell approach using the Active Directory module makes creation faster and repeatable. For Kerberoasting, the account gets a service principal name, and a service ticket request event (4769) naming the canary is the alert.

Practical advice: test every canary before relying on it, since untested detections cannot be trusted. Fake credentials placed in user descriptions or honey documents can lure more cautious attackers, but should not be too obvious. Canary Tokens and Honey Badger are noted as other options. The speaker warns that admins, service accounts and vulnerability scans may trigger canaries, so alerts need tuning to avoid fatigue. Overall, canaries are cheap to start and worth trying in a lab first.

talks.title: Dahvid Schloss | To Emulate a Criminal, Act like a Criminal | WWHF Purple Team Roundup | Talk 3
talks.teaser: Argues red teams should mirror modern cybercrime by focusing on objectives, native tooling and quiet Windows techniques.
talks.summary:
Dahvid Schloss argues that red team exercises have not kept pace with how criminals operate. He traces cybercrime from early damage-focused malware to a financially motivated industry, dating the shift to the Silk Road marketplace and open credential sales around 2010. He cites remote work during the pandemic, a reported 300 percent rise in crimes for 2020, and breach life cycles of about 286 days, and says many red teamers still chase domain admin instead of the data and money a real attacker would target.

The middle section covers the skills he wants testers to prioritise. For programming, he recommends PowerShell, which ships with Windows and can run tooling in memory, plus native languages such as C, C++, C# and Go, since compiled payloads need no interpreter and custom loaders can get past many antivirus products. He walks through ways to avoid AMSI, load a custom PowerShell host, and fetch tools through web or DNS requests. For domain activity, he favours SMB and LDAP over nmap and ping, which he calls too noisy, and describes BloodHound and share listing as quieter ways to map access. On objectives, he suggests finding documents by file extension rather than searching for password strings, which he says triggers alerts quickly.

He closes by urging testers to blend into normal activity, using living-off-the-land binaries, native communication and C2 frameworks such as Mythic, Covenant or Metasploit rather than relying on expensive tooling. In answer to audience questions, he said WebAssembly and WebSockets are emerging options for C2 that he is still researching. His takeaway is that patience matters, since rushing leads to mistakes that get a team detected and removed from the network.

talks.title: Sustainable Phisheries: Preventing Disease in Farm Raised Phishing | Ean Meyer | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Sustainable Phisheries: Preventing Disease in Farm Raised Phishing | Ean Meyer | WWHF San Diego 2022.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Ian Meyer, Associate Director of Security Assurance at Marriott Vacations Worldwide and instructor at Full Sail University, discusses how to conduct phishing exercises in ways that preserve employee trust and organizational relationships rather than shaming users.

## The Fishing Metaphor and Core Problem
Meyer frames the issue as a "fishing industrial complex" where security vendors make it easy to conduct massive phishing campaigns that shame users. Like industrial fishing with nets that devastates fish populations, poorly designed phishing exercises deplete organizational trust. Meyer emphasizes that while phishing is easy to execute (like casting a wide net), sustainable security requires treating employees as valuable resources, not targets.

## Key Technical and Ethical Points

**Bad Practices:**
Meyer criticizes real examples where companies sent deceptive emails during the pandemic—GoDaddy teasing employees with fake holiday bonuses and Tribune Media offering false hardship assistance—to test if they'd click. These exercises violated psychological safety and used fear-based manipulation.

**The Scalpel Metaphor:**
Meyer uses a surgical scalpel as a metaphor for offensive security tools. A surgeon uses it to heal; an amateur kills. Security teams must think about downstream consequences before deploying phishing tests.

**Building Better Pretexts:**
Instead of fear-based messaging, Meyer demonstrates creating contextual, honest emails that match actual job duties. In a live audience example, he shows how shipping/logistics teams could receive emails about manifest updates (framed neutrally) and banking teams could receive customer inquiry emails—both based on real work patterns, not manipulation.

## Trust and Relationship Building

Meyer stresses that if security teams break trust through shame or punishment, employees stop reporting incidents. He shares a story of an employee who was fired after a social engineering exercise, despite leadership promising "nothing punitive." Result: help desk staff stopped talking to security, losing the organization's best source of threat intelligence.

Meyer demonstrates this through an audience participation exercise, throwing a trinket on a string into the crowd. When asked why the person opened the envelope, the answer was "trust"—the speaker wouldn't put something harmful in it. This trust is what security needs to build.

## Sustainable Security Program Model

Meyer advocates for:
- Removing shame-based language ("you have been fished")
- Using surveys asking *why* people clicked, not punishing them
- Recognizing anyone can be fished under the right circumstances
- Framing security team as enablers, not gatekeepers ("team of yes")
- Making employees security champions through partnership, not enforcement
- Focusing metrics on phishing *reporting* rates, not click rates

One of Meyer's exercises achieved 100% participation rate in a security champions program because employees felt respected and trusted.

## Actionable Takeaways

- Phishing exercises should emulate real threats but not use FUD (fear, uncertainty, doubt)
- Write pretexts aligned with employees' actual job duties
- Ask for help rather than testing obedience
- Partner with business units to gather feedback on controls gaps
- Meyer created a GitHub repository for crowd-sourced ethical phishing pretexts and landing pages
- Success metrics should track reporting and security champion engagement, not shame-based click rates

## Philosophy
Meyer concludes that security is about decreasing risk, not eliminating it. Businesses exist to take calculated risks. Security's job is to enable business while protecting against defined threats—this requires employee trust above all.

talks.title: Vulnerability Discovery, From Bronze Age to Cyber Age | Tony Sager | WWHF San Diego 2022
talks.teaser: Traces decades of vulnerability discovery, from early government red teams to focusing the few controls that counter real attacks.
talks.summary:
Tony Sager, who spent about 35 years at the National Security Agency and has worked in computer security since the 1970s, reviews how vulnerability discovery changed over his career. He starts with his early work in communications security and presents a simple risk model in which vulnerability, threat and consequence are weighed against controls. His point is that risk never reaches zero, so spending should be balanced across the model rather than poured into eliminating every flaw.

He then describes how government testing moved from ad hoc red teams, assembled from whoever had the right skills, to structured blue teams, sampling of live networks and later hunting inside agency infrastructure. His teams kept rediscovering the same weaknesses because findings went to people who lacked the authority or the language to fix root causes such as configuration management. He also recalls a case where a flood of indicators emailed to under-resourced staff was readable but not actionable, since usefulness depends on the receiver.

The later part covers the CIS Controls, which began as a small group of practitioners agreeing on a short list of priority actions and grew into a community effort. He describes a community defense model that maps top threat reports onto an attack technique framework to show which controls counter the most common attacker behaviour. He closes by urging listeners to prioritize a small number of high-value actions, translate threat data into steps owners can take, recognize incentives as the real obstacle, and look after colleagues to avoid burnout.

talks.title: WWHF | Which one of these is not like the others? {Can you Detect Abnormal Behavior?} | Erik Goldoff

talks.title: WWHF | Should you set it and forget it? Intro to IOT Hacking
talks.teaser: Gives newcomers the electronics basics and device research steps needed before starting IoT hardware hacking.
talks.summary:
This webcast previews the hardware portion of an introductory IoT hacking course, aimed at people without an electronics background. The presenters start with what counts as IoT, from smart appliances to industrial controls, and note how quickly connected device counts are growing. They stress that testing a device means looking at its wider ecosystem, including cloud services, mobile apps and network protocols, not just the circuit board.

The core of the session is basic electronics and component identification. Topics include current, ground, voltage, AC versus DC, and why matching a part's voltage rating prevents damage. The presenters walk through resistors, capacitors, inductors, diodes, transistors, voltage regulators and integrated circuits, and explain that ball grid array packages hide their leads underneath, which makes access hard. Common debug interfaces such as UART, JTAG and I2C are presented as typical entry points. For reconnaissance, they recommend gathering manufacturer documentation, firmware downloads, teardown guides, FCC filings with photos and schematics, and datasheets matched to chip markings, while checking for tamper protection and depopulated resistors first.

The session closes with an overview of the two-day course, which adds firmware acquisition, static and dynamic analysis, and checks for network services and other testing disciplines. The main takeaway for a practitioner is to research the device thoroughly and assess it as a whole system before opening it up.

talks.title: WWHF | Breaking and Entering - Tyler Robinson | Red Team Roundup
talks.teaser: Walks through physical penetration testing tactics, from badge reader attacks to door bypasses, and the business case for them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on physical penetration testing, which looks at what an attacker could reach through badge systems, network jacks, and building technology. The speaker explains that physical access often provides initial access in red team work, since a device hidden inside a facility can be hard for responders to find. Physical tests can also show executives the business risk when security teams struggle to win support.

The middle covers tools and examples. A device wired behind an HID badge reader can capture badge data, and USB drop boxes can record activity at a reception desk. At one New York bank, a sheet of paper triggered a motion-based exit sensor and opened a secure door. At a financial firm, white stickers placed over motion sensors that were armed only during the day enabled a night entry through a parking garage and roof hatch. Reconnaissance from sign-in sheets, digital directories, and fire-escape maps supported these efforts, while knowledge of fire-safety and elevator terminology opened restricted areas. Implants with cellular links were left in place to keep persistent access.

The takeaways center on planning and culture. Rules of engagement, local laws, and armed guards all shape the risk, and the speaker advises against physical tests for immature organizations. Defenders should treat janitorial, maintenance, and building-automation staff as part of security awareness, since legacy building systems are often reachable from corporate networks. Positive reinforcement, rather than blame, helps teams improve.

talks.title: WWHF | WhatTheF#$ | Chris Truncer | Red Team Roundup
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in WWHF | WhatTheF#$ | Chris Truncer | Red Team Roundup.

talks.title: WWHF | Why We Red Team : The Real Value of Threat Emulation | Joe Vest
talks.teaser: Argues that red team tests should measure how security operations prevent, detect and respond to threats.
talks.summary:
Joe Vest opens by noting that the red teaming community cannot agree on a definition, so the talk starts from the problem security operations is trying to solve. He describes security programs shaped by compliance, customer pressure and limited resources, which are then validated mostly through audits, patching and standard vulnerability assessments. Vest argues that a threat is not just a tool or a flaw but a threat actor combining intent with tools and techniques across a long chain of steps, so single exploits rarely tell the whole story.

He separates common test types by what they deliver. Vulnerability assessments reduce attack surface, penetration tests map relationships between flaws, and threat-based tests measure how security operations prevent, detect and respond. Vest urges prevention first but detection always, and encourages challenging defensive assumptions. One engagement he describes started quietly, then escalated to a loud phase; the defenders' response was poor, and restoring the network took over eight hours because recovery procedures were not followed.

His takeaways are to give threats a voice in security planning, decompose public threat reports into test scenarios, and report results as an attack diagram with missed detection opportunities mapped to detection strategies. He also recommends training defenders with live-fire exercises on production systems, while warning that overworked blue teams can be pushed too hard.

talks.title: WWHF | What2Log.com-Making your life a bit easier | Mick Douglas | 1-Hour
talks.teaser: Walks through a free crowdsourced site that explains which OS logs to enable, how to enable them, and why they matter.
talks.summary:
Mick Douglas and Flynn present What to Log, a free crowdsourced site they built after finding little usable guidance on which logs to collect. Their goal is to explain what to log, how to log it, and how those records help, using native operating system components so defenders can match the living-off-the-land methods attackers use. The project is meant to be evergreen and is still being built out.

Each entry explains why it matters, which operating system it applies to, and how to enable, view and check it through the GUI and command line. Suggested levels run from a minimum baseline to an extreme setting, so teams can raise collection during an attack. The Log Pile gathers chosen entries into copy-paste commands or downloadable PowerShell and bash scripts. Windows is covered most fully, Ubuntu is the only Linux focus so far, and macOS unified logging remains hard. Planned work includes Sysmon, web and database logs, compliance mappings and multi-language support. Presenters also asked for suggestions on fields that could be dropped to cut SIEM ingest costs.

In the question period, Mick named the Windows event log service stop event as a source of false positives during shutdowns. Flynn described Wi-Fi connection logs as an overlooked attack signal, and recounted an espionage case where one of those logs showed a suspect joining a coffee shop across from the rival that had received stolen data. The talk closes with the point that logs tell the story of what happened on a system, and that the free project needs feedback and contributions.

talks.title: WWHF | Network Protocol Abuse - How Attackers Profit by Playing by the Rules | Troy Wojewoda

talks.title: WWHF | How to Hire Cybersecurity—InfoSec Professionals Who Get Things Done | Kip Boyle | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Offers hiring managers practical advice on screening resumes, building teams and finding security talent that performs.
talks.summary:
Kip Boyle and Wes, who co-host a podcast about landing security jobs, speak to hiring managers who find it hard to build infosec teams. They describe hiring as unpredictable and emotionally demanding, and they note that a bad hire hurts the person, the team and the organization. Wes surveyed hiring managers, and the session groups the main pain points into three areas: sourcing candidates, screening resumes and interviews, and hiring people described as rock stars.

On sourcing, they recommend building a talent pool before a role opens, pairing junior staff eager to learn with experienced people who can mentor them, and writing job descriptions that make sense. For screening, they argue for looking for reasons to say no, since false positives create tension across the team. They suggest using the internal recruiter for basic and broad questions, asking candidates how they would prepare for a ransomware attack, checking whether listed skills match past job titles, and favoring quantified accomplishments over duties. Wes also shows a security organization diagram that helps recruiters place candidates in related roles.

On rock stars, they reject the idea of one person covering every area and favor T-shaped skills, with breadth in business and technology and depth in at least one technical area. Kip describes splitting technical and managerial work across roles or using outside help. The session closes with a Q&A and an invitation for hiring managers to help start an open-source hiring manager handbook. The takeaway is to define roles clearly, involve the team in interviews, and treat every candidate interaction as relationship-building, including when the answer is no.

talks.title: WWHF | Why a Security Awareness Program Isn't Enough to Secure Your Network
talks.teaser: James McQuiggan analyzes WWHF | Why a Security Awareness Program Isn't Enough to Secure Your Network.

talks.title: WWHF | Why the Basics are Hard - AWS Cloud Security Fundamentals Andrew Krug
talks.teaser: Walks through core AWS security fundamentals, from IAM policy logic and organization guardrails to auditing and incident response.
talks.summary:
This session previews an AWS cloud security course and frames "fundamentals" around the security pillars of the Well-Architected Framework. It opens with a review of well-known cloud breaches from about 2014 to 2021. The cases include a leaked privileged access key pushed to a public code repository, a private git server compromise that exposed access keys, a publicly reachable Kubernetes console holding an overly permissive key pair, and a server-side request forgery that let an attacker reach instance credentials. The speaker argues that the same basic failures recur, and that least privilege, multi-factor authentication and simpler system design would have blocked many of them.

The middle of the session focuses on identity and access management. It explains how IAM evaluates policies, how condition keys such as MFA session age and tag-based attributes can limit what a stolen credential can do, and how permissions boundaries and service control policies act as guardrails even against a careless or rogue administrator. Multi-account design is recommended to contain blast radius. The speaker demonstrates generating a least-privilege role policy from CloudTrail activity, and describes CloudMapper, an open-source auditing tool whose reports cover IAM linting and resource inventory. Running audits continuously and moving security group changes into CI/CD are presented as practical steps.

The closing portion covers detection and incident response, emphasizing centralized, tamper-resistant CloudTrail logging and preparation before an incident occurs. The main takeaway is that many serious AWS breaches come from basic gaps that configuration, guardrails and logging can close, and that a tested response plan matters when prevention fails.

talks.title: WWHF Blue Team Roundup | Alissa Torres | IR Pivots : When to Dig into Host Data
talks.teaser: Shows how host memory and endpoint data help analysts pivot past noisy alerts using five triage techniques.
talks.summary:
Alissa Torres argues that security operations analysts are buried in alerts, and that a single detection often lacks the context needed to tell a real intrusion from a false positive. She presents host-based incident response as a way to pivot from an alert to the endpoint and gather that context, organized around five pivots.

The first pivot covers fileless malware, where attackers misuse native Windows tools such as certutil, regsvr32 and WMI. Rather than dumping a full 64 GB memory image, she shows how to extract only the address space of a suspicious process, then recover an obfuscated script from a regsvr32 process in a four-gigabyte capture. Other pivots include trusted applications behaving oddly, such as a BGInfo instance running for hours or a ping process whose loaded DLLs changed after code injection; user processes appearing in session zero; gaps left when an endpoint security tool fails to record command lines; and persistence, where autoruns collected across hosts are reduced by frequency and filtered against a known-good baseline.

Her takeaway is to learn what normal looks like in your environment so that anomalies stand out, and to collect targeted host data when context is needed, since it is faster than full captures. She suggests practicing these techniques in a clean Windows Sandbox virtual machine.

talks.title: WWHF | 2021-03-31 - Interviewee Field Manual: Hack the Interview
talks.teaser: Explains how security pros can plan job searches like an attack chain, covering networking, resumes, interviews and salary talks.
talks.summary:
This Wild West Hackin' Fest webcast treats landing a security job as a repeatable process that a practitioner can plan and refine. Doug Brush argues that networking drives most hiring outcomes, and that candidates should build contacts in person and online well before they need work. He suggests helping people in community forums, researching target companies through their financials, culture and likely acquisitions, reaching out to insiders, and learning about the hiring manager.

The middle of the talk moves through application materials and delivery. He recommends keeping a resume as a living document, leading with what the candidate can do, quantifying accomplishments, and tailoring keywords to each posting. He notes that applicant tracking systems can misread details such as certification names, and that recruiter emails can land in spam folders. For interviews, he advises asking about day-to-day work and culture, preparing for technical and cultural rounds separately, staying honest, and sending individually tailored thank-you notes the same day.

In the closing stretch he covers offers and rejections. He suggests delaying pay discussions, weighing total compensation including stock and time off, and asking interviewers for feedback after a rejection. The Q&A touched on an employer that had cut its security staff, gamified recruiting, and mock interview services. The takeaway is to keep a network active, keep materials current, and treat each interview as practice.

talks.title: WWHF | 2021-03-17- Security DDTTX - Intro to Tabletop Exercises
talks.teaser: Amanda Berlin explores WWHF | 2021-03-17- Security DDTTX - Intro to Tabletop Exercises.

talks.title: WWHF | Abusing Microsoft Office for Post-Exploitation - Kyle Avery
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft Office add-ins, templates, DCOM and document poisoning support persistence, lateral movement and credential theft.
talks.summary:
Kyle Avery, a penetration tester, argues that Microsoft Office, which is installed on many corporate workstations, is useful to attackers well beyond the macro-based initial access it is usually known for. He organizes the talk around persistence, lateral movement and credential gathering, and pairs each technique with detection and defense ideas.

For persistence, he shows Word add-ins packaged as renamed DLLs, which load at startup from trusted locations without an enable-content prompt. Excel needs a registry change to load XLL add-ins, but XLAM add-ins work without one. Document templates such as Normal.dotm and Personal.xlsb run when a user opens a document, and roaming profiles can carry them to other workstations. For lateral movement, he covers Excel's DDE initiate method and Outlook's CreateObject call to ScriptControl, both reached over DCOM, with Visio as a similar option. He also shows in-memory shellcode delivery through Excel XLM macro API calls. For credential gathering, he runs a WebDAV listener on a high port, uses a netsh URL ACL entry to listen on port 80 without administrator rights, and forces authentication through Outlook signature images or poisoned Word hyperlinks.

He closes with detection points: file writes to trusted locations, Office processes spawned by the DCOM launch service, Office started with embedding command-line flags, and suspicious API calls. Defensive measures include Attack Surface Reduction rules, disabling automatic image downloads, and restricting which ports users can listen on.

talks.title: Kevin Johnson - Daleks Performing a Jedi Mind Meld- Communicating Risk and Issues
talks.teaser: Explains why security teams and the business talk past each other about risk, and how shared language and goals help.
talks.summary:
Kevin Johnson argues that many recurring security problems persist less because of missing technical answers and more because people in security and the business miscommunicate. He points to SQL injection, which keeps turning up in new applications even though parameterized queries are a known fix that also performs better than dynamic SQL. He also questions how risk gets rated: in his run of the CVSS calculator, a username harvesting flaw scored close to the top of the scale, above a SQL injection flaw he scored at 7.3.

He gives examples of communication breakdowns. In one engagement, a team used "TCP" to refer to an internal application, not the protocol. At a previous employer, a change-control discussion stalled over a TCP/IP reference that turned out to be mainframe terminology applied to a Linux server. He also criticizes hype around exotic attacks, such as a ransomware-infected coffee machine and a compromised teapot, and argues the useful question is what the threat actually means for the organization. Security and the business often have opposing goals, since a revenue target can conflict with a lockdown that security wants.

His proposed remedies are to accept that the communication gap exists, learn the other side's language and goals, and show up where they work, such as their meetings. He stresses honesty, avoiding exaggerated risk claims, and being seen as ethical. He notes that his firm advises on fixes but does not perform remediation, so its recommendations are not tied to a financial interest. He presents no single solution, only a call to keep working on the problem.

talks.title: Pieter Danhieux - Stop Calling My Baby Ugly!
talks.teaser: Argues that teaching developers secure coding patterns, not just reporting flaws, cuts recurring vulnerabilities like SQL injection.
talks.summary:
Pieter Danhieux starts from a common friction: security teams find flaws, file tickets, and developers fix one bug without learning the pattern behind it. He argues that application security is under-resourced, with one specialist often covering hundreds or thousands of engineers, and that slow, noisy scanners leave knowledge with one or two people in each organization.

The core evidence comes from a hands-on training platform used by roughly 100,000 developers. Players explore a live application and its code, then work out the cause of a flaw and how to fix it. More than half a million players handling SQL injection answered correctly, while about 35 percent did not recognize the bad pattern. Rust developers reached 98 percent accuracy, whereas COBOL and PL/SQL ranked low. Business logic was the least understood category. After being shown a secure coding pattern, players succeeded on the next attempt roughly 90 percent of the time.

His practical advice is to bring checks into the IDE with lint rules or plugins, while making sure they do not block work. In pipelines, favour fast, reliable checks on one or two vulnerability classes. Pick the most common flaws in your own scans, document a secure library or coding pattern for each language, and link it from the ticket so developers stop copying answers from forums. Keep the tone positive, because a helpful security team earns more trust than one that only points at ugly code.

talks.title: Mike Woolard - Automating ZAP to Deliver On-Demand Reports
talks.teaser: Explains how to wrap the ZAP API in Python and a database so product owners can trigger scans and review findings on demand.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how a move from waterfall release gates to agile growth left one assessor juggling dozens of in-house web applications, acquisitions, and inconsistent team practices. Spreadsheets gave way to a homegrown security dashboard where application owners pick an environment, submit a scan, and see results within roughly fifteen minutes instead of retyping commercial or manual reports.

The middle walks through the moving parts: MySQL tables for scheduled scan requests and optional stored findings, ZAP API key generation, persisted sessions with scoped contexts, technology hints, authentication or Zest login scripts, and exclude rules. A scheduled Python job polls the database, imports the right session, clears stale alerts, runs spider and active scan to completion, and either exports HTML or pushes alert details through the API into the dashboard for triage.

Practitioners are steered to customize the published script, run ZAP with the GUI visible while debugging, deduplicate or close mitigated findings before developers see noise, and treat the stack as a use-case layer on top of command-line automation already covered elsewhere. The closing arc positions the same portal for SonarQube, ticketing, endpoint vulnerability tie-backs, and future public release as a broader application inventory, not only scan buttons.

talks.title: Hackin’ Your Career - Top 10 Ways to Stand Out in Your Cyber Career - Russell Eubanks
talks.teaser: 1 Hour analyzes Hackin’ Your Career - Top 10 Ways to Stand Out in Your Cyber Career - Russell Eubanks.

talks.title: Jamie Dicken - Why Developers Don’t Care About Security
talks.teaser: WWHF January Roundup analyzes Jamie Dicken - Why Developers Don’t Care About Security.

talks.title: Mick Douglas - Sebastian Boutin - That’s Fantastic!
talks.teaser: Demos Fantastic, a modular Windows assessment tool that wraps PowerShell checks in guided quests and invites JSON-based contributions.
talks.summary:
Mick Douglas and Sebastian Boutin introduce Fantastic, a Windows-focused tool that places a web interface over a set of PowerShell commands. They start with an installation walkthrough using npm, which needs Node.js and a short setup prompt that creates an admin account. Their stated goal is to lower the learning curve for administrators who otherwise depend on complicated command cheat sheets.

The core unit is an action that runs locally or against remote hosts, and tests check its results. A failed test can trigger a follow-up action, such as enabling a firewall profile. Actions are grouped into daily quests for routine checks and story quests that run in a set order. The demo covered last boot time, firewall profiles, Windows Defender status and a missing hotfix, with the underlying command shown for each step, similar to how Zenmap reveals nmap commands. A visual editor links quests together and can mark them as non-editable by others.

Modularity is a major theme. Content lives in JSON files placed in directories, extra modules can be installed through npm, and authentication can use the default database-backed store or an Active Directory integration. In the Q&A, the presenters said npm is still required, that a standalone Windows executable is being considered, and that protecting the text-based configuration files belongs at the operating system layer. They closed by asking for feedback and contributions, including from people who do not write PowerShell but can build JSON content.

talks.title: BHIS & WWHF Present | Discussing Implications of the SolarWinds Breaches
talks.teaser: Panelists dissect the SolarWinds breach and argue that visibility, logging and fundamentals matter more than chasing indicators.
talks.summary:
The webcast covers the SolarWinds Orion compromise, in which a malicious update reached roughly 18,000 customers and several hundred were targeted. The speakers argue that chasing indicators of compromise is of little use now, because the attacker's domains and IP addresses had already been blocked and signatures are easy to change. They frame the response as a question of basic visibility.

The discussion centers on what organizations should have had in place. Network metadata such as DNS and NetFlow logs, identity provider logs, and DHCP records are named as essential, with retention long enough to look back months. A domain seen for the first time from a server that never contacts external hosts is a strong lead. The speakers stress knowing your hardware and software inventory, since many teams did not know Orion was running, and mapping blind spots. Free tools such as Security Onion, Zeek and RITA help spot beaconing. One example recalled an earlier exercise in which Zeek data alone uncovered a stealthy command-and-control channel in a customer network.

The panel then addresses policy. They debate whether widely used government software should face critical-infrastructure style standards, and whether audit frameworks such as FedRAMP or SOC 2 improve security. Delaying patches is called a poor excuse, and threat intelligence feeds are criticized in favor of durable knowledge of attacker techniques. The takeaway is to return to fundamentals, verify logging on the network and endpoints, and rehearse incident response before the next incident.

talks.title: You Don't Have to Be Crazy to Work Here - Doug Brush
talks.teaser: 1 Hour investigates You Don't Have to Be Crazy to Work Here - Doug Brush.

talks.title: The Dirty Truth Behind Getting Into Cybersecurity - Naomi Buckwalter
talks.teaser: Explains how experience, certification and degree gatekeeping keeps newcomers out of entry-level cybersecurity roles.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why first cybersecurity jobs are so hard to land. The speaker, a mentor to job seekers, says many capable people with degrees, home labs and certifications apply to dozens of roles and hear nothing back. Her main argument is that entry-level openings are scarce. In a review of 1,000 US cybersecurity listings on LinkedIn, she found 87% were mid-senior or above and 12.5% were tagged entry-level.

She pushes back on the idea that little junior work exists. Citing a Forbes report, she says 20% of small and mid-size businesses lack a formal information security program. A Verizon report is cited as putting small and mid-size businesses at 43% of 2019 data breaches. Walking through a NIST-based list of common security services, she argues most tasks can be taught without a CISSP or years of experience. Her figures also show 43% of entry-level postings require a CISSP and nearly 40% require a college degree, which she argues adds to burnout and understaffing on existing teams.

For newcomers, she recommends listing security work already done in current roles, asking managers for technical tasks, volunteering in cybersecurity working groups, and writing plain-text resumes that applicant tracking systems can parse. For interviews, she advises a 30-second personal pitch, pausing while speaking, and avoiding stories about unauthorized hacking. She closes by urging hiring managers to give newcomers a chance.

talks.title: Releasing Your First (Python) Open Source Project to the Masses! - Ian Lee
talks.teaser: Walks newcomers through git basics, contributing to existing projects, and publishing a first Python project on GitHub.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles the common belief that you need to be a developer to take part in open source. Ian Lee begins with a recap of an earlier workshop and explains what version control is, why Git is the dominant tool, and how files move between untracked, staged, committed and modified states. He demonstrates the core ideas in a visual Git playground: local repositories versus remotes, pushing and pulling, branches as movable pointers, merging, rebasing and resetting. He stresses writing clear commit messages and avoiding committing secrets, since removing a file later does not erase it from history.

He then shows lower-barrier ways to contribute. Using only a web browser and a GitHub login, he edits documentation in another project, previews the Markdown, and opens a pull request. He also corrects a documentation typo in a Docker-related project and points to awesome lists as an easy place to add resources. He outlines the git flow model with main, develop, release and hotfix branches, and notes that a fix applied to one tagged version does not reach other versions unless it is copied across.

For the final part he builds a Python project from scratch in a Docker container using Poetry. He initializes a Git repository, creates a matching GitHub repository, adds it as a remote, and pushes the first commit. He then adds a module that uses the requests library, defines a command-line entry point, and reinstalls the package to run it. The takeaway is that a first project can start small and grow through repeated, modest contributions.

talks.title: Intro to Git for Security Professionals - Ian Lee - Deadwood 2020 Workshop
talks.teaser: Teaches security practitioners core Git concepts, from commits and branches to pushing changes and contributing to open source.
talks.summary:
This workshop introduces Git to security professionals who write scripts or tools but have never used version control. It opens with why tracking changes matters, how distributed systems like Git differ from centralized ones such as Subversion, and how to set a user name and email for commit metadata. The speaker then walks through initializing a repository, staging files, committing, and reviewing work with status, diff, log and show.

The middle section covers correcting and organizing work. Attendees see how to amend a commit, how partial staging with interactive patch mode lets you commit only some changes, and how a reset can move a branch back past a commit. The speaker notes that the old commit remains in the repository until garbage collection, which matters for anyone reviewing a developer's machine for leaked credentials. Branching is introduced as movable pointers, followed by a merge that produces a conflict resolved by hand, with rebase mentioned as a more powerful but riskier option.

The final part covers remotes: cloning, fetching, pulling and pushing against a hosted server. It closes with contributing to open source projects through forks and pull requests, using a small documentation fix as an example. The takeaway is that modest fixes to documentation or typos help projects, and that keeping even personal notes and scripts under Git builds habits that pay off later.

talks.title: Infosec Marketing in 2021 - Hacking the New Normal | Jon Barnes & Jason Blanchard | 4-Hours
talks.teaser: A four-hour workshop delivers planning frameworks, audience models, and creative campaign tactics for security industry marketers.
talks.summary:
The session opens as a long-form Wild West Hackin' Fest workshop for people who market security products and services, mixing interactive prizes and chat prompts with a staged agenda: priorities for 2021, content and community, then year-long planning on a shoestring budget.

The core teaching stresses conceptual models over ad metrics or SEO minutiae. Presenters compare technical practitioners and purchasing-decision audiences, warn against clichéd hacker imagery, and argue that crowded podcasts and webcasts demand immediate value, genuine care for recipients, and guarding cultivated email lists from internal monetization pressure. They cite reallocating big conference spend toward grassroots events, partnering with in-house experts to sanity-check ideas, and resisting comparison of 2020 performance to normal years.

Later segments walk through marketing maturity and simple scorecards, hard versus soft measurements, a one-page plan, marketing SWOT, capped initiatives, audience sketches, the six Ps and PESO buckets, publishing calendars, and checklist-driven execution. The close introduces a “stupid idea” method—partnership, performance, parody, props, prizes, PR—illustrated with campaigns that succeeded or flopped, plus book and swag giveaways.
