talks.title: Marcus J Carey | Definition of Insanity | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Traces how security tooling has cycled from firewalls to browsers, and argues for hands-on fundamentals and coding skills.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security keeps repeating old approaches. It traces the back-and-forth from antivirus and firewalls to network scanning, file integrity monitoring and endpoint tools, and sees the same pattern in today's focus on endpoints. Ransomware gets special attention because it hits confidentiality, integrity and availability at once. The speaker also points to attackers living off the land with PowerShell, and to the speaker's own PowerShell-based ransomware built for testing.

The middle section looks at the browser as the new operating system. WebSocket traffic and encrypted DNS are hard to inspect, and browser extensions can read activity across sites, which makes them a risk. The speaker says MITRE ATT&CK gives red and blue teams a shared vocabulary, and that continuous testing on live networks matters more than training in isolated cyber ranges. He then demonstrates a browser-based escape-room training app he built in JavaScript, which teaches basic weaknesses such as default passwords and codes written down near the lock.

The closing part is career advice. The speaker argues that newcomers need solid fundamentals and the ability to code more than they need to become wizards, and that admitting "I don't know" and sharing knowledge are signs of a strong practitioner. The practical takeaways are to run the same tools attackers use against your own network, automate repetitive work, and build low-cost training that lowers the entry barrier into security.

talks.title: The War for Control of DNS Encryption | Paul Vixie | WWHF Deadwood 2020 Virtual
talks.teaser: Examines how DNS encryption protocols like DoT and DoH shift control away from network operators and firewalls.
talks.summary:
Vixie argues that pervasive monitoring by governments, companies and criminals has pushed the internet toward encrypting nearly everything, and that DNS, which acts as a directory for the internet, is especially sensitive. He places this in a longer history of lock-in, from proprietary networking in early computing to cloud and platform control, and argues that information is now the main domain of power.

The middle of the talk walks through the protocols. Traditional DNS let a device take its resolver from DHCP, so a local operator could inspect and filter lookups. DNS over TLS on port 853 added privacy but stayed easy to block, so DNS over HTTPS moved queries onto port 443, where they blend with web traffic. Browsers and platforms from Google, Mozilla, Microsoft and Apple are rolling this out. He also covers HTTP/3 over UDP, which hides connection events from the operating system, and encrypted SNI and ECH, which hide destination names from inline firewalls. Workarounds he describes include DNS taps and DNS firewalling on recursive servers.

He closes by arguing that bypassing local filtering shifts control to vendors and to states that can absorb the cost, while families and enterprises lose visibility. He calls smart devices a form of surveillance capitalism and says standards decisions favour people who can afford the time and travel. In the Q&A he urged listeners to question what their devices send and to fund work on resolver-to-resolver encryption, which he says is not yet ready.

talks.title: Tao and the Art of Tshark Fields | Chris Brenton | WWHF Deadwood 2020 Virtual
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Tao and the Art of Tshark Fields | Chris Brenton | WWHF Deadwood 2020 Virtual.

talks.title: BB King | Free Tools For Webapp Hacking | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Walks through Firefox's built-in developer tools for finding hidden behavior and testing web apps from the browser.
talks.summary:
This talk is a semi-guided tour of the free developer tools built into Firefox, drawn from a longer web app pen testing class. The speaker asks attendees to follow along in their own browser. He explains that client-side JavaScript means the page a user sees often differs from the source the server returned, so the built-in tools reveal more than view source. He notes that Chrome's tools overlap with Firefox's but are not identical.

The console is shown as the place to watch for logged messages, browser warnings and content security policy notices, such as blocked inline scripts or blocked tracker requests. The network tab filters traffic by content type and text, can disable caching so cached responses do not hide activity, and lets requests be edited and resent without leaving the browser. Response headers such as content type and no-sniff explain why a script served as plain text never runs. The storage tab covers cookies, IndexedDB, local and session storage, and cookies can be edited in place. The inspector shows live page changes and style rule cascades.

The last section uses console JavaScript against the live page: listing every link or image, appending a parameter to each link, and pulling YouTube links out of a chat room page as a real-world example. Autocomplete can search the page for names like password, key or token. The closing advice is to leave the console open even while browsing, since it reveals how a site is built and where it might break.

talks.title: Exploits, Research, Tools, and the Impact to Security | Dave Kennedy | WWHF Deadwood 2020 Virtual
talks.teaser: Reviews two decades of exploit and tool releases, weighing whether publishing offensive research makes defenders stronger or weaker.
talks.summary:
Dave Kennedy looks back over roughly twenty years of the security field. He describes early days when researchers posted exploits openly and built reputations by publishing them, then the move toward responsible disclosure after Dan Kaminsky's DNS flaw. He also explains how operating system protections such as data execution prevention made exploit development harder, and how his own early PowerShell research fed into security features in later versions of the scripting language.

The middle of the talk turns to defense. Kennedy argues that many organisations measure only whether a control covers an attack, not whether it still works when the attack changes. In one demo, a regsvr32 technique was blocked by a Windows Defender signature, then rebuilt with bitsadmin to fetch the payload and got past it. A PowerShell payload from his Magic Unicorn tool was caught by the AMSI interface until a small change to the string let it through. He also cites a Windows Defender download method that Microsoft disabled shortly after it was disclosed, as an example of publication shrinking an attack surface.

The closing debate covers whether offensive tools such as Cobalt Strike, Empire and Metasploit should be released. Kennedy argues that hiding tools and research leaves defenders unable to test their controls. He recommends baselining normal behaviour, restricting PowerShell to users who need it, and enforcing basics such as multi-factor authentication over relying on signatures alone. He ends by urging red and blue teams to work together.

talks.title: Travis Palmer | Cracking Beyond 15 Characters, Under $500 | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Travis Palmer | Cracking Beyond 15 Characters, Under $500 | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: Don C. Weber | Detecting Encrypted Radio Communications Using Universal | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Shows how to capture and decode industrial 900 MHz radio traffic with Universal Radio Hacker and check its encryption.
talks.summary:
Don C. Weber shows how to capture and analyse radio traffic from industrial control devices, using Phoenix Contact 900 MHz radios as the example. His starting point is that these radios leave AES encryption switched off by default, and that frequency hopping does not stop a signal from being captured. He first recommends a quick configuration review: export the settings from a Windows system and search for the word encryption, comparing a configuration with and without it.

The core of the talk is a walkthrough in Universal Radio Hacker, driven by a HackRF One. Weber finds a hop in the spectrum view, records it, sets the noise threshold, isolates one transmission and centres the waveform. Setting samples per symbol from the fastest transition reveals the preamble, the sync word and a plaintext test string. He then labels packet fields such as device ID, sequence number and checksum, and compares that plaintext capture with an encrypted one. The encrypted payload is 24 bytes against 12 bytes of plaintext, which leaves open questions about padding, cipher mode and initialization vectors.

He closes by noting that capture is always possible, that anyone can send packets the radio may still parse, and that denial of service is hard to defend. Practitioners should verify encryption settings, question how vendors implement them, and treat a radio-dependent process as a risk. Sample captures and slides were published so attendees could repeat the analysis without owning a radio.

talks.title: Whoops. I accidentally helped start a foreign intel service | David Evenden | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: A former intelligence operator recounts how an overseas contract drifted into questionable targeting and the lessons he drew.
talks.summary:
David Evenden, a former NSA red team operator and Persian linguist, describes a contract he took with a US firm after leaving the agency. The work was based in a villa in the UAE and was framed as tracking ISIS-linked activity online. The team used modified open-source datasets to link social media accounts to likely supporters, and in some cases accounts were taken over after the people behind them were detained.

Requests gradually shifted from following militant funding to tracing the travel of prominent people, and then to targeting a UK journalist who wrote about human rights abuses. The speaker shows a phishing email and a macro-enabled document sent to that journalist, which researchers later reported on. Realizing the team lacked proper permission and was taking tasks from local government, the group was told to leave. Colleagues who stayed later moved to a firm the speaker describes as a front for the UAE's version of the NSA.

He closes with practical lessons: if something seems too good to be true, it probably is; vet leadership; be alarmed if a foreign government holds your passport; carry signed authorisation; plan an exit strategy; and let personal values act as a compass. He also describes the lasting toll of reviewing violent imagery and how his team rotated that work.

talks.title: Jeepers Creepers: Advanced OSINT | Forrest Kasler | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Jeepers Creepers: Advanced OSINT | Forrest Kasler | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: A Pitmaster's Guide To Security | Alyssa Miller | WWHF Deadwood 2020 Virtual
talks.teaser: Uses brisket-smoking lessons to explain how to build a security program that wins executive support and improves continuously.
talks.summary:
The talk uses barbecue as a metaphor for building a security program. It opens with breach patterns: misconfigured cloud storage, and a pen-test review where configuration management was the top finding, holding at about 40 percent for three years. It also flags official Docker Hub images, where the standard node image had 642 vulnerabilities, and notes that cross-site scripting remains the most reported flaw in open source projects.

The core is five rules drawn from smoking brisket. Planning comes first: pitch initiatives to executives in business terms, such as cutting help desk time spent rebuilding machines after ransomware, rather than relying on fear, and lead with the key points because boards give little time. Low and slow means continuous improvement, starting from critical business assets and building defenses outward in layers like a castle. Good smoke means metrics that tell a story of improvement rather than arbitrary targets. Security should also be a paved road integrated with developers, not a gate between pipeline phases, and teams should know their tools: enterprises average more than 60, about 35 percent overlap, and 80 percent are underused.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to plan around business value, prioritize what matters, measure progress over time, and make existing tools work harder before buying more.

talks.title: Dr. Brizendine, Austin Babcock, Dr. Stroschein | Exploits with the JOB ROCKET | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Dr. Brizendine, Austin Babcock, Dr. Stroschein | Exploits with the JOB ROCKET | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: Hackers Don't Wear Black Hoodies, They Wear Capes | Chloé Messdaghi | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Explores how stigma, media imagery, and laws like the CFAA chill disclosure, and maps practical steps to advance hacker rights.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing information security as a humanitarian issue and dedicating the session to researchers who fear prosecution when they try to report flaws. It walks through real friction points: advance warnings that went unheeded before major breaches, surveys suggesting most hackers skip reporting, and programs that pay bounties without legal safe harbor.

Case studies anchor the narrative, from a drone vendor threatening researchers under broad computer misuse statutes to contracted penetration testers arrested after an alarm at a courthouse. The speaker links public fear to socially constructed stereotypes—hoodie imagery, careless use of “hacker” instead of attacker—and explains how amygdala-driven threat responses echo in everyday reactions when people learn someone works in security research.

The closing arc covers U.S. anti-hacking and anti-circumvention law, the Aaron Swartz prosecution, failed reform efforts, and the stakes of Supreme Court review of “exceeds authorized access.” Takeaways stress distinguishing hackers from criminals, pushing vulnerability disclosure programs, engaging press and employers, contacting representatives, and supporting advocacy hubs such as Hacking Is Not a Crime and allied civil-liberty groups.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Kevin Johnson | Haunted Security | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: RFCs for Rebuilding Civilization Post-Apocalypse | Chris Culling | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: A comedic tour of joke RFCs for rebuilding civilization, ending with a real 2001 test of pigeon-carried IP packets.
talks.summary:
The talk is a comedic mock broadcast by Chris Culling, framed as a late-night show that counts down seven RFCs supposedly needed to rebuild civilization after an apocalypse. The opening entries are satirical: RFC 2550 covers a rollover problem when years reach five digits, and RFC 5841 imagines packets using TCP options to signal their mood. Scenic routing for IPv6 is presented as a way to keep packets in fresh air, and RFC 6592 is praised as the null packet.

The middle entries lean further into absurdity. RFC 2795 describes an infinite monkey protocol suite, with keeper requests and simian replies used to check on monkeys at typewriters. RFC 4824 carries IP datagrams over semaphore flag signaling, which is slow but can send letters and hex values one at a time.

The final item, RFC 1149, covers IP datagrams on avian carriers. The speaker contrasts it with a real 2001 trial by the Bergen Linux user group, which sent nine ping packets by pigeon. Four returned, a 55 percent packet loss, and round trips averaged 87 minutes. In the Q&A, the speaker argues that RFCs leave room for interpretation, so red and blue teams benefit from knowing the standards that attackers may exploit.

talks.title: Nadean Tanner | Secret Thoughts of a Successful Hacker | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Nadean Tanner | Secret Thoughts of a Successful Hacker | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: Stephen Spence | Converting Blue Team into Advanced Host-Based Alerting | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Stephen Spence | Converting Blue Team into Advanced Host-Based Alerting | WWHF Deadwood 2020.

talks.title: Dave Klein | The Era of Software-Defined Segmentation | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Shows why VLANs and firewalls struggle today and how software-defined segmentation brings granular, platform-agnostic policy.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that traditional segmentation, built from VLANs, access control lists, firewalls and cloud security groups, struggles in environments that change quickly and span data centers, clouds and containers. The speaker, Dave Klein, says these tools are hard to manage, give little visibility, and cannot write rules by process, user or fully qualified domain name. That makes it hard to block clear-text protocols or force traffic through a web proxy.

He then describes software-defined segmentation, also called microsegmentation, as a platform-agnostic approach that applies one policy set across legacy systems, bare metal, hypervisors, cloud, containers and serverless. The suggested workflow is to visualize the environment, label assets, define policy, monitor traffic and then enforce it, starting with the highest-value targets. He stresses broad operating system support, metadata integration, a host firewall that administrators cannot quietly change, and a REST API for pulling in CMDB and vulnerability data. Use cases include protecting unpatchable medical devices and legacy systems.

The main case study involved a top-five global bank whose production and UAT environments shared more than 800 overlapping VLANs, after a developer nearly made a money transfer in what turned out to be production. Instead of re-addressing tens of thousands of servers, the team mapped the environments, pushed agents with playbooks and separated them in a few weeks rather than the years the VLAN changes would have taken. A second case isolated security cameras and building controls from the data center. The takeaway is to start with high-value segments and connect the approach to existing monitoring, directory and ticketing systems.

talks.title: A Quickstart Guide to Insider Threats | Adam Mashinchi | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Shows how red, blue and purple teams can emulate and detect insider threats on user endpoints.
talks.summary:
The talk treats insider threats as something red, blue and purple teams should test together, starting from the premise that organizations will eventually be compromised. Post-exploitation activity matters more than exploit testing, the speaker argues, because allow-listed tools and social engineering can get past defenses. The user endpoint is the weakest point: unvetted devices, third-party visitors, home-office laptops outside monitoring, and approved cloud services make malicious data movement hard to separate from normal use.

Red teams should emulate adversaries rather than run one-off penetration tests: identify crown jewel assets, define the techniques a user might take toward them as whole behaviors rather than fixed commands, and repeat the tests over time. Blue teams face the harder job of learning normal user behavior, which is refined iteratively, and the talk notes that tracking slow beacons becomes costly as intervals grow. Breach simulation tools suit controls validation but are often driven by threat intelligence and offer less flexibility.

The purple team step is a joint risk and priority assessment that ranks harms by impact and ease of detection. Teams begin with easy-to-catch cases, such as moving a terabyte in an hour, to build a baseline, then work toward slow, low-volume exfiltration. The takeaway is to baseline normal activity, prioritize scenarios that fit the organization, and run the engagements again and again.

talks.title: Hunting by Numbers: Defensive Hunting Program and Outcomes | Chris Crowley | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Describes a prescriptive defensive hunting cycle with plans, reports, starter hunts, and metrics that show value to leadership.
talks.summary:
Chris Crowley frames threat hunting as research and development that makes security operations adaptive rather than script-bound. He argues organizations need governance, impact scoring, and mature SOC functions—steering oversight, monitoring, intelligence, incident handling, forensics, and self-assessment—before chasing the most sophisticated adversaries. Use cases should start from business scenarios and mapped data, not from whatever logs happen to be available.

The core program assigns roughly two hours per week per team member, keeps hunts lightweight, and separates hunting from SIM use-case engineering. Each hunt uses a planned spreadsheet structure and a report capturing detects, operational capture such as scripts or rules, posture improvements, and use-case candidacy. He prescribes five repeating hunts: inventory your own tools, run a least-frequency-of-occurrence analysis, map constituent systems and owners, pursue outliers such as unusual command-line lengths, and run themed team hunting parties.

Practitioners should treat successful finds as incidents, automate repeatable steps without automating analysis, and report aggregates upward: detections, implemented posture changes, owner correlation, and estimated coverage across known systems. References include threathunting.net, outlier-detection approaches, and supply-chain hunting guides as idea sources.

talks.title: EWWW! Zeek Ate a Worm! | Jonathan Ham | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Walks through hunting worm-style SMB activity with Zeek logs, using a WannaCry packet capture as a worked case.
talks.summary:
The talk frames threat hunting around behavior rather than malware names. The speaker opens with a loose malware taxonomy, arguing that naming schemes from different vendors do not line up, so grouping threats by what they do is more useful. He separates trojans, viruses and worms, and explains why worms are the hardest to handle: they spread without user action, exploit network-facing weaknesses, and move at machine speed. A short history follows, from the 1988 Morris worm through Code Red and Blaster to the SMB-based spread used by WannaCry in 2017.

The core of the session is a walkthrough using Zeek on a packet capture. The example is a WannaCry capture with other traffic mixed in. Using Zeek's connection and SMB mapping logs, the speaker runs simple command-line queries to find one internal host making a large number of connection attempts to port 445 against outside addresses, while never reaching other hosts on its own subnet. The same logs reveal a hard-coded share path that works as an indicator of compromise. He then shows how a short Zeek script can raise alerts in real time, while noting that the manual approach is too slow for real response.

The takeaway is to hunt for anomalies such as connection failures, rarely used ports and unusual SMB volume, and to move repeated checks into detection tooling instead of relying on one-off searches.

talks.title: Jorge Orchilles | Emulating Adversaries Via Attack Chains | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Shows how chaining a few mapped techniques into an adversary emulation tests defenses faster than full red team runs.
talks.summary:
The speaker traces how red team and penetration testing programs at a large financial institution evolved. Narrowly scoped pen tests tended to miss what attackers actually do, and a MITRE ATT&CK view showed that only a handful of techniques involve exploitation, so an initial-access focus leaves much untested. Early end-to-end red team exercises, including a 2015 phishing test that flooded a commercial tool with reverse shells, eventually turned into repeated external engagements that kept teaching the same lessons. Because the red team was rerunning the same work, the team began working with defenders as a purple team, using threat intelligence to choose the actor to imitate.

The central case study is WastedLocker, the ransomware used by Evil Corp in an attack on Garmin that the speaker says lasted seven days and carried a 10 million dollar ransom demand. The attack was broken into the techniques it used, mapped to ATT&CK, and only the new impact behaviors were treated as untested. The emulation avoids touching production data: it creates new files, encrypts them, deletes the originals and downloads a ransom note. Tools discussed include the C2 Matrix for choosing command-and-control frameworks, RedELK for centralising red team logs, and Vector for planning engagements and tracking detection results over time.

The main takeaway is to emulate short chains of relevant behaviors rather than rerunning full engagements, and to deviate from a plan when a real attacker would. Teams should document blue team wins, automate repeatable techniques, and push for machine-readable threat intelligence so emulation can scale.

talks.title: Dan DeCloss | Purple Teaming With Runbooks for Plextrac | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Shows how a reporting platform's runbooks module coordinates red and blue team evidence for purple team engagements.
talks.summary:
This session is a product demonstration of the runbooks module in Plextrac, a reporting automation platform, aimed at purple team engagements where red and blue teams collect evidence together in real time. The speaker explains the motivation: cutting the time spent on reporting so testers can focus on finding and fixing issues. Runbooks act as reusable checklists grouped under methodologies. The platform ships with MITRE ATT&CK tactics, techniques and procedures, with procedures drawn from Atomic Red Team, and custom methodologies such as an OWASP web testing guide can be added.

The walkthrough builds a runbook by filtering tactics, techniques and procedures, then starts an engagement for a client. For each procedure, the red team records execution steps, timestamps, attachments and affected assets, and marks which items should appear as findings. Blue team operators add their own notes, log references and timestamps, showing whether activity was logged without raising an alert. Submitting the engagement generates a report carrying the ATT&CK tags, evidence and artifacts. Repeating the same runbook under one client feeds analytics that compare campaigns over time.

The speaker also shows a custom web authentication runbook, video evidence attached to a finding, and a remediation workflow with customizable sub-statuses, such as ready for retest, before a finding is validated and closed. The takeaway is that keeping evidence, collaboration and reporting in one place saves tester time and lets teams track trends across repeated purple team exercises.

talks.title: Everything You've Been Told About Threat Hunting is a Lie | Lesley Carhart | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Clarifies what threat hunting really means, how it differs from alert triage and incident response, and how to build testable hypotheses.
talks.summary:
Threat hunting is used loosely across marketing, products and training, so this keynote sets out a working definition. The speaker, an incident responder working on industrial control systems, traces attacks from manual intrusions to automated malware and then to living off the land, using stolen credentials and legitimate tools that slip past signature detection. Machines spot known patterns well, but a valid account misused by a human needs analyst judgment.

Hunting is proactive, so the talk separates it from alert triage, indicator sweeps, threat intelligence and incident response. It stresses groundwork first: an asset inventory, a network map, vulnerability tracking, basic detection, risk modeling around crown jewels and knowledge of available data sources. Good hypotheses draw on situational awareness, threat intelligence and domain expertise, and must be falsifiable and scoped in time and space. One example is an adversary moving laterally over SMB during a network merger week.

The hunt lifecycle runs from purpose and scoping through testing and feedback. Outcomes are evil found, which becomes incident response, a disproved hypothesis, or an inconclusive result exposing logging or training gaps. Failures come from skipped prerequisites, oversized scope, vague hypotheses and expecting a product to hunt for you.

talks.title: Doug Brush | You Done Have To Be Crazy To Work Here | WWHF Deadwood 2020
talks.teaser: Explores burnout, stigma, and practical self-care habits for security professionals under relentless operational pressure.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames mental health as a neglected cost of defending networks and data. Security work rewards constant vigilance, long hours, and crisis response, while industry culture often normalizes alcohol, macho toughness, and always-on availability. Cited research on chief security officers highlights widespread stress, poor disconnect habits, and short tenures that undercut program maturity.

The speaker recounts a personal path from teenage anxiety and panic through startup grind, family strain, a debilitating injury, job loss after relocation, and severe depression, including how therapy, medication, acceptance and commitment therapy, and peer support enabled recovery. He ties pandemic disruption and rising despair to pressures already inherent in the field, and contrasts harmful coping with deliberate self-care: boundary setting, reduced alerts, sleep and exercise routines, gratitude practice, and honest talk about treatment.

Practitioners are urged to treat mental wellness like preventive security work, challenge stigmatizing language, model time off and non-alcohol team bonding, and remember that responding with kindness—to themselves and colleagues—is a skill they can control when workloads are not.

talks.title: Upping Your Defenses and Detections For the Low Low Price of FREEEEE | Kent & Jordan
talks.teaser: 1 Hour details Upping Your Defenses and Detections For the Low Low Price of FREEEEE | Kent & Jordan.

talks.title: Enumerating Azure AD and ARM | Leron Gray | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting
talks.teaser: Walks through Azure AD and Azure Resource Manager concepts, then shows enumeration and privilege escalation with Storm Spotter.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) and Azure Resource Manager (ARM), the identity and deployment layers of Microsoft's cloud. It covers Azure AD objects such as users, groups, applications, service principals, devices and directory roles, and explains how an application relates to its service principals. For ARM, it walks through tenants, subscriptions, resource groups, resource providers and role-based access control, including why control plane and data plane permissions differ.

The speaker reviews the tools used to query these services, including the Azure CLI, several PowerShell modules and REST APIs, and points out that the CLI stores access and refresh tokens in the user's home directory. The main focus is Storm Spotter, a beta project that is not an official Microsoft product. It enumerates Azure AD and ARM and loads the results into Neo4j to draw an attack graph. In a live demo, enumeration with a sales employee's credentials shows that the account holds contributor rights over an entire subscription, not just the resources the department needs.

From there, the demo follows the graph to a resource group holding a virtual machine. Contributor rights allowed the demo account to reset the local administrator password on that machine. A cached Azure CLI folder on the virtual machine contained a refresh token belonging to a global administrator, which was copied over to take on that identity. The talk closes with defensive advice: apply least privilege, scope roles to single resources rather than whole subscriptions, audit and log permission changes, and use just-in-time access for sensitive machines.

talks.title: API Keys Now ? Taking Pen Test Into Amazon Cloud | December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting | Jim Shaver
talks.teaser: Walks through finding AWS API keys and scripted quick wins for a cloud penetration test, plus defensive checks to fix them.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at how a penetration tester can start an assessment of an AWS environment and find quick wins. The speaker explains where API keys tend to turn up: shared credentials files, environment variables, source code, infrastructure templates such as CloudFormation and Terraform, and the instance metadata service. A key found this way can be checked for validity and permissions before going further.

The middle of the talk walks through a set of Python scripts built on boto3. One checks whether a found key is valid, which groups it belongs to, and whether MFA is attached. Another confirms that CloudTrail logging is enabled in every region. A third dumps EC2 user data, which can contain embedded keys. For S3 buckets with versioning enabled, a script lists deleted object versions so earlier copies can be downloaded. The speaker also shows how a Windows administrator password can be recovered by supplying the instance's private key, and how a volume can be snapshotted, attached to another instance, and its files such as the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives copied out through S3, all using only the API.

The closing section turns to defense. The speaker recommends limiting who can change network configuration, restricting management access with security groups and VPN tunnels, logging every region even unused ones, enforcing least-privilege IAM, and confirming that keys can actually be rotated. Auditing tools mentioned for further reading include Scout Suite, Cartography and Prowler.

talks.title: Fantastic Conditional Access Policies | Dirk-jan Mollema | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Fantastic Conditional Access Policies | Dirk-jan Mollema | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting.

talks.title: Functional Testing/ A New Era of Pentesting | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting | Jon Helmus
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Functional Testing/ A New Era of Pentesting | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting | Jon Helmus.

talks.title: Do yer best! Preparing for a Cloud Pentest | The December Roundup-Cloud Pentesting | Andrew Krug
talks.teaser: Offers 101 advice on preparing an organization and its cloud environment for a penetration test.
talks.summary:
This 101-style talk offers advice on preparing for a cloud penetration test, aimed at people arriving at pen testing from a systems administration or defensive background. It starts with the team. Scopeless red team exercises are harder on staff than scoped tests, so the speaker suggests starting small, informing stakeholders where possible, and agreeing in advance on when people should be brought into a live exercise. Testers should be onboarded like team members, communication channels should not reveal the test early, and the cloud provider should be notified beforehand.

The middle of the talk covers preparing the environment. A shared global allow or deny list of tester IPs can live in a place like an S3 bucket and be pushed to firewall and WAF tooling, then removed after the engagement. Testers should also supply an observable artifacts list with timestamps, showing which detections fired and supporting a kill chain review. That depends on tamper-resistant logs, so the speaker describes copying logs into a separate security account and notes a recent S3 object lock feature as a simpler option. Consistent tagging and AWS Organizations help trace activity later, and patching beforehand reduces noise.

The talk closes with identity. The speaker recommends moving developers from long-lived access keys to single sign-on, which now supports hardware tokens for both console and command line use. Final advice is to start small, iterate, and look after the team.

talks.title: Securing a Remote Workforce with Technology and Training | Ryan Hendricks | 1 Hours
talks.teaser: Covers how a distributed workforce changes endpoint, VPN, DNS and access controls, plus awareness training ideas.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by separating an office workforce from a distributed one, where staff work from any location on portable systems and there is no clear trusted network edge. The speaker argues that remote work offered temporarily is different from an organization that has deliberately become fully distributed. Web attacks, phishing and malware still reach the endpoint, but the proxies, filtering and network-based tools that once protected it no longer sit in the path, and incident response, forensics and tech support all struggle without network control.

The middle of the talk covers the network. A full VPN tunnel sends all traffic through corporate controls but can overwhelm the tunnel at scale, while a split tunnel leaves home traffic unprotected, which creates a false sense of security if staff assume the VPN covers everything. Overlapping RFC 1918 address ranges with home networks can cause routing faults. Home ISPs may hand out globally routable IPv6 addresses to devices even when the corporate network does not use IPv6. Because DNS often comes from the ISP, the organization loses control over resolution, and cloud access rules based on corporate source IP addresses stop working. The endpoint firewall, endpoint device management, network inspection and single sign-on with multi-factor authentication become the controls to rely on.

The closing section recommends updating security awareness for the new setting. Topics include VPN use and when to disconnect, home router and public Wi-Fi risks, printing and data destruction at home, and phishing. The speaker suggests showing staff live demonstrations of a phishing macro, remote access and ransomware in a controlled environment, rather than only describing them. The main takeaway is to adapt controls to a distributed workforce and to explain those changes to staff.

talks.title: Move Aside Script Kiddies–Malware Execution in the Age of Advanced Defenses | Joff Thyer | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Move Aside Script Kiddies–Malware Execution in the Age of Advanced Defenses | Joff Thyer | 1 Hour.

talks.title: Play to Win: Getting Your Dream Cybersecurity Job | Kip Boyle | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Gives job seekers a hiring manager's view on choosing, preparing for, and landing a cybersecurity role.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a hiring manager's perspective on breaking into cybersecurity and becoming a candidate that employers want to hire. The speaker frames the search as four blockers: not knowing the exact job title and the kind of employer that suits you, unrecognized skill gaps, convincing a manager to take a chance on you, and weak job-hunting habits. To tackle the first, he suggests a career mind map, the CyberSeek site for demand and career paths, and a DISC personality assessment to clarify preferred working conditions.

For skill gaps, he recommends choosing three target employers, comparing their job postings with your own experience in a matrix, and writing the gaps down. Certifications should be picked from job descriptions because applicant tracking systems screen on them, and a home lab, ideally built in a cloud free tier, provides hands-on practice. Hiring managers mainly ask whether a candidate can contribute on day one and shows real passion, which can be demonstrated through transferable experience, volunteering, open-source work or conference involvement.

For job hunting, he advises defining work conditions, filtering LinkedIn job listings, and applying even when you match only about half the requirements. He also suggests finding an insider at the target company, then posting about the role and tagging that person with a tailored resume attached. In the Q&A, he advises a small, low-pressure question when following up with a contact, and notes that entry-level security jobs often expect more than people assume, so feeder roles can serve as stepping stones.

talks.title: You’re* Adversary Within: The Golden Age of Insider Threats | Adam Mashinchi | The Roundup
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of You’re* Adversary Within: The Golden Age of Insider Threats | Adam Mashinchi | The Roundup.
talks.summary: Adam Meushaw frames remote-work insider threats as easier than ever thanks to consumer VPNs, Firefox Send-style exfil, unmanaged BYOD, and sanctioned cloud drives. He urges red teams to emulate post-compromise insiders without exploits, focusing on crown-jewel theft via Dropbox or Google Drive while blue teams baseline DNS, PowerShell in HR, and heartbeat beacons with realistic jitter limits. Purple teams should run joint risk priority assessments ranking easy-to-detect disasters such as terabyte exfiltration, then iterate repeatable Dropbox versus Drive tests. He cautions breach-and-attack simulation agents miss human-context abuse and highlights masked NTLM password auditing for enterprises.

talks.title: FIN6 Emulation Plan | Forrest Carver | The Roundup
talks.teaser: MITRE's public FIN6 adversary emulation plan pairs CTI-backed scenarios with markdown and YAML for purple team defense testing.
talks.summary:
The session introduces the first public release of a FIN6 adversary emulation plan from MITRE’s Center for Threat-Informed Defense, a nonprofit effort that partners with industry to publish threat-informed research. FIN6 was chosen as the inaugural project because public reporting is solid, the group relies heavily on commodity tooling, and many sponsors sit in financial services. The presenters frame the work as lowering the bar for faithful purple teaming without replacing skilled red team operators.

The plan stitches together an intelligence summary, a graphical operations flow, and phased procedures mapped to MITRE ATT&CK sub-techniques. Three scenario branches cover historic point-of-sale targeting, e-commerce-style compromises, and more recent ransomware and extortion patterns. Human teams can walk the linear markdown steps line by line, while automation-focused groups can mirror the same logic in YAML shaped like familiar Atomic Red Team and Caldera patterns, with CTI citations and procedure groups tying the formats together. Execution examples emphasize accessible tooling such as Metasploit alongside alternatives when licenses differ, plus living-off-the-land actions on hosts.

Practitioners are pointed to the open GitHub library, encouraged to file feedback, and told that a Caldera plugin is planned to ingest these plans directly. Upcoming library entries will broaden beyond finance-focused actors while keeping the same template discipline and public-intelligence-only sourcing unless partners can safely release newer details.

talks.title: Unicorn Evangelism: The Case for Purple Teaming | Kent Icker & Jordan Drysdale | The Roundup
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Unicorn Evangelism: The Case for Purple Teaming | Kent Icker & Jordan Drysdale | The Roundup.

talks.title: From 0 to 1: Getting Your Adversary Emulation Program Up and Running | Dan DeCloss | The Roundup
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding From 0 to 1: Getting Your Adversary Emulation Program Up and Running | Dan DeCloss | The Roundup.

talks.title: Attacker Emulation in the Age of Endpoint Detection and Response | Joff Thyer | The Roundup
talks.teaser: Shows how assumed-compromise tests evade well-tuned EDR through stageless C2, proxied reconnaissance and quieter lateral movement.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at attacker emulation against mature environments that run endpoint detection and response, application whitelisting and script logging. The speaker places a tester on a standard Windows 10 workstation with an ordinary user account, then focuses on establishing a command-and-control channel with minimal indicators. Recommended tactics include a stageless payload relayed through a content delivery network and running .NET tooling through that channel instead of dropping executables on the endpoint.

Later stages cover reconnaissance, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Directory queries are proxied through a SOCKS listener so that the traffic lands on domain controllers rather than the host, and Kerberoasting is run early with offline cracking. Password spraying over Kerberos is used to avoid detections keyed to logon failure events, while SMB relaying, WMI and RDP are favoured for lateral movement because they produce fewer events than PsExec. The speaker also demonstrates how AMSI flagged harmless strings, and how stripping comments from scripts or downgrading PowerShell reduced scanning.

The main takeaway is to start quietly to reach objectives, then raise the noise so defenders can see which activity their tooling catches. Each technique should be mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and timestamped for the blue team, and blocking responses should be avoided so the exercise can continue. Results are most useful when they feed back into detection tuning.

talks.title: The Secret Thoughts of a Successful Hacker | Nadean Tanner | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Explores imposter syndrome and pluralistic ignorance among security practitioners, with practical mindset advice for overcoming self-doubt.
talks.summary:
Nadine Tanner opens by describing imposter syndrome as a widespread experience among skilled security professionals, noting that high achievers feel it especially strongly. She sketches several forms it takes, including the perfectionist, the expert, the soloist and the multitasker, each of which measures competence differently. She also introduces pluralistic ignorance, where people in a room assume they alone are lost while everyone else seems to understand.

The middle of the talk points to public figures who admitted to feeling like frauds, including Albert Einstein, a civil rights activist and poet, actress Emma Watson and former WHO head Margaret Chan. Tanner presents a four-stage model of competence, from unconscious incompetence through to unconscious competence, and warns that complacency is a danger for experienced people. Her practical advice is to drop self-limiting words such as "but", "never", "impossible" and "try" from internal dialogue, to take stretch assignments, and to treat mistakes as part of learning. She also shares her own doubts around writing books and sitting certification exams.

She closes by encouraging listeners to find a mentor and to become one, reminding them that a little self-doubt keeps people grounded. In the question session she argues that apparent overconfidence often hides a fear of looking incompetent. The main takeaway is that awareness and open conversation with trusted peers make the feeling easier to manage.

talks.title: The Swag Bag Lab and Hardware Hackin’ | Rick Wisser | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap SPI programmers, binwalk and recon turn router and car firmware into a hands-on hardware lab.
talks.summary:
The session centers on the Swag Bag Lab, a remote hands-on exercise created after the speaker's in-person labs proved hard to run virtually. Attendees received a CH341A USB programmer and a SPI flash chip whose firmware had been modified to hide a chain of clues in its strings. Participants dump the chip with flashrom, run binwalk recursively to extract the filesystem, and follow the clues through strings output, a base64 string and a simple substitution cipher.

The speaker then walks through an intermission on firmware taken from a Mazda head unit, using the same chip and programmer. The analysis used binwalk to surface a developer name and a kernel version with publicly known vulnerabilities, and a password file whose hashes were cracked with John. The speaker notes that FCC ID records can reveal the manufacturer and wireless protocols, and that schematics and datasheets help map a board's signal paths.

The closing discussion frames a methodology of preparation, reconnaissance, scanning, analysis and attack surface, with reconnaissance revisited as new findings appear. Practical advice includes starting with inexpensive electronics from garage sales, reviewing responsible disclosure before publishing findings, and avoiding cellular networks and live servers that are not authorized for testing. The speaker also previewed a planned IoT pen testing class and a possible hackable badge.

talks.title: Offensive Maldocs in 2020 | Joe Leon & Matt Grandy | 1 Hour | 4K
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Offensive Maldocs in 2020 | Joe Leon & Matt Grandy | 1 Hour | 4K.

talks.title: Workshop: Linux and Security Basics Hands On | Bill Stearns | 4 Hours
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Workshop: Linux and Security Basics Hands On | Bill Stearns | 4 Hours.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This hands-on workshop, presented by Bill Stearns alongside contributors from Black Hills Information Security and Active Countermeasures, provides an introductory yet practical guide to navigating, managing, and securing Linux systems via the command line. Designed as a safe learning environment, the session walks participants through foundational administration tasks, remote access setup, essential shell commands, system inspection, file navigation, and secure remote operations using SSH.

### Key Topics
- **Initial System Setup and Package Management:** Connecting to Linux instances (cloud VMs such as DigitalOcean, local VMs, or physical hosts), immediately resetting root passwords to prevent brute-force attacks, testing network/DNS reachability, using `apt update` and `apt full-upgrade`, and managing administrative rights via `sudo`.
- **Command Line Essentials & Process Management:** Viewing running processes using tree/forest views (`ps axf`), managing long outputs using the `less` pager, filtering strings with `grep`, capturing errors/stdout redirection (`2>&1`), and editing configuration files with `nano`.
- **System Hardware & Storage Inspection:** Querying hardware characteristics with `lshw`, reviewing block storage devices and partitions using `lsblk`, checking mounted file systems with `df -h` and `mount`, and distinguishing between physical filesystems (ext4) and virtual/kernel pseudo-filesystems (`/proc`, `/sys`, `tmpfs`).
- **Network Configuration & Monitoring:** Evaluating network interfaces with `ifconfig` and modern `ip addr` commands, inspecting routes via `route -n` and `ip route`, determining public IP addresses using simple HTTP queries via `netcat`, and tracking live performance metrics with tools like `top`, `atop`, and `gkrrelm`.
- **Filesystem Navigation & Remote Operations:** Navigating paths, utilizing the File System Hierarchy Standard (FHS), leveraging text-based file managers like Midnight Commander (`mc`), transferring files securely over the network with `scp`, and configuring passwordless authentication with SSH keys.

### Technical Details
- **User & Privilege Configuration:** Stearns emphasizes avoiding daily administrative operations as the root user. Instead, administrators should create non-root user accounts (e.g., via `useradd -m -G sudo labuser` or `adduser`), manage passwords with `passwd`, and utilize `sudo` for elevated tasks.
- **Process & Text Manipulation:** Running `ps axf | less -s` enables horizontal and vertical scrolling across process trees without wrapping. Stearns shows how chaining pipes—such as `sudo ps axf | grep nginx | grep -v grep`—isolates targeted daemon processes, while standard output and standard error redirection can be combined into files using `> file.txt 2>&1`.
- **Network Discovery & Verification:** Verifying ICMP and DNS connectivity is demonstrated via `ping -c 5 -n 8.8.8.8` and pinging hostnames. Stearns demonstrates raw socket HTTP interaction by echoing `GET /` into `nc icanhazip.com 80` to retrieve an outbound public IP address from NAT/virtual environments.
- **Remote File Management & SSH Hardening:** File transfers across hosts are executed using `scp [source] [destination]`. For SSH access (`sshd` on port 22), Stearns explains troubleshooting connection handshakes with `ssh -v`, and replacing standard password-based authentication by generating RSA key pairs (`id_rsa` and `id_rsa.pub` at 3072 bits) inside permissions-restricted directories (`chmod 700 ~/.ssh`).

### Takeaways
Command-line administration relies heavily on understanding core diagnostic tools, standard file locations, and secure administration habits. Stearns stresses avoiding root logins, inspecting system performance bottlenecks using granular tools like `atop`, moving data via encrypted SSH channels, and using accessible tools like `nano` and Midnight Commander to comfortably manage remote Linux infrastructure.

talks.title: Linux Forensics Magical Mystery Tour II: It's All About the Logs | Hal Pomeranz | 1 Hour | 4K
talks.teaser: Shows how to read Linux syslog, web, login and auditd logs, and recover deleted entries from unallocated disk space.
talks.summary:
Hal Pomeranz opens with the core problem: on Linux, logging is left to each application, so a custom backdoor may leave no record, and attackers often delete or trim entries. He suggests comparing local logs against any copies shipped to a central collector, and alerting when a host stops sending logs, since silence can signal compromise.

He then walks through the formats an investigator will meet. Classic syslog lines omit the year and use local time without an offset, which complicates archived data and multi-timezone systems. Apache-style web logs include an offset but use a date format that is hard to sort, and their timestamps can appear out of order because they are recorded when a request completes. For deleted material, he runs strings over unallocated blocks and greps for timestamp patterns to recover old entries. For binary login records, he demonstrates last and lastb against wtmp and btmp, and explains that lastlog from a mounted image may need a chroot into that image because its format varies across systems.

The final section covers kernel auditing with auditd, which records system calls and is harder to disable than ordinary logging. Audit records use epoch timestamps and grouping IDs, and he shows how ausearch, aureport and aulast turn them into readable output, including decoding hex-encoded command lines. He closes by advising teams to configure auditd before an incident and to select high-value rules, since broad auditing can slow a machine.

talks.title: Keynote Roundtable | Paul Vixie, Lesley Carhart, Marcus J Carey, & John Strand | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Keynote Roundtable | Paul Vixie, Lesley Carhart, Marcus J Carey, & John Strand | 1 Hour.

talks.title: Improve Your Security Posture with TrustedSec | Ben Ten & Larry Spohn | 1 Hour
talks.teaser: Walks through a pen test path from nmap scanning to Tomcat login and RDP session hijacking, with matching detections.
talks.summary:
This session, presented by two penetration testers from TrustedSec, argues that many defensive tools look for known exploits and payloads, while a penetration test can often reach domain admin without using any exploit. The speakers walk through an attack path built in a lab, beginning with network discovery. They explain how Nmap options affect visibility: choosing a source port that resembles Kerberos on internal tests or DNS on external ones, using half-open scans, skipping ping and DNS lookups, and scanning one port at a time so that results stay organized and scanning is less noisy.

The demo then moves to a Tomcat host on port 8080. Default credentials were recovered with a Metasploit module, and the valid login was used to upload a web application archive that gave a command shell. From that foothold, the presenters listed domain users from the domain controller. They then showed how a local administrator can take over a disconnected domain admin's remote desktop session using tscon, started through a newly created service, with no exploit and no credential theft.

For defenders, the talk focuses on the Windows events that reveal this activity. Service creation events (7045) and process command-line auditing (4688) can surface the sc create and tscon commands, and Winlogbeat can forward those logs into Elastic and Kibana. The main takeaways are to enable command-line logging, to watch for tscon with a destination session, and to have administrators log out rather than leave privileged sessions disconnected, since any local admin on that machine can hijack them.

talks.title: Intro to Tabletop Exercises with Amanda Berlin & Jeremy Mio (1 Hour)
talks.teaser: Walks through building tabletop exercises, playbooks and after-action reports, with a short PowerShell detection scenario.
talks.summary:
The session introduces tabletop exercises as a way to test defensive detection and response. The speakers say a useful exercise can be as short as fifteen minutes, with a clear goal, a scenario read aloud to everyone, and an after-action report that records gaps and action items. They suggest starting with IT staff and bringing in business units such as HR, legal and executives gradually, framing the scenario around each group's own impact. A sample scenario involves a backdoor found on surveillance cameras in an executive conference room, which raises questions about asset inventory, firmware, vendor support and internet exposure.

Playbooks are the next topic, presented as flexible guidance rather than rigid procedure. Useful playbooks include an objective statement, a defined scope, escalation paths, and a split between high-fidelity playbooks that must be followed closely and investigative ones that allow judgment. As teams mature, playbooks can point to hunting queries, detection rules and MITRE ATT&CK techniques, so a procedural exercise can grow into a technical one. One technical example covers a PowerShell execution policy bypass dropper, where module logging and event viewer entries reveal the activity. In the Q&A, the speakers suggest tying risk to compliance or business impact to win management sign-off, with short- and long-term recommendations.

The multi-day class version uses role-played companies in sectors such as healthcare, manufacturing and banking, where budgets, weaknesses and dice rolls shape outcomes. The main takeaways are to start small, keep the tone constructive by recording strengths, and connect every playbook to the controls it depends on. Management should also approve the gaps the organization accepts.

talks.title: Excellent Architecture : Avoid Common Mistakes in Security Operations w/ Chris Crowley (1 Hour)
talks.teaser: Outlines a reference architecture for security operations centers and the common design failures that undermine them.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how security operations centers should be organized and where they commonly go wrong. It opens with a threat model that sorts adversaries by resources: a low-cost group reusing public vulnerabilities, a mid-tier group that discovers its own, and a well-funded group that can exploit almost anything. From there it lays out a reference architecture of functional components, including a steering committee, command center, monitoring, threat intelligence, incident handling, forensics, and self-assessment.

Each component gets practical guidance. The steering committee sets success criteria and gives the center one consistent direction, with system owners rating each system's impact on function, information, and recoverability. Incident handling is split into janitorial cleanup, firefighting during active incidents, and early identification of sophisticated attackers. Self-assessment covers configuration monitoring, vulnerability management measured by patching rather than scan counts, penetration testing that demonstrates impact, and regular exercises. For maturity, he points to a free SOC-CMM spreadsheet and a MITRE ATT&CK defensive gap analysis.

The main failures are having no architecture vision, skipping the steering committee, and never self-assessing. The takeaways are to agree on an architecture before buying technology, involve constituents early, embed pen testers with defenders, schedule short daily training, and try a self-assessment before paying for a third-party audit.

talks.title: How to Give Technical Talks w Bill Stearns (2-Hours)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in How to Give Technical Talks w Bill Stearns (2-Hours).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Wild West Hackin' Fest webcast, Bill Stearns (Active Countermeasures and Black Hills Information Security) presents a comprehensive guide on how to prepare and deliver effective technical presentations. Drawing on more than twenty years of industry and training experience, Stearns emphasizes that the primary goal of a technical talk is not merely reciting commands or facts, but motivating the audience and conveying genuine enthusiasm for the topic. The session offers practical advice spanning preparation logistics, slide design, vocal delivery, hands-on lab development, handling stage fright, and interacting with attendees.

### Key Topics
- **Audience Understanding and Topic Scope**: Selecting a topic requires understanding the specific audience background and experience level. As demonstrated by the "cooking chicken" exercise, a general topic cannot be developed effectively without knowing the audience's preexisting knowledge and interests.
- **Preparation and Logistical Redundancy**: Presenters must arrive early to test equipment and audio-visual setups. Stearns strongly advocates for hardware redundancy, advising speakers to carry multiple laptops, backup presentation remotes, spare batteries, display converters (DVI, HDMI, VGA), and backup internet access like cellular Wi-Fi pucks. Presentation files should exist on the laptop, online, and on a USB thumb drive kept in pocket.
- **Slide Design and Pacing**: Slides should feature high-contrast formatting (dark text on light backgrounds) and readable fonts. Speakers should use concise phrases or visual cues rather than full scripts to avoid sounding robotic. A baseline pacing rule of approximately two minutes per slide is recommended, along with reserving 15% to 25% of time for questions.
- **Overcoming Nervousness and Filler Words**: Rather than addressing a crowd collectively, speakers should treat presentations as a sequence of one-on-one conversations. To eliminate filler words, Stearns suggests practicing with an assistant who drops dollar coins into a glass jar whenever a filler is spoken.
- **Hands-On Lab Design**: Technical labs should prioritize the "light bulb moment" over laborious setup. Stearns outlines a three-tier lab structure comprising a basic goal description, optional hints, and explicit step-by-step commands. Using packaged cross-platform software or preconfigured cloud VMs is encouraged over requiring students to compile source code.

### Technical Details & Speaker Equipment
Stearns shares his specific setup and recommendations for virtual and in-person speaking:
- Hardware: Razer webcam, Blue Yeti microphone, in-ear monitor, and dedicated LED lights to properly illuminate darker spaces.
- Live Setup: Presentation remotes (such as Keyspan or Targus) with separate high-powered AAA laser pointers, avoiding low-power built-in watch battery pointers.
- Power and Travel: Verifying multi-voltage compatibility (110–240V, 50/60Hz) and bringing appropriate plug adapters for international events.

### Takeaways
- **Practice and Validation**: Rehearse presentations end-to-end with a timer. Record short video segments to review audio and video independently before combining them. Validate technical slides and lab walkthroughs with peer reviewers on fresh systems.
- **Humility and Authenticity**: It is critical to admit when you do not know an answer rather than fabricating explanations, followed by researching the answer and delivering it later.
- **Audience Connection**: Ditch protective physical barriers like podiums. Engage attendees visually, adjust the technical depth based on audience feedback, and provide persistent discussion channels (such as Discord) for continuous learning.

talks.title: Zoom isn’t Insecure! So Why is it so Insecure w Doc Blackburn 1 Hour BHIS HEVC
talks.teaser: Argues that security means managing insecurity, using Zoom's default settings and meeting exposure as a case study.
talks.summary:
When many organizations moved to video conferencing during the pandemic, the speaker used Zoom as a case study for a wider point: asking whether a product is secure is the wrong question. Products ship with many features enabled by default, and each added feature tends to reduce security. Since no one can guarantee full protection and attackers need only one weakness, defenders are really managing levels of insecurity within a limited budget.

The Zoom examples show how this plays out. Short numeric meeting IDs could be found by automated number-guessing tools, which let uninvited people join meetings and led to "zoom bombing"; waiting rooms and required passwords were added later. Early encryption used a weak mode with a 128-bit key, and stronger options were rolled out afterward. A personal meeting ID never expires, so anyone who has it can join at any time, and a default password was reused for new meetings unless it was changed each time. The speaker also counted more than 100 settings, many with sub-options, which took hours to review. The vulnerabilities did not change as the product grew; the threat around it did.

The practical takeaways start with understanding the use cases, the data classification and how users behave, then turning off features the business does not need. Defense in depth and an assumption of compromise matter more than any single product setting, and patching needs a timely plan rather than ad hoc fixes. When the business accepts a risk, the residual risk should be documented and signed off by the person who owns the budget. Security decisions are business decisions, and communicating risk with clear stories and cost estimates is part of the job.

talks.summary: Jake Williams shows how to find software vulnerabilities by watching how applications change files and registry entries, start processes, and handle network traffic. talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Not Just Evil: Hacking Mainframes with Network Job Entry
talks.teaser: Shows how Network Job Entry on IBM z/OS mainframes can be abused to run jobs as other users across trusted nodes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a moment the speaker saw at a payments company, where a developer on a development system created a user on production by submitting a job. It then gives a primer on z/OS batch processing, covering Job Control Language (JCL) job cards, steps and data definitions, and the JES2 subsystem that queues and runs jobs. Jobs run under the submitter's identity unless another user is named and the security system permits the switch.

The central section covers Network Job Entry (NJE), which passes jobs and results between mainframes. The speaker explains the node configuration, the TCP connection on port 175, the framing of blocks and records with their control bytes, and the sign-on record that can carry node passwords. Captured traffic can be decoded from EBCDIC for inspection. The attack path involves learning the local and remote node names, using an Nmap script to find remote nodes that accept connections, and impersonating a trusted node. Many sites trust every node, so a connected peer can submit JCL as other users, which the speaker demonstrates by running Unix and TSO commands on a remote system.

The speaker releases a Python library with tools to send NJE commands, enumerate active TSO users, submit JCL under a chosen user, and analyze captured packets. For defenders, the takeaway is to use certificate authentication and TLS rather than plaintext passwords, remove decommissioned nodes from configurations, and limit which nodes and users are trusted.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Help Me Help You Hurt Yourself
talks.teaser: Shows how poor client communication wastes penetration test time and money, with field examples from both sides.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how weak communication between penetration testing clients and testers wastes money, time and the value of an engagement. The speaker treats it as a shared problem, since both sides gain when questions are answered and information flows clearly before and during a test. The examples come from real field work.

One client delivered an application only as screenshots, and it was still unfinished. Pages changed during testing, so an issue found on one day was gone the next, and the test was invalidated. In another engagement, unanswered emails meant one function could not be tested, and the report had to say so. A separate case involved an administrator who did not respond, so the tester stayed within scope, reached domain administrator, and found sensitive personal records that ended up in the report. On the tester side, a colleague who avoided scoping questions could not effectively reach targets in a different region.

A short, large external test went better when the team asked the client directly which assets were the crown jewels and what an attacker would target. A medical device finding discussed at DEF CON stalled because client communication broke down, and a third party extended the timeline. The takeaways are to ask questions early, keep communication open and direct, and stay courteous, because testers and clients will work together again.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Breaking Into Banks Like A Boss!
talks.teaser: Walks through a physical penetration tester's process of recon, cover stories and entry into secured buildings.
talks.summary:
Brice Self argues that physical penetration testing is measured by how well existing controls hold up against someone who gets past the front door, and that the process of reaching a target is the most overlooked part of the field. He presents a repeatable approach built from his own engagements at banks and other large buildings, and he stresses that the process matters more than any single lock or badge.

The approach moves through stages. Observation happens from a distance, using street-level maps and watching foot traffic, entrances, and where employees park. Reconnaissance means entering the building to see who challenges visitors and how, using delivery pretexts and checks such as dumpster searches to learn policies. Final preparation picks guard shift changes and a cover story, such as posing as an internet provider contractor with a fake badge. During execution he separates cover for status, the reason for being there, from cover for action, the reason for each specific movement, and describes feigned confusion, persistence, and tailgating. In one bank, a workstation on a restricted floor was unlocked with its password visible on the monitor.

He closes with lessons learned: clients may blame the tester, imagery such as Street View goes out of date, and remediation tests often reveal new paths. His defensive advice centres on training staff on visitor processes, verifying visitors through the named employee, refusing to tailgate even familiar colleagues, and not giving internal details to strangers.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): 30 Minute Demo - PlexTrac
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a platform that turns pentest findings into reports, tracks remediation, and hands results to blue teams.
talks.summary:
The talk is a live demo of PlexTrac, a platform for writing penetration test reports. The presenter, a sales engineer, shows how work is organized by client and report, and how each finding holds standard fields such as severity, affected assets, screenshots and code samples. Findings can be started blank, copied from a shared write-ups database, or imported from scanner output such as Burp.

Once a finding is handed off, the blue team can assign it and log remediation steps in a running history, with two-way Jira and ServiceNow ticket sync available. Reports export to Word, Markdown or CSV using custom templates, and tags can map findings to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques for later filtering. Clients can be given analyst-role access limited to their own data, and an assessments module turns questionnaires such as CMMC or NIST RMF into report content.

The demo closes with analytics on severity, tags and remediation trends, including whether new findings outpace closed ones. The main takeaway is that keeping testing data, reporting and remediation in one place cuts copy-and-paste and makes handoffs easier to follow.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): 30 Minute Demo - Guardicore
talks.teaser: A live walkthrough shows how agent-based microsegmentation maps east-west flows and hardens billing apps in hybrid cloud.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why multi-cloud and hybrid estates often lack cohesive controls over sensitive workloads, then shifts to Guardicore’s focus on visibility, segmentation, breach detection, and response. The presenter contrasts classic firewall VLAN projects with east-west traffic reality: flat networks, many unnecessary open ports, and painful change windows when apps move between segments.

The core narrative is microsegmentation delivered through host agents and a proprietary kernel driver that sees process-level communication without relying on native host firewalls. A billed production example walks from discovery (Tomcat to database flows) through application ring-fencing in alert mode, allow rules for legitimate jump-box access, and tightening to block. Labeling groups assets from naming, CMDB feeds, or ad hoc UI tagging; historical connection maps support compliance evidence and filtered views of internal traffic.

The close briefly covers dynamic deception for suspicious outbound probes, quarantine orchestration, and reputation scoring for IPs, processes, and domains. Practitioners should take away a phased model—visualize, alert, allow known dependencies, then enforce—and the mention of Infection Monkey as a free open-source way to stress-test segmentation before policies harden.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): KEYNOTE - Time Travel & GPS F*ckery
talks.teaser: Explains how GPS and other satellite navigation signals can be spoofed and presents Whelan, an open-source sensor for detecting it.
talks.summary:
The keynote gives a high-level look at satellite navigation, where satellites broadcast their position and transmission time and a receiver uses signals from several of them to work out location. It explains that civilian signals are unauthenticated and weak, so they can be spoofed with inexpensive software-defined radio hardware and open-source tools. Many industries, from financial trading to shipping and trucking fleets, depend on these signals for time and position.

The speakers reviewed reported spoofing incidents. Fishing boats on the Black Sea and facilities around Moscow saw false positions, and Syria was described as an area where spoofing was reportedly used to protect locations from guided munitions. Anomalies near the port of Shanghai involved both satellite navigation and AIS vessel data. They also noted that the US Navy reinstated celestial navigation training after two Pacific ship incidents, a link they framed as speculation. Few civilian tools existed to detect such manipulation, which motivated their project.

The project, called Whelan, is an open-source sensor built on a Raspberry Pi with three GNSS receivers that compare position and time across GPS, GLONASS and Galileo. Readings are stored in InfluxDB, processed with Grafana, and alerts go to Discord when values drift beyond expected bounds. Planned work includes a shared site for crowdsourced data, more RF inputs such as ADS-B and AIS, and faster alerting. The closing call was for listeners to identify other unauthenticated RF signals their organizations depend on and build detection for them.
