talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Mapping and Testing Your Network to ATT&CK with Free Tools
talks.teaser: Shows how a small team maps detection coverage to MITRE ATT&CK using free tools and validates alerts with Atomic Red Team.
talks.summary:
The speaker's manager asked what the team could detect and how that coverage would be tracked. An early attempt to document alerts across eleven Confluence pages, with Sigma rules for about 60 techniques, did not scale. The speaker then turned to the free MITRE ATT&CK Navigator, which renders coverage as JSON-driven layers that can be embedded in other pages, and to ATT&CK's publicly available group and tool data for threat intelligence, checked against the update dates shown on each entry.

The core of the talk is a Python 3 tool that turns hand-written YAML files into Navigator layers. The first file grades data sources, such as file monitoring, on completeness, timeliness, consistency and retention. The speaker found this the hardest part, since colleagues were slow to respond. The second file lists verified alerts with dates, confidence scores and EDR locations, producing a layer that separates logged techniques from detected ones. Overlaying techniques used by Iranian groups on that coverage gave a gap analysis the speaker used when that threat was in the news. Atomic Red Team then tested the alerts by ATT&CK ID, with the speaker running tests by hand first to understand them.

The takeaways are that a documented grading rubric makes the inventory repeatable, and that testing works better in small sections than by firing everything at once. Alerts can also be pulled from security tools by script to keep the detection file current. The speaker estimated the whole effort took a small team about a month.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Teaching And Mentoring Others
talks.teaser: Guidance on teaching and mentoring in information security helps practitioners share knowledge even when they feel unqualified.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by describing imposter feelings about standing in front of a security audience, then walks through a personal path from a rural high school typing class through liberal arts detours, an IT degree, college help-desk work, and a first security analyst role where senior networking staff patiently answered basic questions. A professor’s invite to guest-speak at a cybersecurity club despite feeling brand new later resurfaced when former students became colleagues, including a supervisor and a full-time threat intelligence teammate.

The middle ties encouragement from mentors to outward sharing: an unpolished OSEP study blog, a failed first exam attempt, and a joking “ask me anything” tweet that grew into peer support online. The core message is that audiences already know teachable things—technical or not—and can teach, encourage, challenge, and still learn from the people they help. A memorable line from a high school teacher frames the mindset: you have got to learn to learn.

The close lists low-barrier ways to engage: CyberPatriot or computer classes, career fairs, short blogs, videos, lab mentoring, and conference or meetup talks, with room to be bad at first. Q&A contrasts an original interest in offensive lab work with landing in threat hunting, and briefly notes shifting defender focus from hot indicators toward behavioral context and richer analytics—while agreeing defenses are gaining better environmental understanding than log-triage alone.

talks.title: WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Labours Of Hercules - Be Like Phil
talks.teaser: Kevin Johnson analyzes WWHF 2020 (Virtual): Labours Of Hercules - Be Like Phil.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Kevin Johnson, CEO of Secure Ideas, presents 'Labours of Hercules—Be Like Phil,' using Disney's Hercules movie and its mentor character Phil as a framework for addressing the cybersecurity industry's real problems: not a talent shortage, but high training costs, unclear career paths, misinformation, and inadequate ethics education. Johnson advocates reframing cybersecurity as a skilled trade with formal mentorship pathways rather than an exclusive high-level profession.

## Key Problems Identified
Johnson highlights critical barriers: (1) training costs of $6,000–$7,000+ per course exclude many learners; (2) people lack understanding of career progression and where to focus learning; (3) incorrect technical information spreads online (citing a YouTube 'next-gen hacker 101' video that misinterprets traceroute output); (4) ethical and legal boundaries of security work aren't consistently taught—he describes a company scanning internet hosts without permission and questions how to teach people when and when not to apply penetration testing skills.

## The Apprentice-Journeyman-Mentor Model
Johnson proposes a three-stage progression: Apprentice (entry-level with defined foundational skills), Journeyman (competent practitioner capable of leading projects and consulting), and Mentor (guide for the next generation). Mentorship is bidirectional; mentors learn from mentees, and everyone at every level should mentor others. Johnson explicitly rejects the term 'master' due to negative connotations, emphasizing instead that reaching mentor status is only the beginning of responsibility, not an endpoint.

## Building Formal Mentorship Programs
Johnson outlines five implementation steps:

1. **Formalize the program:** Define goals, structure, communication plan, and schedule before launch. Clearly communicate expectations to all participants. Avoid ad-hoc mentoring ('we'll figure it out when we have time').

2. **Identify mentors actively:** Don't post open calls; actively recruit and engage potential mentors. Drag them into the program and work with them on adjusting plans.

3. **Provide multiple learning paths:** People learn differently. Some learn through reading, others via video, audio podcasts, hands-on practice, or group discussion. Secure Ideas uses written materials, recorded videos, live webcasts, Slack workspaces, and consultants available for real-time questions.

4. **Set clear SLAs:** Establish and communicate response time expectations (e.g., 30-minute response time during business hours). This is critical because mentees feel hesitant to ask questions and need assurance they won't be ignored.

5. **Ensure active engagement:** Reach out to all participants regularly. Track progress through assignments, quizzes, and practice exams. Pay attention to subtle feedback—if mentees say 'you haven't checked on me in weeks,' you're failing. When students say 'yeah yeah, I got it' without genuine understanding, probe deeper.

## Example Programs
Secure Ideas offers a CISSP mentorship program structured as recurring 9-week cycles with fixed start and end dates. Students can retake the program multiple times. Between cycles, previous participants naturally become mentors to new cohorts, creating sustainable community growth. Additionally, Johnson released Professional Evil Fundamentals—a free YouTube playlist of 2–4 minute definition videos covering foundational concepts.

## Guiding Philosophy
Johnson emphasizes that security professionals' primary responsibility is knowledge-sharing. He draws parallels to woodworking YouTubers like Steve Ramsey, who share crafts with genuine passion. Key principles:
- Everyone needs a mentor or hero; no one succeeds alone.
- Don't pursue applause or recognition; do the work because it matters.
- Follow ethical and legal rules; this distinguishes practitioners from those they oppose.
- Develop agility and broad competency, not isolated specialization.
- Aim with a flexible plan rather than rigid lists that guarantee imposter syndrome.

## Takeaways
The industry's real crisis is not talent shortage but accessibility and ethical education. Formalized, structured, bidirectional mentorship with multiple learning paths and active engagement prevents overwhelm and dropout. As practitioners gain expertise, mentoring the next generation becomes their primary responsibility.

talks.title: Develop Technical Recall Skills: Spaced Repetition with Anki w/ Josh Wright (1-Hour)
talks.teaser: Shows how spaced repetition and the Anki flashcard app can build long-term recall of technical skills.
talks.summary:
Josh Wright opens with a familiar problem: a steady stream of new tools, commands and techniques that he keeps looking up because he forgets them within minutes. He explains the forgetting curve and spaced repetition, the idea that reviewing material at increasing intervals, in short sessions, builds lasting recall. Before starting, he asks attendees to decide why they want a skill, whether for a certification, deeper expertise or career goals.

The core of the talk is a live walkthrough of Anki, a free flashcard app that schedules reviews based on how well a learner answered each card. Wright builds a deck of Linux command line cards, using cloze deletions with screenshots or formatted command output as visual aids, and rates his recall as easy, good or no. He keeps the app open all day and adds items as he learns them. In the Q&A he says he writes cards by hand rather than generating them automatically, because each learner understands a concept differently, and he keeps separate decks for each subject.

Wright stresses that the app does not solve motivation or time. He recommends finding enjoyment in the work, building a daily routine and being patient with frustration, and suggests trimming small blocks of other activities to make room for short study sessions. He closes by reminding listeners that security work matters, citing a school whose files were lost to ransomware.

talks.title: Mapping Your Network to Mitre ATT&CK to Visualize Threats, Logging, and Detection w/ Wade Wells
talks.teaser: Shows how to map logging and detection coverage onto MITRE ATT&CK using free open-source tools.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a manager's request for a clear view of which attacks the team could detect. Wade Wells, who works in threat intelligence and threat hunting at a financial company, first tried a Confluence page per MITRE ATT&CK tactic, but that only covered about a third of the framework. He moved to the ATT&CK Navigator and to Detect, a Python tool that turns YAML files into Navigator layers. One YAML file grades each logging source on completeness, field quality, timeliness, retention and consistency. A second file scores detections per technique and records dates, so coverage can be shown over time.

Overlaying the two layers exposes gaps between what is logged and what is alerted on, which Wade used to direct threat hunting. He hosted the YAML files in a repository, ran a daily script on a small cloud server, and embedded the Navigator view in Confluence so colleagues did not need to visit the server. To verify detections, he ran Atomic Red Team tests by hand, which showed when alerts failed to fire, and later began renaming alerts to include their ATT&CK IDs so a script could update the map automatically.

The main takeaways are to understand logging before writing detections, to centralize logs, and to expect the YAML files to take the most effort. Wade said the layered view helped him show leadership where coverage stood. He also cautioned against treating threat actor technique lists like signatures.

talks.title: Hackin' Cast: How to Sell Security to C Levels w Chris Brenton
talks.teaser: Explains how security leaders can frame projects in business terms to win executive funding and shorten sales cycles.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a common problem: security projects such as better patching or threat hunting lose budget fights because executives weigh them against sales, product and support needs. The speaker argues that security should be pitched in business terms, as a way to remove obstacles and grow revenue rather than as overhead. Problems should be traced to process gaps instead of blamed on individuals, which leads to fixes that last.

For a newly hired security lead, the suggested first steps are to learn the company's biggest business risks and to align with sales and legal, not only IT. Long customer security questionnaires can add months to deals, so a measured sales-cycle metric makes a stronger case than anecdotes. Compliance frameworks such as SOC 2, PCI DSS, ISO 27001 and EU privacy rules act as a shared reference that builds customer trust, and the Cloud Security Alliance control matrix helps find overlaps between them. The speaker also notes that contradictory questionnaire answers can expose vendors who are simply checking boxes.

Delivery advice centers on a short deck of about ten slides with a high-level plan, backup slides for technical detail, and a rehearsed pitch to a manager first. Budget requests should include a small buffer, since timelines and staffing usually run longer than planned. In the Q&A, a case where recorded incidents rose after a new leader arrived was reframed around how long attackers stayed undetected before removal.

talks.title: Hackin' Cast: Adversarial Emulation with The C2 Matrix

talks.title: Hackin' Cast: Hacking Dumberly Redux - More Dumberer
talks.teaser: Shows how simple, well-known techniques like default passwords and replayed requests keep producing real breaches.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that real attackers usually start with the simplest route that works, so testers should try basic techniques before building custom exploits. The speaker cites the 2017 Equifax breach, which used a known Apache Struts flaw about two months after it was announced, and a case in which a teenager reportedly breached Apple. Recurring findings from testing include accounts whose password matches the username, predictable passwords shaped by 90-day rotation rules, passwords printed in help screens or welcome letters, cleartext passwords stored in an Active Directory attribute, and forgotten test accounts.

Several device and app examples follow. Using an online guide, the speaker extracted firmware from a TRENDnet camera, split it with binwalk and dd, and found a factory test account in the password file whose credentials were only base64 encoded. A second camera yielded the same result. In an Apple TV and Amazon Prime case, a configuration flag had AirPlay disabled, and the signature check passed once the signature was deleted. A colleague bypassed MFA by requesting a page that should only be reachable after authentication. A MySQL login succeeded roughly one attempt in 256, which the speaker called a "soccer trophy" flaw.

The longest story involves a contest where points came from sending an app's registration request. Replaying captured requests worked until organizers blocked replay. The team decoded a base64 payload, read the Android app's bytecode to learn how its signature was calculated, and scripted forged values, including a platinum status multiplier. Reusing persistent HTTP sessions sped things up further. The talk ends by encouraging testers to try simple steps first, guess boldly, admit when they do not know, and share their work with others.

talks.title: Hackin' Cast: Quickstart Guide to MITRE ATT&CK: the Do's and Don'ts
talks.teaser: Explains how to use the MITRE ATT&CK matrix as a shared language and for behavior-based testing, with common pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a problem: MITRE ATT&CK is cited constantly by vendors, yet many people know it only secondhand. The speaker gives a fast primer on the Enterprise matrix, organized by platform such as Windows, macOS, Linux and cloud, and explains that its technique IDs give red, blue and purple teams a shared vocabulary for adversary behavior.

The core guidance is a set of do's and don'ts. Treat the matrix as a common language rather than a checklist, so one detected technique does not mean a whole category is solved. Seek out behaviors rather than signatures: system time discovery can be carried out with net time or PowerShell Get-Date, and matching one specific command misses the underlying behavior. Decouple techniques from named threat actors, since actors change their ordering and tooling. The attacker's choice is likened to a game of minesweeper, where each technique risks triggering a defender's alert.

For testing, open-source resources help. Caldera suits teams that want a GUI and agent-based emulation, while Red Canary's Atomic Red Team offers command-level tests for those comfortable with PowerShell. Both are baselines, and each command should be understood before it is run. Prioritize tests by value against difficulty, such as screenshot capture for data an organization considers critical, and remember that ATT&CK sits alongside standards like the NIST functions. The takeaway is to use the matrix as a baseline and to get involved in its community.

talks.title: When Logging Everything Becomes an Issue
talks.teaser: Shows how Sysmon and PowerShell logging can accidentally expose plaintext credentials in event logs, and how to reduce that risk.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a side effect of richer Windows logging. Sysmon and PowerShell logging give defenders much more visibility into what admins, developers, malware and attackers do, but the same events can also capture secrets. The speaker argues that admins, developers or even third-party applications can introduce this risk without anyone noticing.

Several cases from the speaker's own environment show the problem. A Black Hills penetration test using MailSniper harvested email addresses, and because transcript logging was on, the password it was passed appeared in plain text in the logs. Command history from creating new AD users stored every username and password in the SIEM, leaving about two weeks before onboarded staff started during which those accounts could be abused. A server administrator's scheduled task exposed credentials for a remote workstation, and a third-party application running with a privileged account logged its password too.

To find this exposure, the speaker searched event logs for common tools that take credentials on the command line, such as PsExec, net use and scheduled task commands, and used Sigma rules to run similar queries in SIEM platforms. Static analysis with PSScriptAnalyzer flags plaintext passwords in scripts so they can use SecureString instead. Remediation options include tuning Sysmon configurations, starting from a community template that excludes chatty events, and enabling Protected Event Logging on Windows 10, though many SIEM vendors do not yet support it. The takeaway is to decide which logs belong on which machines, educate admins and developers, and protect logging configuration from tampering.

talks.title: What I Learned After a Year as a Cybersecurity Mentor
talks.teaser: Offers lessons from a year of mentoring aspiring pentesters, from asking good questions to finding free community resources.
talks.summary:
This short talk draws on a year of mentoring people who want to break into penetration testing. The speaker sorts incoming requests into two kinds. Strong ones show that research has already been done, name the next certification or step, and ask about experience that only someone who has been through it can answer. Weak ones ask for exam questions and answers, or for everything to be handed over, often things a search engine would answer. The speaker says that most of the 50 to 100 emails received each week fall into the second group.

The middle of the talk argues that cybersecurity is not for everybody. The field demands constant learning, and some newcomers quit once they see the effort it takes. A mentor can guide someone but cannot supply passion or drive. Mentoring is also rewarding. One student who kept working on his own and checked back after a month of effort later landed a job at a top penetration testing firm. Because one-on-one replies cannot keep up with demand, the speaker suggests other ways to help, such as blogs, videos and streaming, where a familiar topic can still be shared with a personal angle.

The closing section points to resources. These include a weekly Mentor Monday thread run by Tanya Jenkins that pairs mentors with people seeking help, a women-focused cybersecurity group, and Discord and Slack communities with several thousand members each where people answer one another's basic questions. The takeaway is that anyone can mentor, and answering a single question each week in such a community is a real contribution.

talks.title: Be Evil: A Toolset for Tier 1 Threat Emulation
talks.teaser: Presents Ravenclaw, a Rust-based backdoor for tier 1 threat emulation that supports CLR, Win32 API and PowerShell-style post-exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk separates threat emulation from ordinary red teaming. The speaker argues that a red team should make the blue team better, while threat emulation tests whether an organization's defenses hold up against the behaviour of a specific intrusion set. He ties this to the ransomware economy, describing an incident-response case in which one group reportedly held domain admin access for months before launching its attack. FBI figures he cited for a single group suggested ransom demands in the range of hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, across more than a hundred compromises.

On the offensive side, the talk covers why post-exploitation activity often gets caught. Windows Server 2008 R2 is described as still common on internal networks, and credential theft from LSASS is treated as an early priority once an attacker has a foothold. Well-known command-and-control tools are often detected through their known signatures, and PowerShell is increasingly visible through script block logging. The speaker suggests that a backdoor should offer flexible execution paths, such as Win32 API calls, the .NET CLR and Python, rather than depending on one tool or one interpreter.

The talk closes by introducing Ravenclaw, an open-source backdoor written in Rust that is designed to run CLR assemblies, Win32 API calls and PowerShell-style execution. It is paired with a control interface meant to manage several backdoors from one server. The practical takeaway is to measure whether defenders actually detect the emulated activity, treating a detection as a successful outcome rather than a failure of the test.

talks.title: Post Exploitation: Striking Gold with Covert Recon
talks.teaser: Explains how to map an environment quietly by mimicking user activity and mining logs, caches and configs instead of noisy scans.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, the speaker explores stealthy post-exploitation reconnaissance techniques, cautioning offensive security professionals against noisy, default actions such as immediately running Nmap upon gaining a foothold. Grounded in a systems administration background, the speaker advocates for adopting a "packet economy" mindset—minimizing network packets and blending in with standard user behaviors to avoid alerting blue teams and anomaly detection systems.

### Key Topics
- **Packet Economy and Avoiding Noisy Scanning:** Why relying immediately on tools like Nmap, full port scans, or heavy VM installations gives away an attacker's presence, and why testing detection monitoring requires discreet behavior.
- **Mimicking Normal User Activity:** Understanding normal operational hours, system local time, and baseline tools so post-exploitation activity does not stand out as anomalous.
- **Passive Network and Host Discovery:** Utilizing existing host artifacts—such as DNS caches, ARP tables, and mounted remote file systems—to map architecture and vendors without transmitting excessive traffic.
- **Internal OSINT and Data Mining:** Extracting metadata from internal documents (using concepts behind tools like FOCA and PowerMeta) and hunting credentials across logs, shell histories, and scripts.
- **Cloud Post-Exploitation Hygiene:** Caution regarding cloud metadata endpoints and API logging, advocating for checking scripts and cron jobs before making direct API calls.
- **Purposeful Escalation of Noise:** Transitioning from stealthy reconnaissance to intentionally raising noise levels once objectives are met in order to test and improve defensive detection capabilities.

### Technical Details
- **Activity Baseline Analysis:** Checking local system time, update/application logs (e.g., yum, apt, crontabs), and authentication records to pinpoint manual user interaction versus automated cron tasks. Application logs also reveal server usage peaks.
- **Host Footprinting via Built-in State:** Reading DNS caches to discover hostnames and domain naming conventions. Querying ARP tables (`arp -a`) exposes MAC addresses, allowing identification of hardware vendors (e.g., Cisco, Juniper) or hypervisors like VMware to detect virtualized/sandbox environments without slinging packets.
- **Credential Harvesting Artifacts:** Examining developer/debug logs for leaked credentials or failed password entries typed into username fields (such as seasonal passwords like `summer2019!`), reviewing `.bash_history` for passwords or S3 bucket references, and inspecting unencrypted SSH keys, `known_hosts`, and SSH config aliases to map pivoting paths.
- **Mounted File Systems and Query Methods:** Exploiting remote mounts (NFS, SMB via `mount` or `/etc/fstab`) to inspect remote systems without triggering active network inspection. On Linux, tools like `netstat`, `lsof`, and `ss` query network state differently (`proc` filesystem vs. direct kernel system calls), providing different operational visibility.

### Takeaways
Covert reconnaissance centers on patience, gathering context before acting, and looking for "permission" within the environment before running commands like Windows `net` utilities or specialized offensive tools. Offensive operators should conserve network packets, leverage built-in OS artifacts to infer network architecture, and throttle file downloads or search scripts. Finally, after silently meeting objectives, operators should systematically ratchet up their noise profile to help defenders benchmark their monitoring and response controls.

talks.title: Hack Apart Your Career: How to Fund Doing What You Love
talks.teaser: Walks through finding and applying for non-dilutive SBIR funding from Air Force programs, from registration to a phase one proposal.
talks.summary:
The talk is a walkthrough of how small companies can win non-dilutive research funding from U.S. government programs. The speaker uses an Air Force open call run through F-Works as the worked example. He argues that many founders and engineers never hear about these programs because outreach tends to reach large contractors and veterans. He describes his own path from consulting and startup roles to running his own company, which he says led him to pursue this funding.

He explains the structure of the program. A phase one contract is roughly $50,000 over three months, and the goal is to find an Air Force customer who signs a memo supporting a demonstration. A phase two contract can reach $750,000 over 12 to 18 months and is used to build a proof of concept. A phase three contract is a sole-source award meant to move the work into production. Registration takes about three weeks and covers a business entity, a DUNS number and SAM registration to obtain a CAGE code. A submission includes a pitch deck of about 15 slides, a short technical document, cost information and a customer letter of support. Phase two adds a recorded video of about 100 seconds. He reports around 600 companies applying in the last round and about 200 phase one awards, and he says a signed customer letter greatly improves the odds.

He then steps through the portal, covering small-business certifications, the work-share rules and the labor-rate section, where overhead and fee are fixed. He notes that payment arrives as 75 percent up front and 25 percent at the end, and that phase two is paid by quarterly milestones. He advises against underbidding and offers to help with proposals, closing with a call for more people from the security community to use these funding paths.

talks.title: First try DNS Cache Poisoning on IPv4 and IPv6
talks.teaser: Shows how off-path DNS cache poisoning becomes practical in one attempt by combining IP ID collisions with fragmentation.
talks.summary:
This talk covers off-path DNS cache poisoning and why it is becoming practical again. Randomized source ports made the classic Kaminsky-style attack much harder, but large DNSSEC responses still get fragmented, and the second fragment carries no DNS identifiers, so it can be matched by its IP ID. The speaker reviews these fragmentation attacks, then shows how Linux's per-destination IP ID handling, which uses a keyed hash into a limited set of bins, can be probed to find collisions.

The new technique finds bin collisions by sending spoofed IPv6 echo fragments from a large pool of source addresses, such as a cloud provider's IPv6 allocation. Because the hash key only changes at reboot, a collision can be reused for a long time. Once one is found, the attacker sends a burst of spoofed fragments that can poison a resolver in a single attempt. The talk also notes that timing the attack around predictable resolver activity, such as morning traffic, makes targeting corporate networks easier. The findings came out of a pen test and were disclosed to the affected vendors before being shared more widely.

Suggested mitigations include lowering the advertised EDNS buffer size to about 1220 bytes so responses avoid fragmentation and fall back to TCP, watching for unsolicited echo replies, and limiting how ICMP is handled. The speaker acknowledges that these measures are imperfect, that the DNS flag day changes are still pending, and that rebooting or rekeying gives only temporary relief. Practitioners should review resolver configuration and should not rely on small DNSSEC signing keys.

talks.title: S1/E3: Do you C2? If you do, ICU.
talks.teaser: Hunts for a red team operator's command-and-control traffic in half-duplex network captures using Zeek and BPF filters.
talks.summary:
Jonathan Ham returned for the third installment of his threat hunting series, opening Wild West Hackin' Fest. This time the target was command-and-control traffic built by Jake Williams, sent over a communications channel he said he had never used before. Ham received one hour of packet captures from a busy enterprise network, with the implant hidden among ordinary activity. The capture held only inbound, half-duplex traffic, so outbound sessions were missing and full content inspection was not an option. Early attempts with Snort, Rita and other tools failed, and hours of manual packet filtering led nowhere.

The turning point came when Zeek was run over the capture. Its connection log recorded sessions even when only the returned SYN-ACK and later traffic had been seen. Checks for DNS tunneling showed no suspicious pattern. Ham then examined TLS certificates, looking first for unusually short issuer fields and then for issuers with no common name field. One issuer contained base64 text that decoded to a short message, which identified the endpoint. Several other anomalies turned out to be false positives that the network owner cleared as normal.

The takeaways are to instrument networks before an incident and to confirm that a tool behaves as expected on known traffic before trusting its output. Ham pointed to Security Onion as a free, quick-to-deploy platform that bundles Snort, Zeek and the ELK stack. He also stressed that threat hunts are never truly finished and end only when time or budget runs out.

talks.title: Nerdlist: The Totally Not 1,337 Bad Ideas That Give Infosec Noobs A Foot In The Door
talks.teaser: Explains a crowdsourced list of joke passwords that gives newcomers an easy first open-source contribution and a path into infosec.
talks.summary:
Tarah Wheeler presents the Nerdlist, a GitHub repository of passwords people actually use, drawn from television, comic books, memes and old movies. She explains that people often pick joke passwords they believe nobody else would choose, and that widely shared password lists already show how predictable those choices are. The project was built as a low-barrier way for newcomers to make a first public contribution to an information security project.

The talk walks through contributions the project has received, including a set of Android gesture unlock patterns, one shaped like the Alohomora spell, and a student's keyboard layouts for German and Dvorak variants. Wheeler argues that gatekeeping in the field keeps people out, and cites research she says shows pull requests from people who present as femme are accepted at about half the rate of those from people who present as masculine. She also reports that some administrator passwords for regional ISPs on the list are real and have not been changed in years.

To close, she asks attendees to contribute, to teach newcomers credential stuffing, and to test systems only with permission, reporting what they find so it can be discussed publicly. Rewards are silver challenge coins made from Scrabble-style tiles. The Q&A covers which community values she would like to see spread, and she encourages even small additions to the list.

talks.title: Story time with Johnny Long
talks.teaser: Traces a hacker community member's move from burnout to service, and profiles peers using their skills for charity.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's career peak in the mid-2000s, when he led red team work and public speaking but felt empty and out of balance. A turning point came through extended family trips to Uganda, where he used technical skills to repair donated computers for local nonprofits, which eventually led to a training center and a hacker space. Members of the hacker community funded much of that work, which inspired him to found Hackers for Charity to link community skills with real needs.

The middle of the talk is a series of short profiles of community members doing service work. Mubix and Ben 10 started Hackers in Education, which teaches online safety in schools alongside police officers. Canadian robotics teachers trained a Ugandan hacker space's robotics team, and those students now teach younger kids. Matt Svensson founded We Defend Charities to help nonprofits with security, and Amanda Berlin started Mental Health Hackers, which brought stress relief to conferences. Chris Sanders' Rural Tech Fund donates equipment to remote schools, Chris Cox's Operation Safe Escape helps abuse victims, Bill Pollock's No Starch Press Foundation funds STEM education, and the Innocent Lives Foundation helps law enforcement track down child predators.

The stories share a pattern: a small personal step spreads as others pick it up. The speaker urges attendees to match their skills to existing organizations through a website and Slack channel, or to launch a new project under a 501(c)(3) shelter that Hackers for Charity offers.

talks.title: The Hacker's Apprentice
talks.teaser: Mark Baggett explores The Hacker's Apprentice.

talks.title: Assumed Breach: A Better Model For Penetration Testing
talks.teaser: Explains why assumed breach testing from a compromised user better mirrors real attacks than traditional internal pentests.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that typical internal penetration tests, where a tester drops a Kali box on the network and runs loud scans and exploits, do not reflect how real attackers operate. As an alternative, the talk presents assumed breach testing, which starts from a user who is already compromised, uses a representative workstation and a real user account, and looks for high-value data rather than domain admin rights. Two models are described: a compromised user who ran a payload, and a malicious insider who wants to cause damage.

The middle of the talk walks through tradecraft used in these engagements. Initial code execution can come from HTA files, with obfuscation through tools such as Unicorn and Invoke-Obfuscation, or from environmental keying that only decrypts a payload on a matching host. Command-and-control traffic can be disguised with malleable profiles. Access is gained through targeted password spraying and low-and-slow Kerberoasting, which avoids the flood of event 4769 entries that gives away scripted requests. Further credentials come from group policy preference files, Active Directory description fields, web.config files, file shares, and SSH keys. Tools such as BloodHound, PowerView, and PowerLine are mentioned for mapping access and running PowerShell when it is restricted.

The closing section covers trade-offs. Attackers may have months rather than weeks, so assumed breach tests often have to be noisier, and they rarely include vulnerability scanning. Whether to test against AV and EDR should be agreed with the client in advance. The main takeaway is that clients get more value when their test uses realistic users and systems and when scoping focuses on what would hurt most. Defenders can use the same techniques to find weaknesses in their own environments.

talks.title: WWHF 2019 Keynote
talks.teaser: A keynote urges newcomers and leaders to share knowledge, welcome diverse voices, and help others grow in security.
talks.summary:
This keynote at Wild West Hackin' Fest focuses on skill building, experimentation and how the security industry can improve as a community. Ian Coldwater argues that security problems are not solved yet and that the field needs more diverse voices. The talk speaks directly to people who feel they do not belong, whether because of age, background, a lack of a security job or working outside IT. Drawing on a path from DevOps into penetration testing, the speaker says that skills from other fields, such as cloud and container work, have value that security has been slow to use.

On finding a direction, the talk suggests trying capture-the-flag categories to see what appeals, then going deep and learning how things work internally rather than memorising lists of tools. Generalists are valued, and well-known experts are shown to be human and not know everything. Sharing knowledge is presented as essential. A story about a DevOps conference and a security conference illustrates that something considered basic to one group can be unknown to another, so security and developer teams should talk more, without condescension.

Toward the close, the talk addresses leaders: lift others by giving them tools and power, build guardrails and bridges rather than gates, stop gatekeeping, and avoid drama that wastes time. To move the industry forward, it recommends that people sponsor underrepresented colleagues, share speaking chances, and that employers invest in staff through conferences and training. The message is that each person has value to offer and room to grow, and that the community rises when people help each other.

talks.title: Hacking a Security Career
talks.teaser: Offers practical career and business advice for security newcomers, covering networking, contracts, money and soft skills.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at how people build a security career and how they might run a security business, arguing that technical skill alone rarely gets someone hired or keeps a firm going. It starts with the idea that most jobs come through weak social links rather than mass resume submissions, and that small, friendly gestures at conferences, such as sharing knowledge, volunteering, or publishing writing, tend to pay back over time. The speaker stresses that introverts can build a reputation through these routes too, and that middle-of-the-road competence is enough for most employers.

The middle section covers the practical side of starting a firm. Startup money can come from savings or small business loans, and a side business demands a lot of personal time. The talk then goes through contract and billing habits: making NDAs mutual, setting clear payment terms such as net 30, asking for upfront deposits to cover travel and equipment, invoicing properly, and agreeing on a rate schedule. It also covers white labeling work through other firms, sanitizing client stories before sharing them, and keeping company devices owned by the company.

The closing section argues that soft skills are what most often sink people, including emotional intelligence, communication, conflict de-escalation, and respect for others' time. It asks what success or "finished" means for a given person, whether that is a published CVE, a conference talk, or a changed industry standard. The takeaway is that behaving badly is not permanent: a genuine apology needs admission, explanation and accountability.

talks.title: Elevating your Windows Privileges Like a Boss!
talks.teaser: Covers common Windows misconfigurations that enable privilege escalation, from weak file permissions to unquoted service paths.
talks.summary:
The talk covers privilege escalation on Windows through misconfigurations rather than binary exploits or unpatched bugs. The presenter argues that vulnerability scanners rarely flag these problems because they have no simple signature, and that many of the techniques are the ones used routinely on red team engagements. Much of the problem comes from administrators making their own jobs easier, and from vendor and installer defaults that leave directories open.

The middle of the talk walks through permission and configuration checks. Directories where ordinary authenticated users can create files or append data let an attacker drop a DLL into the path of a privileged third-party program, and a proxy DLL or a simple add-user payload keeps the service from crashing afterward. The presenter recommends icacls, since the default GUI hides special permissions. Other cases include writable entries in the system PATH, where a service calling netsh would run a planted binary first; writable service image path values; unquoted service paths containing spaces; the AlwaysInstallElevated policy, which lets a crafted MSI run as system; unattended install answer files holding plaintext passwords; and leftover COM registrations. Process Monitor helps reveal services that look for missing executables.

The closing advice is to audit directory and registry permissions under Program Files and similar locations, and to put confidentiality and integrity into system administrator job descriptions so they are rated on them. The presenter also urges red teams to work with incident response teams, since attackers use these same tricks and defenders should recognise them.

talks.title: Adversarial Emulation
talks.teaser: Argues that red team exercises should emulate real adversaries using bounded, repeatable attacks that help validate defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that red team engagements often leave a business without a clear answer about whether its defenses work, since they are one-off snapshots and defenders tune against the same tools each time. The speaker proposes a bounded attack space: instead of covering the whole kill chain, a team constrains a test to a part it can repeat and measure. Cheap shortcuts, such as whitelisting a tool to see what happens further down the chain, let teams test later stages without costly exploit development.

Threat intelligence built on hashes, IPs and domains goes stale quickly, so the speaker urged describing adversary behaviour instead, ideally in machine-readable form. MITRE ATT&CK is useful as shared vocabulary but often becomes a checklist, when the order and context of techniques is what matters. On the network, attackers must blend into normal traffic, so defenders should understand their own pattern of life and use segmentation to add friction at each lateral movement step.

The talk closed with an open-source project evaluating about 30 command-and-control frameworks, with a planned decision tree and public walkthroughs for emulating specific threat groups. The main takeaways were to build repeatable scenarios that blue teams can replay to validate detections, to bring defenders into the exercise, and to show executives how a real adversary gathers information over time.
