talks.title: ELD Device Security
talks.teaser: Walks through hardware testing of electronic logging devices used in trucks, from FCC ID lookups to UART, JTAG and flash dumps.
talks.summary:
Brian Fehrman and David Fletcher explain why electronic logging devices matter: most US freight moves by truck, and federal rules require these devices, which connect to a vehicle's CAN bus. They cover the rules that replaced paper logbooks, the exemptions, and the sparse security requirements, since manufacturers can self-certify. Vendor claims that the devices only read bus data and encrypt their traffic are then compared with earlier research on J1939 access and a Black Hat talk on ELD firmware.

They list possible attack paths, including vendor servers, companion phone apps, wireless interfaces and physical access. Their methodology starts with FCC ID lookups, datasheets and forums, then moves to passive bus monitoring, wireless analysis and board-level hunting for UART and JTAG interfaces. Across five devices, one stayed in Bluetooth pairing mode and accepted firmware updates through an app, another exposed its MAC address in its Wi-Fi network name, and a third leaked command strings and web endpoints linked to a fleet management company. Several debug interfaces were disabled, and one board's main processor was fried during probing.

The main takeaway is that a device able to read the bus should not transmit by default, and that open pairing modes, firmware update paths and debug headers deserve scrutiny. The speakers close by calling for better tooling to dump flash from high pin count parts.

talks.title: Aggressive Autonomous Actions - Operating with Automation
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how Cobalt Strike Aggressor scripts can automate post-exploitation, phishing alerts, EDR detection, persistence and reporting.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at using Cobalt Strike's Aggressor language, an event-driven scripting layer, to reduce manual work during red team engagements. The speakers frame automation as a way to handle repetitive steps that need no analysis, keep operators consistent, and limit user error, rather than as a replacement for creative offensive work. They walk through the main event types, such as beacon initial, heartbeat timers and SSH initial, and the functions and hooks that let scripts act on beacon metadata, read command output and extend the client GUI.

The demonstrations cover several use cases. A heartbeat-triggered script dumps credentials whenever an administrator beacon is present on a jump box. A phishing helper sends a text message through email gateways the moment a new beacon checks in. Another script lists the system driver directory for known EDR minifilter driver files, then highlights security tools in process listings so the operator knows what to avoid. Further examples add registry, scheduled task and WMI persistence through pop-up menus, generate payloads in batches across HTTP, SMB and DNS listeners, and run commands remotely through MSBuild with unmanaged PowerShell. The talk closes with a custom report generator that collects compromised hosts and accounts for the final deliverable.

The speakers point to a public GitHub repository with the scripts organized by engagement phase, so attendees can adapt them to their own work. The main takeaway is that automating predictable, non-analytical steps helps keep access and evidence consistent while operators step away from the keyboard.

talks.title: The Lexicon, Risk Management and You
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Lexicon, Risk Management and You.

talks.title: Hack Dumberly Not Harderer
talks.teaser: Pen testers show how expired domains, weak macros, and password reuse still beat flashy exploits in real engagements.
talks.summary:
Tim Madine and Derek frame penetration testing and real breaches around unsophisticated wins rather than APT mythology. They cite Equifax as a case where a published vulnerability sat for months before compromise with off-the-shelf exploit code, and argue defenders and testers should try lazy approaches first.

They walk through operational examples: acquiring already-categorized expired domains to slip past mail and web filters for phishing and command-and-control; hiding a Cobalt Strike payload in a white-font Excel cell to evade Defender instead of reverse-engineering it; downloading Ncat from the Nmap site to obtain a reverse shell past EDR; seasonal helpdesk passwords granting VPN access; MailSniper against public Outlook Web Access; webcam firmware extraction with Binwalk and Base64-encoded credentials; a Cisco SSH private-key acceptance quirk; LibSSH accepting a premature success message (CVE-2018-10933); and a MySQL authentication flaw that occasionally grants access after repeated bad attempts.

They close by prioritizing risk over headline CPU flaws, encouraging testers to ask junior colleagues for fresh ideas, and using a SANS CTF challenge where repeated simple Burp decoding beats premature shellcode analysis. Practitioners should validate obvious misconfigurations, reuse existing tools, and share straightforward techniques locally.

talks.title: What Could It Hurt?
talks.teaser: A pentest leader shows how web frameworks breed false safety when teams adopt them without understanding limits, misuse, or patching cost.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a red-team consulting viewpoint: breaches keep piling up, victims get blamed, and applications—not only users—drive most failures. Security advocates once steered developers away from hand-rolled code toward frameworks so teams could focus on business logic while libraries handled session management, database access, and common controls.

The core argument compares that trade-off to an infamous attempt to dispose of a beached whale with far too much dynamite: frameworks do heavy lifting until implementers treat them as magic shields. The middle walks through public and client examples—Django validation gaps and defaults, Apache Struts deserialization and Equifax’s patch and WAF timing, a Ruby on Rails shop claiming SQL injection was impossible until Active Record was exploited in seconds, stale jQuery and the limits of migrate shims, and single-page apps exposing logic in the browser—plus pressure from executives who treat coding as trivial and timelines as impossibly short.

The close rejects “developers are stupid” while urging organizations to fund understanding: know what a framework actually provides, test assumptions, and plan real upgrades instead of trusting branding. The speaker also mentions free training for veterans and gratis services for qualifying charities before wrapping.

talks.title: Extracting Data from Slack: Hackers Will, You Should!
talks.teaser: A PowerShell module pulls Slack data via the official API and audit-log alerts that flag bulk downloads and abused tokens.
talks.summary:
Organizations store chat, files, and credentials in Slack at scale, and authorized API access can copy everything a user can see without exploiting a platform bug. The first segment introduces Slack Extract, a PowerShell module that authenticates with a browser D cookie or API token, archives messages and attachments per channel, exports metadata and user directories for reuse in password spraying, and supports scoped runs such as private channels only or admin access logs when privileges allow.

The second segment treats defender visibility. Slack’s Audit Log API (admin-only, bearer token) structures actions like file downloads differently from routine user API traffic, which any authenticated session can drive. The speakers ingested audit events into Elasticsearch and Kibana, tuned alerts on volume such as hundreds of files in a short window, and documented setup friction, pagination quirks, header formatting for authorization, schema drift, exaggerated logout counts, and rate limiting.

Practitioners should treat offline bulk extraction as distinct from normal browsing, search pulled data locally to avoid keyword search alerts, rotate and protect tokens including bot credentials, and periodically run extraction-style review to gauge exposed secrets. Real engagements reportedly surfaced Wi-Fi passwords, shared drive paths, user passwords, S3 keys, and source with embedded credentials, while sanitization and policy alone rarely keep pace with how people share in chat.

talks.title: Copying Keys from Photos, Molds & More
talks.teaser: Shows how an intruder can duplicate a key from brief access, phone photos, lock pins or molds, and why the entry may leave no trace.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a physical intruder can copy a key without stealing it, and why the resulting entry can be almost impossible to detect. The speaker separates overt, covert and surreptitious entry, explaining that a surreptitious attack leaves no evidence even for a trained specialist. Duplicating a key is presented as one of the few realistic ways to reach that level, because a copy cuts and wears the lock the same way the original does.

The middle of the talk covers several methods, each with its own trade-offs. Calipers and key gauges read cut depths when a key is in hand for a short time, while a clay or mold impression captures the full profile for later analysis. When someone is only briefly distracted, a phone photo of a key on a grid overlay, ideally against a dark background, can be decoded into bitting values. Stamped direct or blind codes on keys and packaging can be reversed with lookup tables or software. Without any key access, a lock can be removed and its pins extracted by rear shimming. A punch machine or a cast metal key can then produce a working copy in the field. A demonstration showed a cylinder being swapped at a data center door after a door sensor was masked.

The takeaway is practical. Keys visible in photos, on social media or hanging from a belt can leak enough data to reproduce them, so people should keep keys out of view and avoid posting them. For defenders, the talk shows that a key-based intrusion may leave marks that only a specialist would ever find.

talks.title: Android App Penetration Testing 101
talks.teaser: Walks through Android app pentesting setup, tooling, file system and intent analysis, and embedding a payload into an app.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Jeff (Yoda66) and Derek Banks from Black Hills Information Security deliver an introductory overview of Android mobile application penetration testing. The speakers discuss the Android security model, market share landscape, key architectural components, required tooling, and practical testing methodologies. The session culminates in a technical explanation and live demonstration showing how to disassemble, modify, back-door, recompile, and sign a legitimate Android application with an embedded Metasploit Meterpreter payload.

### Key Topics
- **Android Market Share and Risk Landscape**: Android commands over 80% worldwide market share, featuring an open ecosystem where users frequently run older operating system versions (such as Lollipop, Marshmallow, or Nougat). Risks include enterprise data stored in applications, insecure dependencies, cleartext credential storage, and malicious or modified side-loaded apps.
- **Testing Environment and Tooling**: Setting up a dedicated mobile testing workbench requires tools like Android Studio (with AVD), Genymotion (x86-based emulator with VirtualBox), real rooted hardware devices (such as Google/Motorola Nexus devices), Jadx/Jadx-GUI for decompilation, Drozer for inter-process communication assessments, apktool for smali disassembly, and Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) for automated static and dynamic analysis.
- **Testing Methodology**: Pen testing mobile apps encompasses reconnaissance, filesystem analysis, network communication interception, and code review. Common methodology references include the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and Josh Wright's mobile device report cards.
- **Inter-Process Communication and Intents**: Android apps communicate via intents and broadcast receivers. Improperly filtered intents or vulnerable upstream libraries can expose internal functionality—such as accidentally exposing debug logging containing sensitive session cookies to the system log (logcat).

### Technical Details
- **Filesystem and Storage Analysis**: Android applications install by default into `/data/data/<app-package-name>/`. Testers can use `adb pull` before and after authenticating or interacting with an app, then run a diff to identify insecure data storage, including cleartext credentials and session tokens.
- **Network Traffic Interception**: Web traffic can be proxied using Burp Suite by generating its CA certificate, pushing it via `adb` (e.g., to `/sdcard/Download`), and installing it into the device's trusted credentials. Full packet capture can also be conducted using a software AP combined with Wireshark, tcpdump, or Bro.
- **Intent Exploitation with Drozer**: By port-forwarding TCP port 31415 using `adb forward tcp:31415 tcp:31415`, testers connect a host Drozer console to an on-device Drozer agent to stimulate exported activities, broadcast receivers, and services.
- **Backdooring APKs**: Disassembling an APK with `apktool` produces smali assembly files and extracts the binary `AndroidManifest.xml`. Meterpreter stagers generated by Metasploit can be disassembled into smali, copied into the target app's package structure, and called inside `onCreate` in the main activity file. Jeff demonstrated his Python automation script (`Android_EmbedIT` on GitHub) which decompiles both APKs, parses the XML to find the main activity entry point, injects the stager call, randomizes directory paths to evade simple detection, merges permissions, reassembles the app, and signs it with a newly generated keystore before launching a live reverse TCP Meterpreter handler.

### Takeaways
Android's openness and decoupled components provide substantial attack surface, especially when apps accept uncontrolled intents or rely on third-party libraries. Manual checks via ADB, decompilers like Jadx, and tools like MobSF and Drozer allow testers to rapidly locate serious flaws such as cleartext storage, leaky log files, and tampering opportunities. Organizations and users must exercise caution with side-loading APKs outside official app stores, and developers should use practice targets like DIVA (Damn Insecure Vulnerable App) to learn secure coding and validation practices.

talks.title: Integrated Security Testing
talks.teaser: Shows how to fold security payloads into existing Selenium integration tests so QA teams can catch XSS, SQLi and XXE bugs.
talks.summary:
Morgan Roman, who works on application security at DocuSign, argues that dynamic web scanners struggle with business logic and produce many false positives. The talk proposes reusing the test framework that QA teams already run, such as Selenium with Gherkin or Cucumber, and adding security payloads to existing workflows. A payload is sent in during a test, the test runs through its full multi-step flow, and the output or failed assertions reveal the problem.

The examples cover several bug classes. For XSS, the payload logs to the browser console with console.error rather than alert, because an alert would stop Selenium. Angular injection uses very large numbers so that evaluated math is a reliable signal instead of a coincidence. SQL injection is checked by sending quote-heavy input through API automation and tracing the errors through a proxy. XXE is detected by watching file system access in a test environment, and CSV injection is prevented by prefixing cells with a single quote so Excel does not evaluate formulas. Cookie checks confirm the Secure and HttpOnly flags, and a browser monitoring snippet records outgoing calls to catch scripts loaded from unexpected hosts. A live demo ran a sample note-taking app through these tests, and a proxied run through ZAP produced passive scan findings that could feed a CI/CD pipeline.

The talk closes with authorization testing, using a matrix of users, such as Alice, Bob and an attacker named Eve, to check sharing and access rules on every deploy. The practical takeaway is that functionality outlives the features that implement it, so tests that already run in the pipeline catch regressions. Making QA staff allies by giving failures clear messages that name a security contact helps push these checks earlier in development.

talks.title: Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).

talks.title: Covert Attack Mystery Box: A few novel techniques for exploiting Microsoft "features"
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Covert Attack Mystery Box: A few novel techniques for exploiting Microsoft "features".

talks.title: Take a Break
talks.teaser: Survey results and practical hobby ideas help security practitioners step back from screens and reclaim time outside work.
talks.summary:
A UK freelance penetration tester frames the session around keeping work from crowding out family and personal time. He shares results from a community survey on daily screen hours, evening and weekend habits, overtime, and whether work has intruded on school events or social life. Many respondents report long days and feeling they spend too much time on screens, while others deliberately carve out offline time.

The middle of the talk walks through why hobbies matter—stress relief, learning, confidence, and meeting people—and offers starting points from sports and arts to volunteering and low-commitment challenges like watching one film a week. He describes committing to a long multi-day endurance event, using trainers, public announcements, group accountability, streak tracking, and visible records of achievements, while also allowing burnout breaks and switching activities when interest fades.

Practical takeaways include muting notifications, politely declining extra hours, separating work devices, blocking calendar time, and fitting movement into travel or conference mornings. Short case material covers a colleague’s fitness streak and an extreme body-suspension hobby as examples of confidence transfer, plus pointers to blog posts and an honest conference talk on what happens when rest is neglected. The speaker stresses that startups, new families, and crunch periods can legitimately prioritize work—and that the goal is conscious choices, not a fixed eight-hour rule.

talks.title: Open Source Intelligence 101
talks.teaser: Shows how public posts about one employee can build an attack profile, and how to reduce that exposure.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces open source intelligence as the reconnaissance stage of an attack on people. Information gathered from publicly available sources is not secret, yet it can still be valuable to an attacker, and the details people share on social media can expose them, their employers and their friends. The speaker separates this passive research from pretexting, befriending targets or reaching private data, which can be illegal or breach terms of service.

A single public photo of a new office badge became the starting point for profiling one employee. Linking posts, tagged friends, a repeated username and a people-search listing revealed the employer and job role, a likely email format, the software in use, and personal interests that could support a tailored lure. A birthday was confirmed against a leaked license photo after conflicting posts gave different dates. The talk also covers job listings that name firewall brands, Wayback Machine snapshots, breach lookup services, credential dumps, exposed cameras, and map imagery.

The closing section turns to defense through operational security. Practical steps include auditing what is posted, removing background details and photo location data, not relying on privacy settings alone, reviewing third-party app permissions and contact uploads, teaching friends and family about their own exposure, trimming LinkedIn details, and opting out of people-search sites. The takeaway is that anything public today may stay visible and be combined with other data later.

talks.title: Privilege Escalation FTW
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Privilege Escalation FTW.

talks.title: Red Teaming in the EDR age
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Red Teaming in the EDR age.

talks.title: Using PowerUpSQL & goddi for Active Directory Information Gathering
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Using PowerUpSQL & goddi for Active Directory Information Gathering.

talks.title: Seriously, I Really Can Still See You.
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Seriously, I Really Can Still See You..

talks.title: Automating Creating Disposable & Secure Red Team Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Shows how Terraform modules automate disposable red team C2 servers and redirectors, with generated SSH keys and firewall rules.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through using Terraform, HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool, to stand up red team infrastructure on demand. It starts with the core concepts of providers, provisioners and the state file, then builds a single Digital Ocean droplet that generates its own SSH key pair, saves the keys to disk, and removes them on destroy. The speaker pitches the material at people who already know what redirectors and C2 servers are.

The middle of the talk turns the single configuration into reusable modules, with variables as inputs and outputs as return values. A C2 module feeds its server addresses into a redirector module, which uses socat to forward port 80 to those servers, and Terraform orders the builds from that dependency. Ansible playbooks run through a null resource that re-triggers when the playbook's checksum changes, and per-host SSH config files are generated so hosts can be reached with tab completion. Firewall rules limit access to the operator's current public IP by default.

The live demo deployed one C2 server and one redirector, installed packages on both, and then tore everything down with a destroy command. The speaker presented Red Baron, a tool they wrote that packages these modules with support for AWS, Digital Ocean, Azure, Google Cloud and Linode. The takeaway is that engagement infrastructure can be rebuilt quickly, kept separate per engagement using Terraform workspaces, and destroyed afterward. The speaker also noted that the SSH private key is printed to the terminal, because the sensitive flag does not yet work with some provisioners.

talks.title: Passive DNS Collection and Analysis -- the ‘dnstap’ (& fstrm) Approach
talks.teaser: Shows how in-server dnstap and fstrm enable passive DNS collection without blocking resolvers or packet sniffing.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that DNS sits at the center of almost every online transaction, so understanding and monitoring it matters more than treating it as invisible infrastructure. It contrasts older approaches such as BIND query logging and BPF or libpcap packet sniffing with their production pain: disk I/O that stalls name servers, fragment reassembly, growing TCP use, and blindness as encryption spreads.

The speaker describes dnstap as an in-server telemetry path that records questions, answers, intent, cache events, and bailiwick context, paired with fstrm (frame streams) as a transport designed for constructive loss under backpressure rather than blocking the resolver. Performance charts compare Unbound with logging, disabled dnstap, discard mode, and file output. The work is open source and integrated into major open-source authoritative and recursive servers.

For defenders and researchers, passive DNS above the recursive avoids stub-client PII while supporting cross-reference hunts: newly seen names, historical answers after takedowns, and permuted lookups from indicators to related domains and infrastructure. A live demo walks a REST API for MX and IP pivoting. The speaker also warns that DNS over HTTPS undermines enterprise monitoring and policy, and encourages operators to run sensors and analytics locally or in shared communities.

talks.title: See Sharper
talks.teaser: Surveys .NET runtime and build-tool abuse for in-memory execution and delivers fusion logging, CLR ETW, and behavioral detections.
talks.summary:
The presenters open by framing .NET tradecraft as an escalating problem that often flies under defenders’ radar compared with PowerShell-focused monitoring. They explain core runtime primitives—loading assemblies from byte arrays via Assembly.Load, P/Invoke into arbitrary Win32 libraries, and COM misuse—and why those capabilities exist for legitimate plugin and performance scenarios yet double as execution paths.

The middle of the session walks through abused utilities that ship broadly on Windows endpoints: MSBuild tasks and XSLT that pull and run JScript or inline C#, InstallUtil running arbitrary C# from a compiled DLL, and dotnet-to-JScript transforming .NET into script formats. They cite red-team and threat-report examples—including MSBuild abuse in the wild and InstallUtil sightings—and stress that compilation and in-memory loading make process telemetry look like ordinary development activity.

They close with defensive options that are imperfect but actionable: Fusion logging, CLR and kernel ETW for DLL loads such as mscoree.dll, awareness of CLR Guard tradeoffs, a simple GitHub ETW listener example, behavioral detections along the kill chain, baselining when build tools should appear, network anomalies such as MSBuild reaching GitHub, and application control. They note deeper hands-on coverage is reserved for a follow-on workshop.

talks.title: Hack for Show, Report for Dough
talks.teaser: Clear techniques turn pentest findings into actionable reports that technical teams can reproduce and executives can prioritize.
talks.summary:
Clients hire penetration tests for written outcomes that help them block repeat attacks, not merely for proof of access. The speaker frames the assessment report as the durable product: it may face legal scrutiny, must stand without the tester present to explain it, and should map the environment as attackers see it versus how developers imagine controls such as short input fields.

The middle of the session splits every finding across two readers. Technical staff need reproducible steps—hosts, commands, URLs, parameters, and timestamps so logs can be checked—while skipping trophy details like full password-cracking walkthroughs. Business leaders need levers: policy weaknesses, perimeter gaps, and training priorities stated without insults or wizard posturing. The talk urges documenting blocked attacks as positive evidence, noting WAF-style friction without dictating scope changes, and building screenshots that are accurate, precise, and explanatory rather than decorative full-window grabs. Public report examples illustrate strong text evidence and weak captions, including redacted recon write-ups contrasted with confusing desktop images and contradictory summaries.

Practitioners should aim for cover pages, tables of contents, one-page executive summaries, severity tables readable without color alone, and focused validation screenshots such as highlighted curl output. The close warns against copying prior client content or scanner blurbs, avoids rhetorical shaming in write-ups, and mentions Word features—insert screenshot, custom autocorrect, and caption macros—for faster consistent production.

talks.title: What to Expect When You Are Expecting...a Penetration Test
talks.teaser: Explains how scoping, paperwork, communication and reporting determine whether a penetration test succeeds for both sides.
talks.summary:
The talk, from two penetration testing consultants with more than 20 years of combined field experience, examines why engagements stall or disappoint and how both testers and clients can prevent it. Before issuing a request for proposal, buyers should define what a pen test means to them, since vendors may read the term differently, and review sample reports. Buyers should also inventory in-scope hosts and domains, identify stakeholders, set blackout windows and decide how testers will connect, whether on-site, by VPN or by drop box.

Once the contract is signed, the speakers recommend confirming dates, third-party hosting approvals, purchase orders and test credentials early, so access problems do not push back the start. For phishing or red team work, pretexts should be approved in advance, and only a small circle of people should know the test is happening. The kickoff call should include every stakeholder. During testing, both sides should agree on contacts for critical findings, a way to separate the testers' traffic from real attacks, and a reporting cadence, without over-communicating in ways that distract the team.

Scope that is too narrow can hide real risk, so realistic restrictions matter. The speakers argue that the final report should be clear and actionable rather than raw scanner output, and that clients should expect to review findings and discuss severity with the testers afterwards. Their core advice is to set expectations early and prepare paperwork and access ahead of time.

talks.title: Six Sick Systems, One Hour: Investigate with Host Forensics
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Six Sick Systems, One Hour: Investigate with Host Forensics.

talks.title: The Top 10 Reasons It's GREAT to Be a Pen Tester... And How You Can Help Fix that PROBLEM
talks.teaser: Argues that pen tests should deliver business value and offers tips on reports, verifying fixes and blocking SMB abuse.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a lighthearted list of reasons penetration testing is appealing, then turns to the industry problems those perks can hide. The speaker argues that too many engagements are weak: the term pen test is loosely defined, some vendors sell vulnerability scans as pen tests, and many customers only want a checkbox. He urges testers to tie findings to business goals, be transparent about how they got in, and write reports that help defenders act.

The central case study is a WebEx flaw found during a customer engagement. The WebEx installer registers a Windows service that can be controlled over SMB on TCP 445. A domain user without admin rights could use the service control command to point that service at arbitrary commands and run them as SYSTEM on other machines, though on Windows 10 an admin login was needed. The team worked with Cisco, which shipped a patch before the details were published, and then released Nmap scripts and a Metasploit module. The speaker also described testing from a standard employee laptop image over VPN, which cuts travel costs while still reaching internal systems.

For practitioners, the closing advice focuses on what happens after the test ends. Ask testers how they will help you verify that a fix works, and reject reports that cannot be understood or that simply paste scanner output. On the defensive side, block client-to-client SMB where possible, remove Java and Flash when feasible, and consider offensive countermeasures that raise the cost of an attack.

talks.title: Peekaboo - I own you: Owning hundreds of thousands of devices with a broken HTTP packet
talks.teaser: A security researcher demonstrates remote root on mass-deployed cloud IP cameras using malformed HTTP requests and command injection.
talks.summary:
Cheap cloud IP cameras sold under brands such as VStar and white-labeled to other vendors appear hundreds of thousands of times on internet-wide search, often for roughly thirty dollars. The presenter describes teaming with a collaborator to break one open physically, reach a serial console, dump flash with common Unix tools, and unpack firmware that runs an old Linux kernel, BusyBox, and the GoAhead web server.

The core chain starts where the server only rejects malformed verbs, not malformed paths. A GET that omits the leading slash can retrieve the protected system.ini file and reveal a fixed admin username and cleartext password. From the admin UI, unsanitized fields—including motion-alert email settings—reach the system() call, yielding root command execution because the daemon itself runs as root. A custom client sends the non-standard HTTP form that off-the-shelf libraries refuse to emit.

Live demos spawn a telnet-backed shell on the camera, then abuse the device’s UPnP client so a home router forwards ports through NAT, including toward unrelated LAN hosts. Disclosure produced CVEs later seen in botnet activity; the missing-slash class had prior art on printers. Takeaways for defenders include turning off UPnP, not exposing cheap camera admin ports, and treating vendor “no vulnerability worries” marketing skeptically.

talks.title: 2017 Wild West Hackin' Fest Labs
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in 2017 Wild West Hackin' Fest Labs.

talks.title: I Can Still See You!
talks.teaser: Hands-on PCAP review with Bro, Snort, and ARPwatch shows how default tooling still catches lateral movement and C2 when taps exist.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames detection as a visibility problem: attackers still emit packets, while defenders often watch only the internet perimeter and miss lateral movement and post-exploitation inside server and desktop enclaves. A Wild West Hackin’ Fest challenge supplied unknown packet captures from the Black Hills testing lab, analyzed with deliberately modest means—capinfos timelines, Bro/Zeek connection and DNS logs, default Snort, ARPwatch, and command-line greps—without Splunk, full PCAP GUI deep dives, or session reconstruction beyond Bro’s defaults.

On the “initial” capture, unusual concentration on port 5000 isolates a suspicious host, repeated HTTP hits to login/process.php suggest a web shell, and flow history implies an internal aggressor at the console rather than a classic patient-zero phishing chain. Another host beacons outward before being driven via SMB from the first evil box. Snort’s long-tail SMB alerts corroborate players without packet-by-packet rule tuning. On “bettercap,” ARP-cache flip-flop syslog lines expose aggressive man-in-the-middle poisoning; the victim’s outbound traffic, including odd high ports treated as command-and-control indicators, routes through the attacker’s MAC at layer two even when content inspection and VirusTotal report nothing on related file hashes.

The operational message is that stage-one exploitation may stay invisible, but post-exploitation activity is far more detectable if switches and critical segments are tapped and logs aggregated—including Windows event 4688 for whoami—so responders can squish one box instead of dozens. The session closes by announcing a planned second volume of the speaker’s network forensics book, filling gaps such as deeper DNS-centric tradecraft.

talks.title: Windows Operating System Archaeology
talks.teaser: Walks through COM object hijacking, moniker abuse and scriptlet execution for persistence, evasion and AV bypass.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with background on the Component Object Model (COM) for attendees who have not worked with it. It explains how COM classes are registered in the registry, how Windows resolves them at runtime, and how monikers such as scriptlet URLs let a script be fetched and executed. Scriptlet (SCT) files, which are XML-based, are presented as a way to run code in memory when dropping an executable or DLL is not an option.

The middle of the talk covers techniques built on that resolution process. Hijacking a class ID that Explorer loads at logon gives a persistence mechanism, and a TreatAs key can redirect a legitimate object so its code runs without anything suspicious on the command line. The speakers show how a Microsoft-signed script can be abused for command injection through a scriptlet moniker, how a hijacked scripting dictionary object can run a payload while still behaving normally, and how redirecting an anti-malware scan interface COM class can make scanning fail open. They also cover registration-free COM through activation context manifests, dotnet-to-jscript for Win32 API access, and remote DCOM launch of Outlook on a host where the user is a local administrator.

The closing section points defenders toward registry changes under COM keys, unusual scriptlet URLs, and processes running under an unexpected user. Enumeration with OleView, Process Monitor and certutil-style inspection helps find hijack candidates. The speakers argue that COM is a large attack surface that few products monitor well, and they encourage researchers to keep examining it.

talks.title: Bitcoin At The Gates Cybersecurity & The Coming Global Financial Revolution
talks.teaser: Connects cryptocurrency metadata, capital controls and monetary policy to how hacking shapes the global economy and inequality.
talks.summary:
Tara Wheeler opens by framing the talk around how cybersecurity is reshaping the global economy. She argues that finance and information security are converging as banks pursue frictionless transfers, and that metadata from cryptocurrency transactions can be worth more than the payments themselves. She contrasts this with cash, which reveals little about where it has been.

The middle of the talk walks through monetary theory. The unholy trinity holds that a government cannot control monetary flows, capital controls and fiscal or interest-rate policy all at once. Wheeler suggests cryptocurrency can move value across borders beyond the reach of capital controls, using Venezuela as an example, and points to local currencies as a more fungible alternative. She links recurring Bitcoin price swings to manipulation, and notes that its fixed supply means it cannot be priced or managed like fiat money. She also describes a bridge currency created by a startup and used by IBM, which keeps transaction data away from regulators.

She closes by pointing to shrinking middle classes and growing inequality, citing a comparison that 3.6 billion people hold as much wealth as eight men. Her takeaway is that people building and using these systems should understand their economic effects and help design better solutions.

talks.title: I'll Let Myself In: Tactics of Physical Pen Testers
talks.teaser: Shows how physical testers get through doors with cheap tools and common installation mistakes, and how to fix each one.
talks.summary:
This talk argues that physical penetration testers rarely pick locks; most entries come from poor door installation and overlooked hardware. The speaker walks through common weak points, including hinge pins that can be knocked out of a frame, oversized strike plates on retrofitted electronic doors, and latches that were never set up as dead latches. Reaching through gaps to hit crash bars, frameless glass doors with exposed thumb turns, and gaps under doors also appear as repeated entry routes.

Other cases involve a passive infrared exit sensor tripped by a canned gas cloud, an under-door tool that pulls a lever handle, and a door bottom bypassed with thin film. Access panels from several vendors share one widely known key, and a postal switch on one panel can be bridged to release a door. Long-range badge readers, a posed elevator repair technician, and an armed guard desk that yielded only a single read round out the stories, each with a different outcome.

The practical takeaway is that most of these failures are cheap to fix. Jamb pins can turn a standard hinge into a security hinge, correctly fitted dead latches and shrouds stop slipping, dynamic door bottoms block tools beneath doors, and dual-technology motion sensors resist gas and balloon tricks. Staff should also avoid shared keys and confirm that door hardware matches the frame. The speaker adds that confident, belonging-looking behavior helps intruders, so training should cover both hardware and people.

talks.title: What Is the Hacker Community?
talks.teaser: The talk traces how technical skills and collective giving built schools, maker spaces, and relief efforts worldwide.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames “hacker” as someone who solves hard problems, often without manuals, and argues that the scene becomes a tight, creative resource for people who work hard and treat others well. Through personal history from bulletin boards through professional security work, the speaker describes a turning point: conventional conference success felt empty until humanitarian work in Uganda showed that routine technical help could be life-critical for organizations serving vulnerable people.

The middle of the talk documents Hackers for Charity: community-funded moves to East Africa, failed classroom-lab installs, and a consolidated training center that has trained thousands and placed hundreds in IT jobs. It covers fire relief that rebuilt homes, a leather-craft program, portable offline learning kits used with farmers, and a hackerspace that supported street-affected girls and a high school robotics group progressing toward international competition—all backed by small donations and volunteer labor.

The close extends the same pattern to U.S. outreach—privacy coaching for shelters, awareness for nonprofits, education with law enforcement, correctional and veteran facilities, and maker-space kickstarts. Hurricane Maria response in Puerto Rico illustrates rapid community-led solar, radio, and lighting aid before larger agencies arrived. The takeaway is that the community’s adaptability, generosity, and problem-solving habit can be deliberately aimed at local and global needs.

talks.title: Honey, Please Don’t Burn Down Your Office Further Adventures in IoT and Office Automation
talks.teaser: Covers a voice-controlled office built from smart bulbs, Raspberry Pis and vintage gear, with practical build lessons.
talks.summary:
The speaker returns to his home office, which grew from three smart bulbs into a voice-controlled IoT test bed. He moved from Siri to an Amazon Echo after Siri began overriding his custom commands. Alexa skills need an internet-reachable web server, which he rejected for devices such as a Tesla coil. Instead, he used the local WeMo control path, and he ran a Python 3 implementation of that protocol so his own programs could run on a Raspberry Pi or NUC.

Build problems shaped the setup. Raspberry Pi audio dropped out over months, so orchestration moved to a NUC running Ubuntu while the Pis handled individual GPIO devices. Five blinds rose at staggered times over SSH until he sent the same device and button command the physical remote used. Presence detection came from rolling tcpdump captures matched against phone MAC addresses, which let the office greet each person by name.

His closing advice focuses on security and habits. Secure devices as you build them, keep SSH on key-based authentication, and accept that firmware updates may break integrations. He recommends muting the Echo microphone during sensitive conversations, and urges listeners to write code regularly, starting with small tools like a port scanner.

talks.title: 0wning the network with CrackMapExec v4.0
talks.teaser: Explores CrackMapExec 4.0 modules for scaling Active Directory pentests across SMB, WinRM, MSSQL, and SSH.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces CrackMapExec as open-source Python tooling built to own large internal networks under tight engagement timelines. Early versions focused on Windows Active Directory via SMB, concurrent host targeting, credential relationship tracking, and integration with Empire and Metasploit. Version 4.0 broadens the same framework to modular protocols including SSH, MSSQL, HTTP, and WinRM while keeping Impacket-based native protocol abuse.

Live lab demos walk through SMB fingerprinting without credentials, mass authentication to flag local-admin “pwned” hosts, SAM hash dumps, remote command execution, Mimikatz modules, and the CMEDB store for creds, hosts, and group membership. Further demos cover share enumeration and spidering, Group Policy Preferences cpassword recovery, Empire and Metasploit shell deployment, MSSQL xp_cmdshell and module execution, Invoke-VNC, SSH command execution, WinRM remoting, and DCSync-style NTDS extraction with results logged to the database.

The talk closes with roadmap items such as Windows Script Host execution paths, AppLocker bypass work, and module chaining, plus defender guidance on lockout policies, logging, segmentation, LAPS for unique local admin passwords, and detecting CrackMapExec activity with open-source telemetry.

talks.title: Make Email Great Again - Lessons Learned from a Year of Malicious Emails
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Make Email Great Again - Lessons Learned from a Year of Malicious Emails.

talks.title: Building a Successful Internal Adversarial Simulation Team
talks.teaser: Outlines automating purple-team exercises, pipeline validation, and continuous detection measurement beyond spreadsheet workflows.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that conventional red-team work and vulnerability metrics fail as flight simulators for defense. Penetration findings matter less than whether defenders reliably detect and respond to realistic attacker behavior, yet most programs still depend on manual spreadsheets that rot the moment tools or rules change.

They describe a year of operational lessons from standing up internal adversarial teams, mapping detection rules to MITRE ATT&CK phases, and confronting brittle logging pipelines. To address scale, they built an internal automation stack that executes tagged simulation commands on instrumented hosts, checks endpoint and SIEM outcomes, and records timing and success in a database instead of ad hoc phone calls. Detection rules moved into versioned YAML with technique metadata. They preview open-source purple action lists, scenario bundles tied to threat-group technique pages, and basic reporting for blue analysts. Integration with Unfetter aims to replace static heat maps with assessable, updatable gap views.

Practitioners should treat measurement of defensive instrumentation as a first-class problem: unit-test individual rules, run end-to-end pipeline proofs, and feed structured results into frameworks that leadership can interpret. The long-term vision is feedback loops that flag broken controls quickly and eventually suggest remediation, though the authors stress the industry is still early in defining credible metrics.

talks.title: The World is Y0ur$: Geolocation based Wordlist Generation with Wordsmith
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The World is Y0ur$: Geolocation based Wordlist Generation with Wordsmith.
talks.summary:
## Overview
In this presentation, Stan Jeff Kawa and Tom introduce Wordsmith, an open-source tool designed to generate targeted wordlists and usernames using geolocation data. After observing in penetration testing engagements that users frequently incorporate local geographic and cultural references—such as sports teams, landmarks, cities, street names, and religious references—into their passwords, the presenters created Wordsmith to automate the collection and generation of location-specific dictionaries. The talk covers the evolution from version 1 to a ground-up modular rewrite in version 2, detailed data sources, tool architecture, CLI mechanics, and real-world penetration testing case studies.

## Key Topics
- **Geolocation-Based Wordlist and Username Generation:** Moving beyond generic dictionary lists to create focused wordlists based on specific countries, states, counties, or cities. Wordsmith also utilizes regional demographic data, such as US Census and Social Security Administration records, to generate plausible user account names for password spraying and enumeration.
- **Data Sources and Ingestion:** Leveraging diverse public resources including the CIA World Factbook (demographics, common languages, religions), OpenStreetMap (roads, cities, counties), Project Gutenberg (religious texts such as various editions of the Bible and Quran), Wikipedia (sports teams, universities, landmarks), and spellcheck dictionaries (Hunspell, LibreOffice/OpenOffice) for multilingual wordsets.
- **Architecture and Extensibility:** Version 2 organizes data into an ISO alpha-3 flat-file directory structure with YAML configuration files and modular text files per attribute, allowing community contributors to add local data sets easily without needing deep coding experience.

## Technical Details
- **CLI Usage and Boundary Selection:** Wordsmith (`wordsmith.rb`) accepts geographic boundaries (`-I`) ranging from entire continents and multi-country aliases defined in a `regions.csv` file, down to ISO country codes, state abbreviations, and specific municipalities. Attributes (`-a` for all, or dedicated flags like `-R` for roads, `-L` for landmarks, `-Z` for zip codes, and `-X` for miscellaneous custom files) define what terms are aggregated.
- **Mangling and Filtering Options:** Wordsmith provides flags to enforce minimum or maximum character lengths, perform basic mangling (such as removing punctuation and splitting strings), strip non-compliant strings matching standard password policy complexity rules (`-D` for Windows default complexity requiring 3 of 4 character sets and at least 8 characters), and prepend or append common patterns like area codes, zip codes, or custom year masks.
- **Username Generation and Kerb-Guessing:** Using the top 100 first and last names by location, Wordsmith can output common enterprise username permutations (`first.last`, `flast`, etc.). In a demonstrated Active Directory assessment, pre-authentication Kerberos requests ("kerb-guessing") against domain controllers allowed the tester to validate 505 active user accounts out of a generated list without triggering failed authentication lockouts, uncovering nearly half of the organization's valid user accounts.
- **Hash Cracking Results:** In an engagement demo targeting an Irish client, an 800,000-word geolocation-focused wordlist was generated in 12 seconds. Paired with Hashcat and the 50,000-rule `dead_hob0` mangling ruleset, it recovered 101 out of 533 unique NTLM hashes (approximately 20%) in roughly 80 seconds, uncovering local street addresses, landmarks, and regional surnames.

## Takeaways
- Targeted, location-aware wordlists significantly increase the efficiency and success rate of credential recovery and password spraying against regional and multinational organizations.
- Wordsmith version 2 offers a fully modular, community-driven structure across more than 230 countries and territories, supporting multilingual text and custom attributes.
- Future plans discussed for version 3 include radius-based wordlist generation via geographic coordinates, API development, and broader integration with OpenStreetMap and lyrics databases.

talks.title: The Art of the Jedi Mind Trick
talks.teaser: Shares listening, rapport, and persuasion methods that help practitioners win executive and customer trust and drive informed change.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from decades in defense, NSA, PCI QSA work, and consulting, arguing that major breaches persist partly because security experts preach to each other yet fail to persuade bosses, customers, and executives who control budgets. He frames security advocacy as persuasive communication, outlines informative, persuasive, and special-occasion speech, and contrasts impromptu, extemporaneous, manuscript, and memorized delivery.

The middle ties consulting lessons to practice: research audiences (including a Corvair club anecdote), read rooms with hacker-movie polls and nonverbal cues, listen actively, speak “bilingual” business and technical language, use repeat-back checks, offer choices instead of ultimatums, simplify encryption goals without jargon, respect business drivers, document agreements, compromise in steps, and lead pen-test conversations with positives before findings. Movie references and crowd exercises illustrate adjusting technique when one approach stalls.

He closes that these habits build trust, change culture slowly, and define success as informed customer decisions—not winning every argument—and points listeners to a free extended course on Cyber AIT. The session is dedicated to mentor Becky Bass.

talks.title: Authenticated Code Execution by Design
talks.teaser: See how legitimate access to everyday services can expose systems and data, and how defenders can reduce that risk.
talks.summary: The speaker surveys services that let an authenticated user run commands, deploy code, or access data, including remote login, file sharing, administration, web, and database tools. Attendees learn how ordinary access can lead to code execution or sensitive data exposure, and hear defensive advice to disable unneeded services, restrict access, segment networks, and audit successful logins.

talks.title: A Flapper, a Rodeo Clown, a Cockroach and a Milkshake Walk Into a Bar
talks.teaser: Practitioners share daily work habits, tester-led company models, and ways to nurture a healthier security community.
talks.summary:
The session opens with humorous fear-themed banter, then Ed Skoudis steers a wide-ranging panel with John Strand, Dave Kennedy, and other longtime operators. Each describes a typical day balancing meetings, customer work, family time, and deliberate blocks for hands-on technical work so skills do not erode under business pressure.

The middle turns to how Black Hills Information Security, InGuardians, TrustedSec, Binary Defense, and Counter Hack grew, headcount in the twenties to fifties, profit-sharing or employee-first economics, subcontractor relationships, and delivering strong assessment reports as part of the engagement legacy. Dave Kennedy recounts leaving a Fortune 1000 CISO role after Chris Harrison’s physical test exposed weak guards and datacenter controls, which pushed him toward building a trusted team rather than optimizing for one employer.

The closing focuses on industry drama, harassment, codes of conduct, and Twitter spats. Panelists argue legitimate equity concerns deserve seriousness while calling for phone calls over flame wars, peer intervention, conference protections, and community support when people post about bad days. They urge attendees to protect family time, do excellent work, and leave the field better than they found it.

talks.title: Programming with Google
talks.teaser: Shows non-developers core programming basics, then builds a short Ruby script that enumerates user profiles in a web app.
talks.summary:
The talk aims to bring non-developers up to a basic level of programming so they can write small helper scripts for testing or everyday work. Robin Wood, who has spent much of a career developing and has published more than fifty small, single-purpose tools, starts with fundamentals: variables and common data types such as strings, integers, floats, lists and objects; the difference between equality checks and assignment; conditionals; boolean logic grouped with brackets; loops; code blocks, including how Python relies on whitespace; and functions that return values.

For the live part, the speaker works against a test web app where profile pages expose user IDs once logged in. Starting from a Ruby HTTP request example found through a search, the script runs into problems that are worked through one at a time: a missing library import, a redirect because the request was not authenticated, which is fixed by sending the session cookie, and a type error when joining a number to a string. A loop then walks IDs one to one hundred and prints the page that contains the admin level. The finished script is about fifteen lines.

The closing advice is to be careful with code found online: only use code you can read and understand, prefer answers from the first page of results, and never run code blindly, since a published exploit can hide destructive commands. Keep working scripts in a private repository so they can be adapted later, and practise regularly.

talks.title: Security Theme Parks: You Must Be This Tall to Ride the Internet
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Security Theme Parks: You Must Be This Tall to Ride the Internet.
talks.summary: Kevin Johnson delivers a blunt keynote arguing security teams stop treating themselves as wizards and start aligning with business risk. He ridicules logo-driven patching, cites Equifax and printer HTTPS removals to appease scanners, and stresses knowing real threats instead of panic over CRACk branding. He urges NetFlow visibility, honest logging review, breach-response rehearsal, and empathy for users who click polished lures. He closes promoting Secure Ideas’ free training for military, veterans, first responders, and approved nonprofits.

talks.title: Extending BloodHound for Red Teamers
talks.teaser: Shows how to extend BloodHound with custom Cypher queries that track compromise waves, password reuse and network pivots.
talks.summary:
BloodHound maps privilege escalation paths in Active Directory by storing users, groups, computers and sessions in a Neo4j graph database. The talk starts with the basics of that model: nodes, labels, relationships and properties. The speaker explains that edge direction always signals movement toward greater privilege, then shows how the Cypher query language behind the app can be read and written. A path from a user to Domain Admins serves as the worked example.

The middle of the talk covers extensions for a penetration test. Compromised accounts are tagged with the method used and the wave in which they were taken, so a tester can query only the new access gained by each action, such as a password spray. A Ruby script loads lists of nodes into the database and sets these properties. Other additions include a shares-password-with relationship for reused local admin passwords, a blacklist property that filters out offline computers, disabled accounts or expired sessions, and a set of custom queries that start from owned nodes.

The final section maps netstat connection data onto the graph. IP addresses are resolved to computer names with a mappings file, and connections are stored as relationships labelled by port, such as RDP, SMB or LDAP. Combined with derivative admin paths, this reveals computers that act as jump boxes or pivot points into other environments. The takeaway is that custom Cypher queries let a team turn BloodHound's path data into a repeatable record of what each compromise step unlocked.

talks.title: Domain Password Audit Tool
talks.teaser: Shows how a Python tool turns domain controller hash dumps and cracked passwords into an interactive HTML password audit report.
talks.summary:
Carrie Roberts presents the Domain Password Audit Tool, a Python script that builds an interactive HTML report on password use in an Active Directory domain. She starts with why LM hashes matter: they split a password into two uppercase seven-character halves, are only stored for passwords of 14 characters or fewer, and appear as a fixed blank-hash value when a domain does not store them. Keeping them is a weakness because they are far quicker to crack than NT hashes.

The core of the talk is a walkthrough of the sample report. It covers total hashes, unique hashes, cracked percentages, LM hash counts, password length breakdowns, top passwords and password reuse. One example shows domain admins whose regular and admin accounts share a password, which undermines separation of duties. Optional group files, such as domain admins or enterprise admins, add membership details to the report.

Roberts then demonstrates the workflow on a fresh Kali install. She copies the NTDS database and the SYSTEM registry hive from a domain controller with ntdsutil, extracts the hashes with secretsdump, and cracks them with John the Ripper. The tool recombines cracked LM halves into full passwords and runs in seconds on roughly 88,000 entries. She closes with sanitized reports, a SQLite export for custom queries, and her use of the tool on pivot tests, where hash extraction is offered once a tester reaches domain admin. Defenders should disable LM hashes, separate admin and daily accounts, and check for shared passwords.

talks.title: Certification? College?: How do you get into Cybersec really?
talks.teaser: Lays out the routes into security careers, from skills and certifications to degrees, and how to prove what you know.
talks.summary:
Doug White, speaking for Roger Williams University, argues that there is no single route into information security. He lays out the common paths: building hands-on skills, earning training and certifications, going to college, or combining them. Employers, he says, mostly want proof that a candidate can do the work, such as writing code in a language they can name or explaining networking basics, and claims that cannot be backed up tend to fail in interviews.

He shares stories from hiring. One candidate was caught with a fake degree, and another company's low entry-level salaries led interviewees to turn down offers. He recommends free tools such as GNS3 for practicing networking. For certifications, many entry-level credentials can be earned through self-study. He suggests reading job postings for the roles you want, listing their requirements, and pricing each one in money and time. For degrees, associate's programs at community colleges can be inexpensive and transfer to four-year schools, while a bachelor's usually needs about 120 credits.

He closes by stressing documentation: keep projects in files or videos, and build relationships through conferences and local meetups, since a referral from someone who knows you can get past HR screening. He also warns that stacking too many certifications can make an employer doubt your fit or cost, so the best path is the one that matches your goals.

talks.title: A Google Event You Won't Forget
talks.teaser: Shows how calendar event injection and personalized phishing pages can defeat Google's two-factor options in enterprise attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Google Workspace accounts can be attacked in an enterprise setting, and argues that none of Google's two-factor options is bulletproof. The presenters compare SMS codes, time-based one-time passwords, phone prompts and hardware security keys. They say SMS is the weakest choice, and that security keys are undermined when they fall back to weaker backup methods.

The attack path starts with reconnaissance, collecting contacts from professional networking sites and creating lookalike Gmail accounts. Their tool, Cred Sniper, checks which second factor a target uses and personalizes a fake login page with the victim's profile image, authenticator app name or partial phone number. SMS codes stayed valid for hours and were not tied to a session, so they could be phished and used later. A non-Chrome user agent made Google skip the security key and fall back to SMS. Calendar event injection let attackers place invites with a lure into a user's calendar without sending one, and an API call could make the event look accepted. Once inside, they searched mail, exported account data and authorized an app for persistence.

For defenders, the takeaways are to move away from SMS, avoid security keys with a weak default backup, and train staff on behavior rather than specific red flags. Admins can review Google admin console login logs and search by IP address to find other compromised accounts. The calendar injection issue had been reported to Google, which later added a setting limiting automatic events, but the presenters said the API route still worked.

talks.title: Open Source Pentesting
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Open Source Pentesting.

talks.title: Vapor Trail
talks.teaser: Data Exfiltration via Faraday's Law examines Vapor Trail.
talks.summary:
The presenters introduce Vapor Trail, a tool that moves data out of a network over FM radio. The idea grew out of consultants on client sites who had physical access to a network but found that normal egress paths were inspected, while cellular modems and prepaid SIMs added cost and detection risk. Radio offered a channel that few organizations monitor.

The device is a Raspberry Pi with a length of wire as its antenna. It toggles a GPIO pin using pulse width modulation to place a signal on an unused FM channel, which US rules allow at low power without a license. A cheap software-defined radio receives the signal. Each bit is set by how far the signal sits from a center frequency, so timing jitter on the Pi matters less. Data is split into 128-byte blocks with parity blocks added, so any half of the set rebuilds the file, and SHA-256 checksums confirm integrity. At roughly 2,000 bits per second, compression and filtering help. The limits include an encoder that does not yet run on the Pi Zero and no way for the receiver to request retransmission.

A live demo sent a short file and a larger one that needed two parity groups, and the receiver confirmed both by matching hashes. A gzip-compressed log transfer was also shown. Future ideas include a repeater, a custom board combining transmit and receive with a band-pass filter, and encrypting data before transmission. In the Q&A, the presenters reported a range of about three city blocks and reception through several walls.

talks.title: Morphing to Legitimate Attack Patterns
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can blend into normal behavior to slip past PowerShell and lateral movement detections, with a new C2 proof of concept.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how offensive tradecraft is being squeezed as defenders get better at spotting malicious activity. The speaker argues that obvious PowerShell use, encoded commands, and workstation-to-workstation traffic are now easy to flag, so operators need to make their actions look like ordinary behavior. He points to baselining an environment and watching for deviations, such as a server script reaching out to the internet, as a signal defenders can act on quickly.

The middle of the talk covers specific evasion ideas. One example uses MSBuild to load the PowerShell automation assembly without launching powershell.exe, which the speaker says often avoids detections keyed to that binary. A demo of an updated Unicorn generator showed how splitting strings and chunking variables hides commands, though he notes such patterns are still fairly easy to spot. He then introduces Trevor C2, a proof of concept that makes command traffic resemble a normal browsing session on a cloned website, with data carried in image filenames and randomized beacon intervals. A short Python demo showed commands being sent to a client and results returned.

The closing advice mixes both sides. Defenders should use application control, block unneeded workstation-to-workstation SMB and RPC, enable script block logging, and monitor DLL loading and network connections with Sysmon, while watching east-west logon events. Attackers need to adapt to these controls by emulating user behavior. The speaker presents the progress on both sides as a sign that defense is improving, while noting there is still a long way to go.
